An interesting experience, to say the least. The game has very similar vibes to Lust from Beyond, reason being that both of these games were inspired by the same artists (H. R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński), but unlike the other game, this game has more focus on gore, sexy stuff comes much later in the game.

The game just throws you into it's world, leaving you to figure out what's going on and what to do. No monologues, no dialogues, no story/backstory explanation, objectives, etc. Just you figuring stuff out, which in my opinion was really cool. A lot of puzzles, shooting, and very bizarre stuff. More bizarre than Lust from Beyond in my experience; At certain moments I was thinking what in the actual hell is going on in this game, and I loved that. It's more of an artistic, atmosphere experience rather than epic gameplay, and I'm okay with that.

The ONLY downside is that there are ZERO tutorials, which I kinda like, but at least there could've been popups as to which key to press on the keyboard for certain actions. What I ended up doing is just using the most common buttons which did work, but still, at least a popup that appears only once just so you know what to press would be really nice.

Regarding the ending, [spoiler] it was kinda lame. I know that the game has to end somehow, and after what you go through it is really difficult to come up with a good ending, but still. It would be really cool if at the end you fall into a pit of some sort and end up at the beginning of the game, so that it gives 
you the kind of "endless loop" feeling, where the character loses memory and then it starts all over. The actual ending was just him standing there looking like an abomination. But again, just my opinion. [/spoiler]

Also, it doesn't surprise me that this game was made by my fellow Serbians, because after all, we make similar gory/sexual media like "A Serbian Film". I was pleasantly surprised when I found that out by watching the credits, I didn't really know that when I started playing it.

So to close it out, if you like what you see in the screenshots, you're in for a good time! Just make sure to check the key bindings before playing so you can know what to press when the time for that comes.

From the start, Scorn felt like I was playing an early 2000 PC game, when many early titles had a specific feeling to them and studios were not scared of taking risk and trying new things just for the sake of trying. A lot of modern titles miss this specific spark and somehow Scorn was able to recreate it with its unique and distinct art direction.

Game Design wise, Scorn is incredible. Everything has this grotesque look to it with a fleshy, living and at times uncomfortable feeling to it all as your surroundings are mostly made out of living organism. Organic bio-matter is the architecture for almost every place you explore with the equipment as well being biological. The areas you traverse will have you pondering as to what happened prior to you wandering along the path. The Atmosphere of it all sucks you right in as well with the subtle sounds from the distance playing, amazing sound design overall and excellent music choice to wrap the whole thing into one of the most Artistically impressive games out there.

Stylistic-wise the game is incredible, but many users have a problem with the core gameplay and understandably so. I feel like if this game would of just stayed as a puzzle game, it would of been great, as I thoroughly enjoyed the beginning of my play session where I was trying to figure out puzzles on my own. This game tells you absolutely NOTHING and I actually quite enjoyed that as I thought the gameplay would unravel into a Metroidbrania of some sort since the riddles were environmental. The areas that you have to solve puzzles in are also not very big so even if you are wandering for a while clueless as to what to do, you can eventually figure it out. 

However, that is not how the whole game plays and I think the problem lies in the combat sections. Although in later parts they are not bad at all as they always provide you with enough resources to overcome your next challenge, at the beginning of the game it was a bit frustrating having to deal with enemies when all you had was a tool that was like an extended punch, triggered only twice and the cool down was not very short. This lead me into scenarios where I would hit the monster twice, would have to run a few feet away so it wouldn't hurt me, wait for the cool down, then have to run back at it and do it again until it was dead. It became worse with the fact that almost every enemy does a range attack and if you missed one of the punches from your tool then you risked getting hit and it would take longer to kill them. This made certain parts of the experience tedious and annoying as checkpoints were improperly placed and the death animation combined with the time the menu pop up to select continue was not very quick.

I think the price point as well might be factor for many as I do think it is probably a bit too high, especially because the game is very short and does not offer a lot besides impressive Visuals and atmosphere. The story is also very confusing and to me it does not have the best ending but for what the title implies, I think it fits perfectly. 

Scorn is a pretty unique case. If this game released around 2003 on pc it would be a cult classic, but because it was released so late into the industry with other games being grander, bigger and offer much more on their plate, it affected its perception with the current generation of gamers. I definitely recommend this game if you're looking for a short experience that will have you sucked into the game world for the time that it last as I enjoyed my time with it. If price point is a concern, I do recommend getting this game on sale as I think for the price it goes when on sale, it is completely worth it.

Scorn is a visually stunning masterpiece that transports players into a terrifying world. While Steam doesn't offer a [i]'neutral'[/i] recommendation, I find myself leaning towards a positive review, albeit with some significant caveats

[b]In short[/b] - Scorn is a short experience, clocking in just at 3-4 hours for most players, though thorough explorers may find more to uncover. Despite its flaws in combat and navigation, game's unparalleled visual design and atmospheric immersion make it a worthwhile journey for those who appreciate artistic vision in gaming. But If you can push through the frustrating elements, you'll find a hauntingly beautiful world that lingers in your mind long after finishing the game. Now to a more expanded version:

[h3]Visuals and Atmosphere:[/h3]
Scorn's greatest triumph lies in its breathtaking aesthetic. Drawing heavy inspiration from the works of H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński, the game transports players into a living, breathing biomechanical nightmare. Every environment is a little showpiece of unsettling design, making the simple act of exploration a reward in itself. And haunting soundtrack complements the visuals perfectly, maintaining a consistent atmosphere of unease and wonder while giving some chills

[h3]Gameplay:[/h3]
To me personally game presents itself more as an interactive [i]art piece[/i] than a traditional video game. Puzzle-solving forms the core of the experience, with some genuinely intriguing challenges. However, frequent backtracking can make progression feel tedious at times. Combat is the weakest point of the game. Scarce ammunition, frustrating enemy design and clunky movement combine to create encounters that often feel more irritating than tense

[h3]Accessibility and Story:[/h3]
Scorn takes a bold approach by offering [i]no hand-holding[/i] whatsoever. There are no quest markers, no dialogue, and no narrative elements whatsoever. While this adds to the game's mysterious atmosphere, it also can lead to confusion and frustration for some players. Raising such questions as [i]'Am I going the right way?'[/i], [i]'Where am I?'[/i] or [i]'What's the point of all this?'[/i]
The story, or lack thereof, is told entirely through environmental storytelling and symbolism. And it may leave many players feeling lost or unsatisfied

[h3]Thematic Depth:[/h3]
For those willing to dig deeper, Scorn offers a wealth of philosophical and esoteric themes to ponder. References to ascension, various religions and even Freudian psychology are woven throughout the experience in the last quarter of the game. However, it's worth noting that much of the game's lore is only fully explored in the accompanying [b]ARTBOOK[/b], which may disappoint those hoping for more in-game revelations, with also having a need to purchase it in the first place! (I mean just look at the price!)

Recommended for: Art enthusiasts, fans of atmospheric horror, and those who enjoy piecing together abstract narratives.
Approach with caution if: You prefer clear storytelling, user-friendly game design, or action-oriented gameplay 

And remember [b][u]There is a very fine line between loving life and being greedy for it [/u] [/b]

After finishing this game, I was very conflicted. 

First off, the game design, sound, atmosphere, and overall art direction are amazing and really standout as you go through these creepy halls are areas. Multiple times I was grossed out or in awe of the way things looked or worked in this world. The devs and artists had an idea and really ran with it and succeeded. 

My negatives though are that the puzzles are incredibly frustrating some times, making progress feel sluggish in some areas, sometimes an outright slog. The combat is also rough, almost atrocious. The enemies would feel more daunting if they couldn't be killed, or maybe required something in the environment to kill/deter them. I like how the ammo worked, but honestly if they got rid of the combat all together and made it more about escaping/surviving, this game would've shined so much more in my opinion.

I honestly really liked this game and wish it was longer honestly, I wanted to learn more about the world and keep the creepiness factor going for longer. Great job from the devs and artists, I hope to see more from this world one day.

This game's fantastic. The art's phenomenal and the game has several areas with quite distinct atmospheres. There's no dialogue or exposition so you have to piece your own interpretation together.

The puzzles are all challenging but feel fair once you figure them out. There's a bit of back tracking but the game often gives you shortcuts back and you can sprint quite fast.

The combat is the weakest aspect, which does get frustrating once they start piling enemies on you later on. Some enemies twitch too much and are hard to hit, and they take too many hits to die. The boss battle was pretty cool, but a little drawn out. It felt too much like a video game after the other parts were so immersive. The combat helped to build tension at times but other times just distracted you from taking in the environment. 

The music and sound design are very well crafted. The music complements when it should and is tastefully left out at other parts. The sounds are all unsettling and feel like they belong to their sources.

Most of the negative reviews, complaints about the puzzles and so on seem like they're coming from people who don't even like puzzle games and expected an FPS. I recommend this if you like puzzle games and thought provoking imagery.

Scorn Game Review
(Disclaimer - This is just my opinion and may be unpopular or disliked, the game is based on the artwork of H.R. Giger and art is meant to be interpreted and felt which means we won't necessarily feel the same things and lastly I am just here to share my perspective to assist in whether you might like it or not without spoiling the game)

Please also note that due to the game for me being very art driven and expressive it has become one of my favorite games, but I will try and share my perspectives without being bias or fan-girling over it.

(Positive)
1. As stated above it is inspired by the art work of H. R. Giger (Swiss Artist most widely known for the Alien franchise Xenomorphs, architure, alien artifacts, etc and has even inspired the film franchise Species), due to this I would like to note that I feel the developers really felt and understood some of his work and really did portray it beautifully.

I 100% recommend this game. I almost didn't play it because players seem so split on whether or not it's good. But I saw it on sale for $10, so I finally decided to dive in (3 years later, sadly).

As most have stated, this game isn't for everyone. I hate saying that, because most people see it and think "risk" (like I did) and either put off playing it or never play it at all. But the truth is, it's worth the risk, because if the game resonates with you, it hits hard.

Throughout the entire game, I wanted to see more, know more about this world I was in. This game is special in that it doesn't tell you anything, which means you have to use environmental clues, as well as your imagination. What is my purpose here? What happened to this place? Where am I? Unlike most games that leave you to imagine nothing because it's all explained to you, this game leaves room for plenty of imagination, and I love that about it.

But when I say this game doesn't tell you anything, I mean it. It doesn't even tell you the controls when playing. No map, no objective markers, nothing. I actually quite like this, as it makes me feel more attached and immersed in this world. I really only got stuck twice in this game for a brief period of time. But I wasn't frustrated about it, because I felt this really is part of the game design. This world is supposed to confuse me, disorient me.

The visuals are also superb, as many have already stated. You can tell if the art style is for you pretty easily based on the screenshots and videos. It really gives off Alien: Isolation vibes, and I love that about it. It's a unique style I don't really see in any games, and it made me feel like I am part of this world rather than just a player in it. It all just feels like it could exist, somewhere out in the void. Simply, it feels authentic.

Most reviews I read did not actually enjoy the gameplay. I personally did, in my mind, the puzzles made sense, and while the combat was slow and limited, I actually enjoyed it. Combat is easily avoided if you don't want it (minus a few sections). I don't think it was the best gunplay out there. But it really wasn't as bad as I thought it would be either, based on others' reviews.

I could go on and on, really. But I'll just end this review by saying: The game may not be for everybody, but everybody should try it regardless. Because if it is for you, you'll be more than pleased with what is on offer here. Just like I was.

[h3]My Thoughts:[/h3]
[i]Scorn[/i] is a first person, puzzle game. I usually don't play puzzle games but since it was on sale I decided to give it a try in hopes that the interesting art direction could hold my attention. I've enjoyed it so far and I hope I finish it one day but I might just not be the target audience for puzzle games.

[h3]What I Like:[/h3] 
[*][u][b]Art Direction[/b][/u]
The H.R. Giger inspired art is definitely a unique aesthetic and I greatly enjoy it.
[*][u][b]Lack of Story[/b][/u]
I haven't finished the game yet but so far there is no overarching narrative. And even though I wouldn't want that in most games, in this game it works well. It's refreshing to not have lore dumps in your face every five minutes. You start the game with no information and just get to let your imagination run wild. 
[*][u][b]Start Menu[/b][/u]
This is one of those games where you press start and the game seamlessly transitions to gameplay. I don't know if this mechanic has a name but a few games do this and I'm always impressed when they do. It's such a small thing but when it's done it's such a "chef's kiss" feeling for me.  
[*][u][b]Items[/b][/u]
All interactable items whether stationary or equipable have satisfying animations and are fun to use.
[/list] [h3]What I Dislike:[/h3] 
[*][u][b]Textures[/b][/u]
While the graphics as a whole are great, for some reason the textures for the H.R. Giger inspired art are all low resolution. Since this aesthetic is arguably the main selling point for the game it is a baffling decision to let something which should be the main focus become so third rate. There is a point in the game where [spoiler]you go outside and all the ground and rock textures are very high resolution and look amazing. Why can't the titular art be of the same calibur?[/spoiler]
[*][u][b]Checkpoints[/b][/u]
I died and had to repeat a section. I would understand if this was a survival game but having to solve a puzzle that I already solved and rewatch unskippable animations play out just feels like I'm wasting my time.
[/list]

I think an incredibly important thing of note with this game is each individual element is relatively weak but as a whole it can be an enjoyable experience. Let me break this game down to three elements.
 
- World building and art style: The art style is of course the thing that is driving this game. I think it's relatively strong and the game loves to show it off at every chance it gets. It's kind of one-note but the game is only 5 or so hours so I don't think it overstays its welcome but it may for some. The world however I feel like is extremely lacking. I was drawn in and wanted to explore the world to figure out how it ticks but I couldn't figure out the logic behind this world as I'm not sure there is one. 
- Puzzles: They're nothing that'll really tax your brain. Some of the puzzles aren't really puzzles and more of just an excuse for the character to walk from this area to another. An aspect of a good puzzle is maximizing the time for a player thinking and testing things out in the puzzle and minimizing time walking around and waiting for animations to play. In that aspect, the game fails at it loves to revel in its art style and animation. 
- Combat/survival horror: I understand the idea of adding this in to the game. It promotes more exploration for ammo/health and breaks things up. I think a big problem with it is your melee weapon is absolutely horrendous. You can only use it to hit an enemy twice before you run away and wait for it to recharge. It's more aggravating than engaging when you have to repeat the hit an enemy twice and run away a number of times for an encounter. You also can't sprint to cancel a reload or weapon swap animation to dodge an enemy which will leave to some frustrating deaths. I know your character isn't some 1337 mega soldier and that's fine but I would expect him to prioritize his health and safety and sprint to dodge. Mostly the combat is serviceable but does get annoying at times. 

I would say the puzzle, combat, and world building are poor but they are fine enough tacked onto the art and atmosphere aspect of it. Just need to set your expectations correctly, I'd say it's worth it if you will be fascinated by the weird and disgusting things the artists came up with.

A walking sim best summarized as an HR Giger designed continuous OSHA incident. 
[i]I think I might have Tetanus now.[/i]

In all seriousness, the visual design is [i]amazing[/i] - if you're into the HR Giger / bodyhorror / biomechanical aesthetic.
As is the soundscape, incidentally.

I still wouldn't call it a horror game though. 
It's rife with evocative body horror in all it's aspects, but it's not exactly tense or ... doing anything else "scary". 
More a gross-out & 'conceptual horror' walking sim I guess.

The puzzles are here or there - some are excellent and well tied into the environment, some are just glorified 'connect the dots'- or 'pull all the levers' puzzles. 

Combat is a bit icky and sticky, but then it's [i]not trying to be[/i] an action FPS, so it definitly fits the design brief. You can avoid a lot of enemies or just let them be, if you try.
The rest isn't too hard either, so far. Most of the enemies don't actively threaten you very much.

The game does occasionally struggle with sign-posting stuff well enough - partially because of the "overdesigned" nature of it's environments & assets I guess - but it's not a huge issue. Especially if you're somewhat well versed in how games like this (puzzle/light combat/walking sims) generally go, you should figure out what to do next. 
Since you can't box yourself into a corner / failstate either, you [i]can[/i] just push all the buttons until it clicks.

I do feel the game should've tried harder to not need a HUD & "non-diegetic" indicators at all - playing without [i]is[/i] possible, but you'll be in the dark about a lot of things (most importantly your HP) and you'll have to constantly flip the (admittedly well designed) 'inventory' up to check ammo and healing reserves
Still - a lot of games nowadays manage to put diegetic ammo counters and even sometimes healthbars onto the character- & weapon designs pretty front & center, without it becoming too overtly silly.
And even an artstyle this hyperfocused could've highlighted some things better.

I very much enjoyed it, but I also very much feel okay about waiting so long for a decent sale.

I saw this game's trailer a super long time ago, and was in love with the HR Giger aesthetic it had going for it. Because of the super mixed reviews, I waited for a $10 sale to pick it up. Without spoiling much, I'll try and list some pro's and con's to see if this game is going to be for you.

PROS:
>Very immersive, minimal HUD elements to distract you and being able to check your health reserves and ammo by just looking down at your character model was a really great choice.
>The environment design...wow. Just wow. This place really looks and feels like hell (in a good way). Biomechanical, living structures and lovecraftian landscapes all over. Not something you see represented in games often and I think they knocked it out of the park aesthetically.
>Gunplay feels nice, even the reload animations are visceral. Combat not so much, but I'll talk about that in cons.
>Completely silent story? No dialogue at all? I'm here for that. All-environmental storytelling and leaving a ton of it up to interpretation is a pro for me. I like being able to think about a game after playing it, and when it's not all spoon fed to you it leaves a lot of theory-crafting to be done.
>Graphical fidelity is beautiful. AAA looking graphics are pretty impressive for what I'd assume is a small team of devs.
>Able to 100% in about 6 hours. This could be a pro or con for you, but for $10 I'd say I got my money's worth out of it.

CONS:
>Some of the puzzles really blow. With no dialogue or tutorials anywhere there will be a few puzzles that you will have no idea what the objective is, leading to a ton of time wasted just tinkering around.
>Having to wait an incredibly long time for environmental animations. A lot of the waiting kind of feels like padding the time out. Expect a lot of pulling lever animations and then watching the environment change for the next 20 seconds, it's going to happen a lot.
>The combat isn't great. You don't really have enough ammo to deal with everything which led to me trying to avoid fighting where I could, but this led to a lot of damage taken trying to run past enemies in 4 foot wide hallways.
>The gimmick of the last level [spoiler](not being able to use your hands)[/spoiler] was incredibly annoying and almost led to me getting softlocked. I left one of the final boss battles with 2 hits remaining, then the game forces you to take scripted damage twice after that, leading to me dying over and over. I had to backtrack to find a health station, and after seeing a bunch of other people complaining about it, I don't know how the devs didn't anticipate this happening.
>Ending felt kind of out of nowhere, definitely not a 'traditionally satisfying' ending but that's probably to be expected with the tone the game takes.

All in all, if you are a [i]patient[/i] type of gamer who likes brutally dark storytelling, doesn't mind solving some puzzles (or looking up a guide when stuck), AND you like biomechanical/HR Giger aesthetics, go for it. It's not the best game on earth but I love to see unconventional, weird, crazy games like this. I'm glad it got to see the light of day and didn't get canned by censorship for it's heavy themes. This feels more like an artpiece than a game, and I almost feel like it would be just as good if not better if the combat and puzzles were absent. I had a great time just soaking in the atmosphere and taking screenshots. I'd give it a 7 or 8 out of 10, purely because I want to see more stuff like this get made.

Scorn is a pretty unique experience. The bleak and hostile world that you explore is art direction at its finest. It showcases a very depressing and gruesome imagery of a world that is clearly on the brink of collapse just by observing its surroundings. One of the standout features to me at least is the fact that the entire game is seamless. Once you start first chapter and later the final chapter, you won't encounter a single loading screen at all. The only drawback to this is that you'll encounter some stuttering since the game is rendering new environments as you progress. As for the soundtrack, it helps amplify the experience with its ambiance and eeriness. It further highlights Scorn's tone and visuals to a T. So that alone, Scorn wins in the audio and visual department.

The story for Scorn if you can call it that, doesn't really lead you in on any details. This is mainly due to the fact that you get no exposition, no narrations, or any context for what is going on. All you know is that you wake up and you're on way to your objective. The rest is all left to the world building, the journey, and what you take from it. This leaves Scorn's story up for interpretation and open discussion which in my opinion works well.

In fact, the gameplay itself is minimal too with the information such as your health and ammo only being shown when you have your weapon drawn or how many healing items you have by looking down at your view model. While it adds to the immersion, it goes overkill with the fact that there are some puzzles in the game that are annoyingly difficult to figure out. Then there's the combat which is just ok. Now granted, most encounters can be avoided so you wouldn't even have to engage, but sometimes you are forced into combat since some of the battles with the creatures are in corridors where avoidance really isn't an option. Plus fighting the same enemy type over and over again gets real tedious.

Thankfully once you get through the worst, Scorn gets kicking into high gear towards the end which you need to see for yourself if you haven't already. Now the campaign is very short and there's no bonus content whatsoever. My hours and 100% achievements are proof of that. And while normally there would be cause for complaints for this, I think it works in the game's favor since:

A: Combat is annoyingly tedious and repetitive, 
B: You've just finished a bunch of frustratingly long puzzles do you really want to spend another 30 minutes on another one?

So really, the game ends right before Scorn's shtick gets stale and that's honestly the best way to finish it. 
Would I recommend Scorn? Absolutely.  It's a game you should play at least once... But it is not for everyone. Just be prepared for some of the hard knocks you'll face in its runtime. Also $40 is pretty high considering the campaign's length so grab it while it's on sale. 

TL;DR
Scorn is a masterclass in art direction, world building, and it's soundtrack. The combat is meh and puzzles can be cryptic. It's not that long, but overall a solid experience.

"Scorn," with its striking blend of biomechanical horror and enigmatic puzzles, leaves an indelible mark on the gaming landscape. Its foray into a world inspired by the likes of H.R. Giger presents a compelling, if at times polarizing, experience giving the same feelings I had playing 'I have no voice and I must scream"

Pros:
- Aesthetic and Art Direction: The game's visual presentation is a masterclass in horror and biomechanical design, Though very phallic it is both grotesque and captivating. 
- Puzzles: Offering a challenging yet rewarding experience, the puzzles in "Scorn" are a highlight. They require a blend of logical thinking and environmental interaction, and while few and far between it's a delight when they happen.
-Atmosphere and Sound Design: Beyond its visual horror, "Scorn" excels in it's sound and music design really making everything feel so unnerving like the world it pulls you in.

Cons:
- Combat Mechanics: Combat in "Scorn" often feels clunky and out of place like something they added after but never fully fleshed out... pun intended.
- Save System and Checkpoints: The game's approach to saving and checkpoints is bad. You never truly know when it's saved so you can quit and checkpoint seem to be awkwardly back, so you are stuck watching cutscenes over and over.
- Narrative Clarity and Direction: While "Scorn"tries to tell it's story through the environment it in my opinion found itself falling a little flat (especially in the beginning) and not truly telling a story as strong as I think it could.

"Scorn" navigates the thin line between a masterpiece of horror and a test of patience. It's an unforgettable journey through a beautifully grotesque world, albeit one that might occasionally scorn its travellers with gameplay and technical blemishes. I give it 7/10 suspiciously shaped keys into suspiciously shaped keyhole.

A game I can't enjoy yet it is genius in multiple areas.
There's an era of gaming in the 90's where starting off in a horror scenario with little to no information as to why you're there that this game clearly emulates and does very well.
There are multiple plant and pay offs handled very well. This is the minor of minor spoilers but [spoiler] there is a section where you find a weapon that is also used as a key (essentially). You pick it up off a dead person. You later have a cinematic that leads you to the next area where you no longer have the weapon. You come across another area where a monster (and I'm being literal here) buries itself into your stomach and it's tail is the weapon you just had and just lost. The gap between these moments had no implication on the game at all, you never needed the weapon-key until this belly-creature attachment. But pulling it off a corpse means a whole lot more when you find out the creature in your belly is a life-draining parasite. [/spoiler]
It's small things like this that prove the creators of the game created and respected their lore and took it into account when designing it.

That being said...I don't like this game all that much. The combat is VERY scripted and frustrating at moments, trying to relive what some people found as "tension" in the original Resident Evil 4, where if it's difficult to maneuver you're more likely to panic and thus is a simulation in a horror theme. I've never found this to be effective because frustration and cheap deaths will destroy theming 100% of the time.
The puzzles are built around the protagonist's perspective, in other words all the mechanics of the machinery (loosely using that due to the bio-organic nature of it all) are as much of a mystery to him as it is to you. It's a nice touch at first, because it causes a curiosity to explore and try things out however it becomes clear quickly that the puzzles rely HEAVILY on the player's curiosity because in a game where your movement is very slow (even when running) the puzzles require you to walk back and forth repeatedly in the same level area before you can progress to the next, as if this was another element from the 90's gaming area it attempts to emulate (the dreaded back tracking of "what did I miss?")

In terms of appearance this game is drop-dead gorgeous. The animation of the environment and the...living(?) things in it is near-seamless. The lack of vibrant color allows for certain moments such as "emergency/science lights" to highlight what is important which proves they planned this seemless blend but knew it could cause confusion when on top of a limited exploration a video game can offer. In short, it's literally too beautiful for it's own good. There are times where it somehow breaks the science of reality and makes things seems desolate and claustrophobic at the same time.

However it relies on this a little too much due to the constant re-exploration the puzzles need and the multiple...so many cut-scenes. It handles transitions primarily in 1st person cut-scenes that quickly become annoying as EVERYTHING in this world takes it's sweet time - the protagonist included. The speed that he handles unlocking a door is insufferably slow, most likely in a similar attempt as the aforementioned slow = tension but it falls into the frustrating category fairly fast. Entering a door with a creature that's walking along the ceiling well out of your reach happens in a slow moving cut-scene where I guess the protagonist forgets how to walk because it takes literally 8 seconds for him to walk through it either to show how gorgeous it is and let the ambiance set the tone (which it was doing perfectly before you interrupted it thank you) and to show the creature moving away from you but it takes the entire ceiling in it's movement which is rapid and creepy, there's no way to possibly avoid it. The game relies on it's gorgeous art that it specifically places an immovable camera so you can see what's in it but this is another element that removes the horror aspect because if I was continuing to walk through and saw it move I'd react in game and not have the protection of a cut-scene. Which is hypocritical of me however...because this game loves these cut-scenes so much you can literally die in one. Without major spoilers here you can run through an entire level and succeed just to die in a cut-scene. 

Before ending in a brief summary another commendation this game deserves is Jouni Kalervo Havukainen and the In Slaughter Natives developed an exceptionally visceral, nostalgic, terrifying soundtrack. There is no quip here, it is simply remarkable and they deserve the love they are getting for this score.

In the end it's hard not to see my issue with the game as almost subjective and there is enough well-thought effort and execution in this game that has more love in it's design than most games today that I'm sure there are plenty who pick it up that will rightfully fall in love with it.
I will look forward to the next game this team releases.

Scorn is not a game I like.  Usually, I start with the positives of a game, and that is one.  I hate Scorn because I hate horror, and especially body horror.  This game is a bit too bloody and also extremely unnerving.  The level designs I feel are off-putting and in general, I don’t enjoy this, but I’d also say for all of that, it’s exactly what people are looking for in this genre, and if so, they will almost certainly like this title. 

I’ll also say that points of this game remind me of the darkest moments of a Call of Duty game, or Spec Ops The Line.  You know those impactful moments where you’re forced to do something personally distasteful for story reasons? That’s here too, and again, it’s done for the same reasons, to be unsettling but I feel like it’s more appropriate here.

At the same time, there are some issues I have to bring up.  One big issue is that it’s a little hard to figure out what you’re trying to do or what you are missing mostly due to how alien the world feels, but I think that’s an interesting decision and helps unsettle the player.  The one actual negative is taking that further and saying that it’s sometimes easy to miss things, not because of the universe, but because if you’re not standing in the exact right place you might not notice it. . 

Pick this up if you like body horror, I mean if you’re looking at the screen and not liking what you’ve seen, this isn’t for you, but there’s going to be a decent number of people who will look at this, and can’t wait to play it or already have and… yeah for those people, this game was made for you.

I wasn't prepared in the slightest for what I experienced. I can't put into words the 10 to 15 minutes that proceeded the break through, but when I got a grip I saw that the creature that was just birthed in front of me had died. For about a half second I felt so hopeless and sorry for the creature, before I realized I was staring at a screen. If I was a lesser man I would say something along the lines of "I felt like I lived that things life." But I'm not a reddit shaman and I don't attend burning man in a diaper and a binky. Regardless of my experience, this is a game you play more for it's art style than it's actual game play. It's still a fantastic game though, and I find immense entertainment in imagining how the world of this game came to be, and what it might have all looked like in it's prime. I often find myself simply staring at the walls in this game to take in the detail. Very few rooms, objects, and items in this game lack any detail or prove themselves boring to look at. I imagine the game play and story line to be a similar experience to living in small towns in South Asia; crawling over unidentifiable piles of flesh in a frail pathetic body only to be occasionally met with an ancient monolithic structure who's purpose the world forgot long ago. This game masters an atmosphere of persistent fear and dread of what's to come, and every enemy you encounter reminds you of how weak you are. It reminds you of a primal dread that's forgotten in this modern world, and makes you feel like a monkey that's lost it's tribe in the wild. To put it simply, you feel like a small animal being hunted. The puzzles aren't really that challenging, but the overall experience makes up for a lack of interesting game play and puzzles. I highly recommend all who appreciate this sort of genre of surreal art that artists like Zdzislaw Beksinski and H.R. Giger have brought to this world to pick this game up. My only regret with this game is that I didn't pick it up sooner.

Visually the whole game would probably not feel out of place as a Doom level that you sprint through in 5 minutes, yet the disgustingly intimate exploration of it's detailed viscera summons the feeling of a nightmare that robbed you of your ability to run. There is a beauty to the grime, and it's well optimized with smooth performance throughout. Although the gameworld clearly hates you, the developers don't: The combat is fair, if not too easy, ressources are tight but sufficient and the puzzles make sense in their own twisted way. Scorn is not a test of skill, but a test of will.

Homunculi, classified as an inferior race, also stand apart.

Undoubtedly horrifically beautiful throughout, with the full-on Geiger-style alien biotech being juxtaposed against the rotting decay caused by the infection that's taken hold, there's some suitably brutal scenes peppered throughout your dystopian journey, and some better-than-the-norm puzzles to be solved as part of it. Despite being fairly linear, don't expect this game to hold your hand at any point - you're pretty much alone on this ship, and nothing's there that wants to guide or assist you.

The one weakness is the combat system - most encounters are highly repetitive given the lack of diversity in terms of enemy type, and it felt that they'd have been better served by being rarer and perhaps done without weapons (without wanting to give much away regarding the story, manually ripping some of these things apart in some way, and struggling to do so, would have felt more apt), then there's a battle towards the end which felt both unnecessary and frustrating, simply for the sake of being so. Rather than a sense of achievement, it was much more one of relief that it was finally out of the way, and I could continue with the story. On the plus side, accuracy counts, as this isn't a game to throw ammo boxes out there in every corner.

Scorn's stuck with me since playing, which is something I can't write about many games - the atmosphere is undeniably brilliant, and discovering the alien world plus fragments of the history *is* the experience - so on this basis i have to recommend it pretty wholeheartedly. Given the issues with combat, I still have to qualify this as being a highly unbalanced experience - removing the combat and leaving this as a 'walking-sim' with puzzles might have been a better option in retrospect - but overall it's left the right kind of impression on me, which is very much a good thing. Give me a unique, relatively short experience like this over something mundane that's typically also dragged out anytime.

If you are really interested in large-scale flesh contraptions and a despairing eldritch hellscape, then this game might be for you. The visuals and animations are fantastic, creating a very unique environment to wander through - but that's the game's only real strength... 

The combat should've been entirely removed from this game personally as it is more of a nuisance than anything else, just wasting the players' time between the puzzles. I would've much preferred an approach similar to SOMA, where enemies are given more interesting gimmicks and are instead avoided rather than fought directly.

The puzzles themselves are similarly annoying as the primary source of difficulty comes from figuring out the goal of the puzzle or trying not to get lost in a compact labyrinth of flesh tunnels. Once you actually get to solve them though, they can be kinda neat. They're just an exceedingly small portion of the total gameplay.

That being said, I am still giving a positive review because the visuals and animation work absolutely carry the game. If you are okay with the gameplay largely being that of a walking sim, then I'd suggest picking the it up when heavily discounted. But if you want actual combat, puzzle-solving, storytelling, or action horror elements, I'd suggest looking elsewhere.

Lo, in the shadowed realm of Scorn, there lieth a world most strange and grimly wrought. The air is thick with dread, and each hall and passage doth whisper of despair. The craft of this game is as a tapestry of flesh and bone, where the hand of its maker hath shaped visions both foul and wondrous.

Herein, thou shalt wander in silence, bereft of guide or counsel, left to reckon with the mysteries that sprawl before thee. The game giveth no word nor solace, yet its very silence speaketh volumes to the heart that hearkeneth. Puzzles, cunningly devised, do lie before thee, and thy wits must thou employ to unbind their secrets.

The world of Scorn is as the marrow of night, its hues pale and ghastly, its forms unearthly and grotesque. Each corner doth feel as though it were alive, writhing beneath thy gaze. To tread this land is to be enfolded by unease, for naught but suffering seemeth to dwell therein.

Though the pace be slow, and oft the path unclear, those who delight in grim beauty and dark marvels shall find much to commend. Yet beware, for Scorn is not for the faint of spirit; it demandeth patience and courage of all who dare to enter its fell domain.

Wouldst thou seek a journey most strange and perilous? Then venture forth, and let Scorn weave its eldritch spell upon thee.

Haunting and phantasmagoric, Scorn is a convulsing nightmare of an experience. The game showcases some of the most stunning visuals and sound design the medium has to offer. I frequently found myself stopping just to absorb the striking level of detail in the environments. There is a strange and alien story unraveling before you, solely communicated through Scorn's immaculate environments. Strange whispers echo the halls while gurgling, fleshy masses comingle with machinery. The atmosphere is laid on thick and refuses to let you go until the game's final striking and thought-provoking moments.

Scorn is less of a game and more of a visual and auditory experience. In fact, Scorn is at it's best when it's not trying to be a game. I found that the pacing was disrupted by the gameplay and puzzle elements and would have much preferred exploring the world uninterrupted. What sparse mechanics Scorn does present are never explained. For example, I found myself in a section where I only had one bar of health and copious amounts of enemies. I kept dying in one hit and couldn't understand how I was supposed to complete the area when I die so easily. I only discovered that I could heal myself by accident when I stumbled upon the key to do so in the menus. I don't need or want weapons and combat when the world and the story it tells is this engaging. Scorn really would have benefited from embracing more of a "walking simulator" design principal and forgone the tedious combat though I will say the deliberate obfuscation of all of it's mechanics does lend itself to a sense of this space being truly alien.

Scorn, while rough around it's edges mechanically, is a one-of-a-kind and unforgettable journey through a demented alien landscape that I will be thinking about long after I've uninstalled it from my machine. It's not for everyone but no great piece of art is. Giger and Beksiński would be proud.

- Combat is poor, should really have a passive play option.

- Introduces some mechanics later on and completely abandons them almost immediately. 4 hour length or so reveals a truncated development time and over reliance on art design.

The game “Scorn”, I would classify as an extremely dark, gory, Sci-Fi horror survival exploration puzzle game. Its visual style is heavily influenced by artwork of Swiss painter H. R. Giger and Polish surrealist Zdzislaw Beksinski. The player is a humanoid trying to get out of an unknown area with lots of contraptions, later also facing hostile creatures. Ultimately, I will leave the interpretation of the plot to you and only go as far as to say that the recurring themes which I perceived were death, decay, darkness, the unknown, hostility, survival, birth, declined civilisations as well as an alien planet or parallel universe.
After about 7 hours play time in an exploration approach, my pros and cons are as follows:

Pros: 
+ amazing visual style, like (morbid, abysmal) artwork in itself
+ great lighting effects and stress on objects
+ Geiger & Beksinski influence
+ dark horror atmosphere
+ great level design throughout the game
+ sound design and placement
+ demanding puzzles
+ abandoned ship feeling
+ minimalistic HUD
+ organic-mechanical apparatus mix
+ sense of time passed
+ interpretation possible with recurring themes and mostly conclusive setting

Cons:
-	Gory, creepy, squishy emphasis too much at the beginning and end, had the feeling they deliberately did it for disgust or “shock effects”
-	Sometimes a bit hard to find your way
-	Some low-res textures
-	Sound direction of enemies often unclear when moving about
-	Many invisible walls (typical for console optimised games)
-	Slow battle mechanics
-	Ultimately, missing a story, but could see this as neutral as well

Conclusion: 
To begin with, you will need to stand quite cruel, gory stuff right from the start and ideally like dark, abysmal Sci-Fi horror settings. Secondly you should be a bit fond of survival, exploration and puzzle mechanics. Then you will be able to enjoy this game wrapped in an amazing visual style with only minor flaws. 

Overall rating: 7/10 points

Possibly the most striking art design I've ever seen in a horror game. This game stands mostly as a gallery of the developers' favorite artists, and it's all beautifully realized but quite derivative. The grungy, biomechanical architecture inspired by H.R. Giger is deeply unsettling. The twisted body horror amalgams inspired by David Cronenberg and Harlan Ellison are twisted and harrowing. The iconography and landscapes inspired by Zdzislaw Beksinski are foreboding and captivating. The sound design is excellent as well, creating an incredible horror atmosphere.

The story feels like fanfiction for I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream. Where Scorn's world stands on its own is how it looked far, far into the future past the story of the book. In Scorn, the great machine has begun to imbue itself with flesh to become more like its creators. After what could be eons, the still-living machine suffered the failings of our biology, growing cancerous flesh and being unable to utilize its waste. Finally, the machine was reborn through spirituality. It created the conditions to ascend to its own twisted heaven, leaving behind the world it worked so hard to ruin. Your job in the game is to follow it.

The gameplay, though, is hit or miss. The combat is a huge miss. Your animations are extremely sluggish, the enemies are tanky and have nearly perfect aim, any wrong move can result in losing half your health bar, and healing is very limited. Thankfully, the enemies are pretty intuitive to understand, as their visual and sound designs play into their gameplay function. Unfortunately, around half of the combat encounters are completely pointless. If you see an ammo refill there's about a 75% chance grabbing it will spawn a bunch of enemies to waste your fresh ammo. Exploring naturally yields a lot of dead ends, but enemy placement sometimes leads you down dead end hallways purely to punish your curiosity and waste your time. The more you play, the more running past enemies is the far better strategy, even when it results in having to tank a few passing blows.

The puzzles mostly hit. They are simple enough not to confuse and challenging enough to be satisfying to complete. None of the puzzle types make a return after their first iteration, which has its pros and cons. Exploration puzzles are largely miss because they can only be progressed from a set starting point, despite every subarea's passageways being mostly open from the time you arrive. You spend a lot of time aimlessly walking around and interacting with things you can't access until you stumble upon to the intended first step, but in fairness progression from the first step is usually intuitive.

In the months since I've played Scorn, it has occupied a small space in my brain to ponder on. I lament how derivative it is of other works, how obtuse the story is without knowing its references, and how little time and polish went into the actual gameplay. If you're not a horror superfan, I recommend picking up the artbook instead. This game hits higher highs than some of the best horror games, but lacks the consistency to count itself among the immortal masterpieces. The people behind Scorn are incredibly talented, and I look forward to them learning from the mistakes of this project and creating an original work.

I gotta hand it to my fellow countrymen - if there is one feature that SCORN showcases exemplary, it's its atmosphere. Truly foreboding, gloomy, with certain scenes instilling uneasiness and chill running down my spine. The thorough study of Beksiński and Giger is masterfully reflected in the visuals, to the point where I cannot marvel enough at it! Environmental storytelling is also a big plus given the design of each animate creature, protagonist included. The "puzzles" are also pretty logical, if logic and rationale can even be applied to this somber, unwelcoming world Ebb Software had created. For a "walking simulator", SCORN gets my highest praise.

Alas, it stumbles in a couple of other areas which excite both frustration and sorrow. The first one stems from pretty short game time and unrealized potential as far as hostile interactions go (namely, there are only three enemy types you can encounter (four if you count the parasite, which is passive and sort of a MacGuffin), which is overall pretty low). I do understand that the game is not an FPS in a classic sense (and actually like the hopelessness and vulnerability of the main character, scarcity of ammo for each of its 3 projectile-based weapons, and clumsiness in applying lethal force), but more visual splendor reflected in the gruesome-yet-majestic environments would have been a treat. 

The "sorrow" part stems from two reasons - the protracted, arduous development cycle which skyrocketed expectations of fans worldwide only to crash & burn upon finally releasing (mostly due to the said expectations), as well as ludicrous price for what the game offers (got my copy from Humble Choice way back in February 2024, so this point does not apply to me). Similar games at the time didn't go over 30 (The Invincible), and even the newly released Necrophosis (which is considered to be at least inspired by SCORN) is $15 at release!

So why the positive review then, if there clearly are glaring issues with the game? The reasons are both objective and subjective - subjective because this is by far & hands-down the BEST game to come out of Serbia. The person and patriot in me wants Ebb Software to succeed, to continue doing this kind of thing (albeit a bit more restrained in terms of promises and deadlines), because we need more of SCORN! To be a harsh critic of their first foray into building their dream game would be cruel and inappropriate, for the spark of genius is clearly present in SCORN. It needs to be further nurtured so that, eventually, it grows into something truly genre-defining. As I stepped into the eerie world of SCORN, I was immediately engulfed in its nightmarish atmosphere, where odd forms and somber tapestries danced before my eyes. Designed to immerse players by throwing them into the depths of its unsettling universe, SCORN promised a non-linear exploration filled with interconnected regions, puzzles, and characters integral to its enigmatic story. However, my journey through this grotesque landscape was a mix of fascination and frustration, leaving me with a myriad of thoughts and impressions.

One of the first aspects of SCORN that caught my attention was its combat system, albeit for the wrong reasons. The combat felt slow and clunky, adding little to the overall experience besides hindering my progress. I couldn't help but question its necessity in a game so heavily focused on atmosphere and exploration. In fact, I found myself resorting to mods just to bypass certain combat encounters, highlighting a missed opportunity to enhance the game's immersion.

Despite my grievances with the combat, SCORN excelled in its audio design, at least until Act 5. The squelching sounds and eerie ambiance effectively contributed to the game's unsettling nature, drawing me deeper into its nightmarish world. However, towards the end of my journey, I encountered audio bugs that detracted from the immersive experience, leaving me slightly disappointed.

The story of SCORN, or lack thereof, was a point of contention for me. With no dialogue or traditional lore to guide me, I was left to interpret the surreal narrative on my own. While this open-ended approach has its merits, I couldn't shake the feeling of ambiguity and confusion that lingered throughout my playthrough. Nevertheless, I appreciated the thematic depth exploring concepts of life, death, and rebirth, even amidst the disturbing imagery and sexual content that permeated the game.

Undoubtedly, the star of SCORN is its art direction. Every surface pulsated with grotesque life, blurring the lines between flesh and bone, evoking a sense of visceral unease. However, the game's intricate designs often worked against it, leading to environments that felt monotonous and indistinguishable. Navigating through visually similar areas became a challenge in itself, detracting from the overall enjoyment of exploration.

The puzzles in SCORN fell into a middling category, offering a decent challenge but lacking in innovation. Many puzzles relied on obfuscation rather than genuine complexity, occasionally leading to moments of frustration and confusion. While I appreciated the developers' adherence to the "Rule of Three" for gradual challenge escalation, it often felt more like padding than meaningful gameplay.

Despite its flaws, I can't deny that SCORN is a distinct experience that left a lasting impression. While it may not be everyone's cup of tea, its relatively short length makes it accessible to those willing to delve into its twisted world. I would recommend it, albeit with caution and a disclaimer regarding its disturbing content. SCORN is a journey worth experiencing, albeit one that could have benefited from refining certain aspects, particularly its combat system.

Overall Rating: 7/10

It’s not here to hold your hand or tell you a neat little story—it wants you to feel the story, or maybe squirm through it. You’re dropped into a world that’s equal parts corpse and cathedral, where every door opens with a squelch, and the only guide is your own discomfort. You are no hero—just a nameless, fleshy wanderer in a place where nature lost a long, messy fight against technology. Every puzzle solved feels more like an invasion than a victory. Every machine is a body part you wish you didn’t have to touch.

Scorn doesn’t care about your happy endings. There’s no hero’s journey here. Each puzzle, each encounter, strips away more of your hope until you realize: this world isn’t here to be beaten—it’s here to consume you. Your flesh, your body—it all becomes part of the machine. Scorn isn’t a game about winning. It’s a game about being used. Used by the world. Used by the machinery. 

And when it’s done with you, there’s nothing left but paralysis. Because, in the end, Scorn leaves you with the greatest horror of all—that you never mattered to begin with.

[b]"Scorn" is a dark journey at a weird alien place made by flesh and machinery. A slow pacing experience with amazing visuals, breathtaking sceneries, unique puzzles, peculiar mechanisms, well designed creepy creatures, strong survival vibes, immersive atmosphere and tons of gore. Unfortunately, battles needed some more polishing and they can get annoying after a while. Yet, it's a unique poetic experience inside a living world of high artistic value. 


Manometer: 8/10[/b]


The good
- It's so artistic. Fantastically designed world that gets you immersed right form the beginning with imposing places and breathtaking sceneries. Flesh is combined masterfully with machinery giving you the impression that you're inside a living artificial organism. The atmosphere is tensive, weird, creepy and you definitely don't feel welcomed there.
- Amazing visuals with tons of details, high resolution dirty textures, atmospheric lighting conditions and nice gray-brown chromatic palette.
- Good pacing. It's not a run and gun shooter like most people would think. It's a slow burn, almost sadistic, procedure full of peculiar mechanisms. Balance between puzzles and battles is great so you never get bored.
- It has some nice puzzles. They're not difficult at all, but they're definitely unique. The game lets you figure out by yourself how this world works without on screen prompts or tutorials which makes the experience even more immersive. Exploring new rooms and trying to understand all these mechanisms is pretty interesting.
- Good lore and interesting story. It hasn't many major events or twists. It mostly wants to make you feel the struggle of the protagonist. The ending is amazing and kind of poetic.
- Uniquely designed tools and guns. Although there are only few of them, they look alive like they're merged to the protagonist's body. I can recall only few games with such weird weapons.
- Well designed creatures that are creepy and unique. A little bit bigger variation would be nice though.
- Great animations. Protagonist's hands, enemies, all those huge mechanisms, everything is moving so smoothly and convincingly.
- Awesome audio design full of high quality creepy sounds. Sounds of flesh and machineries are simply perfect.
- Despite not being a pure survival game its tensive atmosphere and limited resources offer some solid survival vibes.
- Gore is designed with lots of imagination. It's a lot more than just blood and guts.

The bad
- There are some gameplay and control issues. Battles have some tedious mechanics and hitting the enemies with your close range weapon is difficult to calculate and inconsistent. Protagonist's movement sometimes feels too heavy and there are minor, yet annoying collisions issues.
- The world and the lore are great but storytelling doesn't give you enough motivation. Your actions aren't connected organically to plot's events so there is no specific purpose of doing things. You solve puzzles just because they are there proceeding to the next location because why not. The end explains most of it though.
- Inside all this chaos of flesh and blood a lot of places look identical and sometimes it's difficult to identify what's interactive. At some points you may do a few circles around the same spot before you realize it.

[h2]TL;DR[/h2]
[b]A lyric body horror, with top tier visual and audio design.[/b]

[h3]Positives[/h3]
[olist]
[*] H. R. Giger's fever dream. Every shape, every creature, every pulse oozes macabre body horror brutalism.
[*] Audio design is absolutely top notch:
[list]
[*] Both in audio effects of everything from the player characters body to various gizmos small and large and
[*] the music, which is used sparingly to great effect as an exclamation mark on scenes of import.
[/list]
[*] Level design is excellent. One can clearly read from the design language and be led through the hopeless halls of civilization fallen.
[*] Ominous set pieces anchor the player on several places. Each of these is done within gameplay by clever use of architecture.
[*] Tool design (including health and ammo stations) is marvelous. Not sure whether I would like to shake the designers hands or hide from them in terror. Well done.
[*] Puzzle construction is fresh with every turn throwing you something new. There is little to no recycling.
[*] Creature design of "the parasite" needs to receive a special nod. Delicious.
[/olist]

[h3]Neutral[/h3]
[olist]
[*] While logically sound, I found the first tool a bit underwhelming.
[*] Not sure whether I like the inclusion of combat or not. Sure the tools at the players disposal are meaty and visceral, but it gives the player a chance to fight back, which to some extent devalues the predatory nature of the environment.
[/olist]

[h3]Negatives[/h3]
[olist]
[*] The final resolution is unsatisfying. There is a bit of deus ex machina going on with a key element of the conclusion (and honestly throughout the story). I would have loved the player character to make a few steps into a place that would turn out to be even worse than the environs they were trying to get away from.
[*] Color desaturation. I would have loved a bit more contrasts at "the citadel" and in several other places. Muting all color and popping a few reds and greens would have done a lot of good to underline certain scenes.
[/olist]

How should I write this review for potential Steam buyers today?

As steam user, I think we want to feel we've got value from our purchase: the higher the price, the highest the expectations. That's a bias that deserves this game at its constant price.

So buyers beware: it's an imperfect, yet mind-blowing work of art, in the format of a 1st person survival horror.

I've binged all of it with delight despite its flaws, thanks to the clear influences drawn from more or less known artists.

[b][u]Art influences[/u][/b]
* H. R. Giger (paintings and sculptures, the creator behind Alien). 
    - his signature theme is a bio-mechanical erotism, weird and horrific, yet arousing (am I a sicko? the last chapter is the giger-est, weird boner material, truly) with a distinct focus on breeding/impregnation.
    - the post-human "population" which seems variously repurposed for infrastructural and logistic tasks, acting on instinct (what those doberman-sized walking penises are for, though? 🤔).
    - structures and contraptions are kinda like bones, sinews, skin, conjunctive tissues, glands and organs
    - various interfaces, gadgets and augments involve some form of penetration, stabbing, parasiting, which you're often the receiving end
    - your weapons are meat and bone, the ammo is bodily stuff (like teeth ; have you seen ExistenZ BTW?)
* Zdzisław Beksiński (less known painter, amazingly creepy landscapes, structures and creatures). His cathedral-looking painting is very reminiscent of some sights in the game, for instance.
* since I've mentioned ExistenZ, I guess David Cronenberg's influence is also there: The Naked Lunch, Crimes of the Future, VideoDrome...

And possibly more influences I wish I knew.

[b][u]Gameplay[/u][/b]
 * explore, fight or hide (ammo and health aren't plenty)
 * solve puzzles to progress (sometimes, gratuitously  gruesome, yet satisfying)

[b][u]Progression[/u][/b]

You'll unlock weapons and more health/kits over the course of the game.
There's no storytelling, you're just a weird naked dude, awakening from an umbilical pod/egg. You seem to breath through apparent lungs and have some bone-looking plating. If you happen to look down, you also have feet... [spoiler]and a long, flaccid dongler which will be used at some point[/spoiler].

You're shambling your way through landscapes, structures, tossed around by rather indifferent living mechanisms and post-human entities, seemingly acting from basic atavisms.

It's a journey without apparent goal besides surviving, harshly, especially [spoiler]after the "game over, man!" moment[/spoiler] from ~mid-game which will sharpen the shape of your struggles a bit.

From then, having a clearer short-term objective of ([spoiler]keeping your invader in check somehow[/spoiler]).. pushing harder through an aggravating condition (whose progress only varies at key progression points, so, no game time pressure).

It's unfortunately short, the gameplay is a bit shallow to my taste but accomplishes its ancillary goal quite well IMHO. You'd find combat and some puzzle rather tedious.
I've played through it with the ironic idea that the gameplay is not the core focus of the game.

If you're not bothered by the format of a journey, from an unexplained beginning, though some enigmatic events and towards an unknown goal (besides the one induced midgame) and a rather open ending (or is it?), then you'll enjoy it.

The game absolutely deserves to be experienced but the price is obviously a big turndown. I have seen sales on GoG (10€) but not on steam.

Alternatively I'd suggest you watch a playthrough VoD or stream if you won't bother with actually playing it.

I have many mixed feelings about Scorn. 

In many ways, I love it. It's a dark journey through a haunting nightmare realm, heavily inspired by the unsettling works of H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński. Every building and machine is a disgusting yet oddly beautiful amalgamation of technology and living flesh, and traversing the game feels like a biomechanical fever dream. The sound design is on point as well, from the sickly squelching of inserting a key to the muffled cries of a disfigured humanoid. Honestly, Scorn is one of the most visually and audibly distinct games I've ever played, and I applaud Ebb Software for creating something so unique.

However, the actual game-play of Scorn is... Not the best. There's no map, so it's easy to get lost in the labyrinth of hallways. Many of the puzzles are quite hard, and you can spend hours trying to solve them and never get anywhere. And don't get me started on the combat. Why do enemies take so much health? Why do you have so little ammo and healing items, and why are the refill stations single use only? I know survival horror is all about feeling helpless against horrific monsters, but there's a big difference between feeling helpless and actually being helpless.

All in all, I feel that while Scorn suffers from a lot of bad choices in game-play, it's a good start for a new studio. Ebb Software had a clear artistic vision, and they definitely achieved it. I would say that I high hopes for  this little Serbian game studio in the future, but unfortunately it seems like they've been shut down since November 2023, which is a damn shame, since I would have loved to see what they do next.

What if a level designer fell asleep on an H.R. Geiger art book? Scorn seems to have the answer to that question. The answers to that and many more are a part of the gameplay of scorn. The best description I can give to this game is "Myst re-imagined as a walkthrough of Geiger's work". Scorn keeps a tense atmosphere while giving the player a look at another world, the soundtrack the scenery and the enemies(and allies) have a grim look and sound. 
The bad parts of Scorn can be boiled down to two elements simplicity and padding. the puzzles and the level design (while gory and beautiful) are simple and small(at least what the player can actually touch). The enemies exist to pad out the play time. They don't seem smart or dangerous. I think the intent is to make the player the monster in this setting. When introduced to gory or horror elements it's as if the player is the main instigator of both violence and action. The only reason the devs didn't give the player a real melee option like a pipe or a knife is so that gameplay and fighting the enemies would take longer. You might be able to better dodge attacks but i found that soaking the hits and healing after a fight was far more rewarding than trying to dodge or manage the enemies in any other way. Scorn is not an FPS even though it could be.
Taking the good with the bad i enjoyed the game and would love to play whatever else they deem worthy to make next. Despite being short and calm Scorn has an amazing feel from the disturbing and beautiful art design to the unnerving sounds, I wanted to see more and hear more about the world we are meant to be exploring. My greatest fear about Scorn isn't what is coming around the corner, it's that the devs might make a "sCoRn 2" now with RAYTRACING and not take the time to craft a world like the one presented here. simple puzzles, dark visuals and a desire to see more, that's what i felt left with.

There is a story in this game, but you need to pay attention to start to see it. Will you ever get the full explanation ? no, and that's the entire point. From HP Lovecraft's explanation of Gothic horror, the "unknown" is the most terrifying thing.

This also allows the player to create their own story to it. What do you think it's about ? You might be totally correct, and most likely, that's how it's supposed to be taken, YOU decide what it's all about.

The combat isn't great, and the game could have worked without it, but I also kind of see why they added it. The puzzles throughout the game are easy. The main focus of the game is mainly the looks, the feeling, the ambience. A solid part of it is that everything is alien, even the UI. It really puts you into the world more.

I would say the game is a bit short, but at the same time I'm not sure it would have been any better if it was longer. This is a one off experience of a game. It's the kind of game that you will keep thinking about for the rest of the week.

I hope we see a sequel that explores the world a bit more, and maybe explains just a little bit more, particularly about the ending. The ending somewhat comes out of nowhere and it does deserve just a scratch more of info.

Alright where do I even begin...
I think I should start by saying that if a walking simulator that heavily relies on atmosphere and environmental story telling with a bit of puzzling and first person shooting sprinkled here and there is something that seems boring/uninteresting to you then sadly this is not the game for you, However, if you truly look at and appreciate games as an art form then stick around, I have a couple things to say about this game.

You probably noticed right off the bat from either the screenshots or the trailers that this game is heavily inspired by the works of artist H.R. Giger (most famously known for being behind the visual design of the Alien movie franchise and specifically the famous Xenomorphs), for the uninitiated H.R. Giger's art style is known as "Biomechanical" - A fusion of human body imagery and organs with cold, metallic machinery that forms something... simply fascinating and awe-inspiring. I could just tell you that this game is basically an interactive art gallery where you just walk around and soak in the landscape, visuals, atmosphere and ambiance and call it a review but there's a little bit more to it than that.

For starters this game does NOT hold your hand in neither story telling nor world navigation and objectives, everything is left to the player to interpret what happened in the world you are currently inhabiting and what you should do next. the gameplay loop consists of 3 parts: Exploration, puzzles and combat.

For the exploration part, as mentioned above, you are left to your own devices to figure out where to go next and what you must do, there are no objective markers and no hints whatsoever which can be a turn off for some but personally it truly enhanced my immersion while playing this game. the environments are very dark and grotesque at first and at some points you'll feel like you're navigating the body of... something, with some structures resembling large organs in a familiar yet quite alien way which speaks volumes to how good the art direction in this game is. At a certain point the game's art direction really kicks into high gear as you explore what appears to be the ruins of a once great civilization and at that part of the game I literally spent no less than an hour just walking around and taking screenshots of every single thing in sight, to say my jaw hit the floor would be an understatement and the ambiance/soundtrack perfectly sets the mood as it shifts from being dark and foreboding in the darker early game areas to being grand and awe-inspiring later on and it just does a fantastic job in grounding you in your surrounding area.

 When it comes to puzzles they are kinda simple enough, nothing groundbreaking or anything you've never seen in a horror game before (although I would not necessarily call this a horror game unless you are squeamish or creeped out by gore) but when you do figure out the solution and it clicks it can be very satisfying as this game has excellent feedback to let you know you have completed what is expected of you without even saying a word.

And finally the combat, yeah this game is not exactly hard but not particularly easy either, you don't start doing combat until a little bit further into the game and even then it takes a while to get going but when it does it can be somewhat enjoyable even though it is slow-paced but it is the aim of this game after all. the enemy design is quite good and it will make your flesh crawl but sadly there is little variety in enemy types as I think there are like 4 or 5 enemy types, 1 of which is a boss that you'll only encounter in one area much later on. this is not a typical first person shooter so health and ammo refill stations are far and few between so sometimes it is best to just run past enemies rather than confront them and waste resources that you might need when running is not an option.

I was surprised by how long the game lasted tbh because I've heard a lot of people complain about how short this game and I guess that is true, however as I said above because I viewed this game as an interactive art gallery going into it I think the 9.6 hours i spent in this game is just perfect. You can probably finish it much faster than I did as I took my sweet time walking around basking in the atmosphere and taking screenshots but I feel like not taking your time to appreciate the effort put into this game's art direction is really missing the point.

Overall this was a very enjoyable experience and one that I think we need more of in the gaming world. I wouldn't say this is one of the best games I've ever played but its certainly been unique enough to peak my interest and keep me thinking about it for sometime and possible even revisit it in the future.

If you are a good shot and don't miss too many times, then the ammo and health can be plentiful. Puzzles can be found all throughout the nightmarish universe that is both haunting and beautiful.

The player can easily spend a lot of time in each section or room and admire the surreal, twisted imaginative minds of the artists and developers. Whether you are looking up, down, all around or questioning what's down that path or around the corner, you will find yourself astonished and horrified at the same time.

The dark ambient soundtrack highlights each location. Reverberating your ear drums while each track tells its own story. Horrifying and ominous at times, that'll leave you on the edge of your seat with a heightened sense of anxiety, while other times cascading the landscapes with a sense of beauty and awe. 

There is no dialogue or story but the way the game and artistry are designed is for the player to decide, while most times it can be obvious. The digital artbook can help put some sense into the backstory of the biomechanical world, enemy names, devices and weapons.

This is one of my favorite games and I hope you enjoy it as much as I have.
