What the f............

I... um....  okay...  Well.....  that was...... a thing....

I mean, I knew it'd be weird, it draws inspiration from H.R. Giger (and of course, Alien).... Buuut.. Yeahhhhh..  

I'm writing this just after I've finished the game, and I went back to try something a bit different (cos I had missed an achievement)...    I have NO idea what the heck is going on..  

[time passes]

OK, I've now read some articles from people that reckon they know what's going on.  Aaaand, I see where they're coming from, but I'd never have picked up on those 'clues'.

The game plays like a horror walking simulator.  A little like SOMA, I suppose, but set .. well, I won't ruin it..   Needless to say, it's full of Gigeresque bodyshock horror, monsters to run away from (or fight) and a LOT of weird puzzles to work out, which entail figuring out what you need to do, and then how to do it with the things dotted around the levels.

Speaking of the levels, they are STUNNING.  Absolute works of art.  Creepy... weird, disturbing... works of art, but still. I don't think there's a rectangle anywhere in the game, it's all organic curves and squishy stuff.

The sound design is great... I played it on surround headphones and it was suitably creepy.  Nice atmospheric music and sounds, lots of environmental FX, and unlocatable squishes, splashes, pops and twangs to keep your nerves on edge.

The story is told through the levels. There's no words, or even the usual UI sounds you get.   It's all very non-traditional up to a point, but has some traditional elements overlaid on it.

The game is really nicely designed, levelwise. And the custcenes, weird body things going on and so on are brilliantly done, telling the tale of a weird place of horrors beyond imagination.

The one thing I found a little less good was the actual game itself.   Once you get over the creepy levels and sounds, the game becomes very familiar in structure and it starts to lose the 'horror' aspects, becoming your standard FPS puzzle. They really went all out to make it feel creepy and weird, making the first act of the game a real horrorfest of weirdness.  But then they seem to have fallen into a rut and and been unable to come up with truly novel  puzzles after that.  They become familiar "go to a room, press a button, watch a mini cutscene, realise there are two more buttons somewhere, and then run around finding the next two mcguffins to complete the three tasks and move forward).         

I died a good few times, but I still managed to finish it in about 8 hours.  I went back and replayed the whole of 'Act 1' again, this time taking my time.... So a total of just over 9 hours.   I'd say that's pretty perfect.  If it'd been any longer, it'd have become repetitive.  By the end of the game, I'd realised how the enemy AI worked and was just running straight past the monsters.

I don't really like scary games, but this game never became too scary, just weird and creepy, so I give it a thumbs up from me.  I hope the devs explain the plot at some point.   It had that same eeriness of the "space jockey" scene in Alien, and like that scene, it felt like there was a whole backstory there that needed telling.

I'm glad this game was made, but honestly, I'm surprised it was. It's Olympic-level Not For Everyone to the extent that it's pushing on not for anyone. But if it's in your taste-range, and you're able/willing to see it and accept it for what it is, you're going to enjoy it.

Scorn is not Call of Duty, it doesn't want to be Call of Duty, and it doesn't try to be Call of Duty, so don't expect it to be, and don't try to judge it by those standards. Despite it being first person, and despite it having guns, Scorn is not an FPS. It has a lot more in common with classic mystery world puzzle games like Myst than it does with Half-Life, and where firearms are involved, they're more about progressing into the next stage of the puzzle than combat. And where there are enemies - and there are maybe 15 - 20 combat encounters in the whole game - you only need to need to actually engage in one of them; the rest you can run from. Even that encounter is more an exercise in timing and problem solving than a fight.

Rather, the vast majority of your time is spent slowly searching your way through this horrid nightmare world, one that, despite being nearly dead, leaves behind an entirely clear picture of a horribly cruel society that saw no value in life beyond how it could be manipulated to serve practical, tangible, yet nightmarish ends. Scorn is outright gruesome in ways even I, someone who loves horror, found disconcerting (especially the first creature you encounter). It's a masterwork in atmosphere and world design. The slow pace and near-total lack of a UI forces you to explore, examine, and pay attention to the detail in the world around you. It's frankly astonishing how, despite there being no dialogue and no texts to teach you the lore, you're still able to fully understand not only what this culture was like, but how it was destroyed. Scorn does a lot with very little. And what you learn is... difficult.

I don't want to use the world "but" because I don't want to present this as a criticism, because I'm not, but Scorn is very slow-paced, so those of you who need constant flashing lights and things to throw grenades at won't like this game. If you want to compare it to a movie, Scorn is more like Blade Runner - slow, purposeful, ponderous, thoughtful - than Transformers. 

This isn't an action game, it doesn't try to be, and it doesn't present itself as though it were, so if you going into it expecting that, it's your fault, not the game's. But if you accept it for what it is (and get past the disgustingly literal "everything is horrible, unmitigated suffering" tone), you will like it.

You were dreaming. Your body lies in the dirt entwined with living tendrils that hold you tight and suck your life juices out of you. Then you wake up. It wasn't a dream!

Scorn throws you into an unknown, strange world. The game gives you the privilege of exploring and experiencing a world like no other. There are no explanations. There are no dialogues. No one will take you by the hand to show you around. And that's exactly what makes the game so unique.

There are many games that take the player into strange worlds. But unlike Scorn, after a while players realize where they are, what is required of them and what they have to do. Scorn throws you into a world so strange and alien that you won't know where you are, what's required of you, or how to escape this nightmare. All you know is that you have to leave the area you are in. This world is hostile. This world is dangerous and you want to live. So you have to get out of here.

Every level is different, looks different, and challenges you with new tasks. The game never gets boring and keeps surprising you with completely unexpected events until the very end. This is euphoric. Again and again, you stare at your monitor in fascination while you think to yourself, 'This can't be true!'. It's absolutely intoxicating.

Beside occasional combat with amazing creatures, Scorn's gameplay is mainly puzzles. Sometimes you have to solve puzzles directly on a wall or in a mechanism, but often the whole map is a puzzle on which you have to activate machines, move levers and find upgrades to open doors or move gates. 

All puzzles are challenging, but at the same time cleverly designed so that you can always solve them. Since all maps are large labyrinths, you often run back and forth trying to solve everything, and occasionally you might feel lost. I was a little frustrated, once in level 4 because I wasn't able to find the last of three mechanisms. But then eventually I found the last one. 

Scorn is an achievement friendly game. Except for the first two achievements, you will collect all of them automatically. As for the first two, you can only collect one of them during a single game. Therefore, after finishing the game once, you just need to replay the first 15 minutes to collect the missing achievement.

Scorn has received overall positive reviews, but some players are annoyed by the fact that the game costs 40 $/Euros but only offers 7 hours play time. I doubt you can complete the game in 7 hours without instructions. It took me 11 hours without guide. Nevertheless, I can understand the criticism. At the same time, Scorn is a very special game, and I can imagine how much work it took the developers to create it. Wait for a sale. Personally, I think $20 is a reasonable price.

If there were Oscars for games, Scorn would collect many of them. In my opinion this game is a masterpiece. It’s a work of art. Scorn is like visiting a gallery of absurdities, where you can't help but be amazed. It's scary and brutal, and there's a lot of blood in this game. Scorn is simultaneously cruel and incredibly fascinating. I only played the game at night with headphones because I wanted to enjoy every moment, and I succeeded. I love Scorn. It's a great game! I strongly doubt I will play anything better this year.

"Scorn is a game where you get to experience the abject horror of being a sentient cow on its way to slaughter. Machines beyond your ability to understand line your path. Scorn is an expedition from the nightmares of H. R. Giger and Z. Beksiński.

It begins without context, there is no narrator or clear clues of what happens or has happened, you do not know where you are, you do not know who or what you are, it is taken for granted that we have a purpose, but we do not know what it is or what it was, you just wake up and walk endlessly through a post-apocalyptic and desolate world, as if you were seeing the ashes of a past civilization. It is through the progression of the game that we are told in broad strokes the meanings and purposes, however, there remains a huge room for interpretation.

The strong point is the artistic design, deeply inspired by works such as Alien, Dune and Prometheus. Scorn seeks to engage and captivate the audience through its landscapes, atmospheres, environments and sound pieces.

Its worst “flaw” is the combat; it feels monotonous and in certain areas tedious, however, it can be counteracted by playing strategically, once you learn to know when to shoot and when to run away the gameplay becomes more fluid. The game does not force you to kill the base enemies in order to continue, a single shot is enough to stun them and take advantage of that moment to bypass them, this allows the progression of the game to be more satisfying and enjoyable. (From a subjective perspective, this section is consistent with what it wants to transmit; it does not have to be polished to be captivating, nor does it have to shine in its mechanical aspect to be a masterpiece. If the environment is crude it is timely and appropriate for the gameplay to be crude as well).

Scorn : By Triple F

"Scorn," developed by Ebb Software, is a unique and unsettling horror game that immerses players in a world heavily inspired by the biomechanical art of H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński. Released in 2022, "Scorn" offers a distinct first-person experience that focuses on exploration, environmental puzzles, and atmosphere rather than traditional combat or jump scares. Set in a surreal, alien landscape filled with organic machinery and grotesque, otherworldly structures, the game pushes players into a strange and deeply disturbing universe without guidance, dialogue, or explicit storytelling. This silent descent into horror is as much an exploration of its aesthetic as it is a journey through a twisted world, and "Scorn" stands out for its dedication to creating an immersive, almost meditative experience of body horror and existential dread.

The visual design of "Scorn" is undoubtedly its strongest element, meticulously crafted to evoke an atmosphere of dread and unease. The environments are a blend of organic and mechanical, with structures that feel alive, pulsating, and decayed. The walls, corridors, and machinery appear to be constructed from bones, flesh, and strange tissues, giving the game an unsettlingly tactile feel. Each area of the game is rich in detail, with careful attention to textures and lighting that cast a haunting, monochromatic glow. This design work allows players to feel as though they’re exploring a decayed corpse on a massive scale, creating a visceral, immersive world that is both beautiful and revolting. It’s a visually striking experience, where every corner feels carefully constructed to invoke discomfort and fascination in equal measure.

Exploration and environmental storytelling are the core of "Scorn’s" gameplay, as players must rely on observation to navigate the labyrinthine world and uncover its secrets. Without dialogue or a clear narrative, the game communicates its story through the environment, forcing players to piece together clues about the world’s history and purpose on their own. There are no maps or quest markers, and the minimal UI leaves players feeling vulnerable and isolated, amplifying the horror of each step deeper into this biomechanical nightmare. This design choice serves to make exploration feel intentional and personal, as players must move forward based on their instincts and memory alone. However, the lack of direct storytelling or guidance may frustrate those seeking a more linear narrative, as "Scorn" leans heavily on abstraction and ambiguity to create its impact.

The puzzle design in "Scorn" is varied, often requiring players to manipulate alien machinery, connect circuits, or navigate complex structures to progress. These puzzles are an integral part of the game’s experience, blending seamlessly with the environment and often requiring players to interact with disturbingly organic controls and mechanisms. While some puzzles are straightforward, others require careful observation and experimentation, reinforcing the game's philosophy of exploration and discovery. The tactile nature of each interaction makes the puzzles feel more unsettling, as players handle machinery that resembles living organs, adding a layer of horror to each task. However, some puzzles lack clarity, and the absence of tutorials can make certain sections feel obtuse, potentially slowing down the pace for players unaccustomed to the game’s cryptic style.

Combat in "Scorn" is minimal and unsettling, more akin to survival horror than action. Players occasionally encounter hostile creatures that resemble malformed beings or twisted anatomical constructs, and the few weapons available feel as organic as the world itself, often resembling skeletal or fleshy tools. Ammunition is scarce, and combat is clunky by design, with slow, deliberate attacks that make every encounter feel threatening. Rather than empowering players, these mechanics reinforce a sense of vulnerability, making it clear that fighting isn’t the focus of the game; survival is. For some, the combat may feel frustrating or unsatisfying due to its deliberate sluggishness, but it effectively amplifies the horror by encouraging players to avoid fights when possible, heightening the tension of each encounter.

The sound design in "Scorn" is hauntingly atmospheric, composed of subtle mechanical hums, organic squelches, and ambient noises that fill the game’s environments with an eerie sense of life. The absence of traditional music allows players to focus on every small sound, from the clicking of strange machinery to the unsettling groans and sloshes of the alien landscape itself. This minimalist approach to audio intensifies the sense of isolation, as players are left alone with the unsettling noises of the world around them. The soundscape builds tension effectively, giving players no reprieve from the dread that permeates every environment, enhancing the immersive horror experience that defines "Scorn."

Narrative interpretation is open-ended, leaving players to piece together the meaning of "Scorn’s" world and its biomechanical horrors through visual cues and environmental details. The game doesn’t provide explicit answers, and players are left to draw their own conclusions about the nature of the world, its inhabitants, and their own purpose within it. Some may interpret the story as an exploration of life, death, and rebirth, while others may see it as a grim commentary on the merging of flesh and machine. This ambiguity makes "Scorn" feel almost like a piece of interactive art, where meaning is subjective and rooted in the player’s individual experience. However, those seeking a more straightforward plot may find this aspect lacking, as the game remains cryptic from start to finish.

In summary, "Scorn" is a unique horror experience that prioritizes atmosphere, design, and environmental storytelling over traditional gameplay mechanics and narrative structure. It’s a game that invites players to explore a beautifully grotesque world at their own pace, immersing them in an aesthetic of surreal body horror that is both captivating and horrifying. While the lack of guidance and minimal combat may deter players who prefer clear objectives or a more action-driven experience, "Scorn" stands as an ambitious and immersive work that challenges conventions of horror gaming. For those willing to embrace its slower, more abstract approach, "Scorn" offers an unforgettable journey into a world that feels disturbingly alive and a dark, visceral descent into a biomechanical nightmare.

If the developers' intention with Scorn was to create a visually striking, disturbing, and horrifying experience, then it's safe to say they've succeeded. Every single graphic element in the game conveys a sense of terror, with environments that seem to emerge from a nightmarish, dystopian world in decay. The aesthetics, inspired by the works of H.R. Giger, dominate the gameplay, constantly making the player feel uneasy as they're immersed in a deforming landscape where nothing is comforting.

The core of the experience lies in the puzzles, which increase in complexity as you progress. In Scorn, the absence of indicators or hints forces players to explore and understand the world through trial and intuition. There are no tutorials or explicit messages, making the progression both intriguing and challenging. You'll feel lost, just like the protagonist, inside a labyrinth of tunnels and rooms that all seem the same, but the compartmentalized structure of the game helps you make sense of each map and discover new corners of this alienating universe.

Unfortunately, the combat aspect represents the weak point of Scorn. While more powerful weapons are provided as you go, the combat system feels cumbersome and unrewarding. Ammunition is scarce and difficult to find, creating a constant sense of shortage. Additionally, health management is equally stingy, forcing players to remain vigilant at all times. The creatures that infest the environments are far from memorable enemies: instead of exciting challenges, they feel more like simple obstacles. This, combined with unforgiving checkpoints, can lead to frustrating moments, where you're forced to repeat lengthy and difficult sections, especially when health is low and resources are scarce.

In conclusion, Scorn is a game that stands out for its unique atmosphere, but falls short in several gameplay aspects. The enemies, unfortunately, are unremarkable, and while the environments are phenomenal, with claustrophobic architectures and desolate spaces that tell the story of a world devastated, the experience doesn't fully leverage its potential. The final "cathedral," with its perverse bas-reliefs, is a visual masterpiece that expresses the theme of the world's transformation into a hell, but it alone isn't enough to elevate the entire experience. In the end, Scorn is a visceral and disorienting journey, but with too many flaws in gameplay to be considered a complete masterpiece.

[b]TL;DR : I played this game in VR through a mod (UEVR), it was a great experience and felt like the game was made for it considering how contemplative and visually focused it is. It's world is left to your interpretation, there’s not a single spoken word in the whole game and no real cut scene. It's great only if you know what you're getting into, I know it was disappointing to some. It's not very long and apparently falls short compared to what was planned and advertised.[/b]


[b]Gameplay in VR[/b] : I used UEVR to be able to "inject" (as it calls it) the game in the headset. You can find here the guide I followed https://youtu.be/4ccaX8Hr1JU?si=-mJiFSlZ4D1NkJTs 
It took a bit of tweaking but after a bit of trial and error it became easy to follow the steps. You might need to disable your antivirus as one of the files you unzip keeps getting deleted by Windows. 

The impressive, goric and dark world of Scorn is perfect for VR, you're often left looking around in awe at the size and weirdness of the place. There's two moments during the game that are probably the most jaw-dropping I've seen in VR. 

Performance wasn't the best, I'm using the first Oculus headset that was released, and a 980ti which is getting a bit old now. The world clearly was less detailed than on a flat screen but the immersion was still totally worth the experience. 

The gameplay itself being very basic it was fine in VR. Only issue was the combat, aiming wasn't easy at all. It's not like in HL:ALyx where you're free to physically move your hands to aim, you need to use joysticks like on a controller, which is even harder to do with the headset on. Maybe I could have tweaked the game a bit more with the tools though, once I managed to set up the camera right I went along with it. I avoided enemies as much as I could, and one specific fight had me reverting to my normal monitor to be able to aim better.


[b]Gameplay in general[/b]

The game is maybe 40% walking, 50% puzzles and 10% combat. 

If the world isn't of interest to you there's not really a point, rushing the game simply to reach the next puzzle without contemplating your surrounding would make it a pretty boring experience. 

The puzzles can be level sized, in a Tomb Raider fashion, or more simple ones that you need to solve like a rubiks cube or something. I found the difficulty perfect, not too hard, not too easy. The very first one is maybe the hardest and it was a weird choice to have it this early in the game. 

Once again, combat is really secondary and it's not the best fps you'll find. The best aspect of it is actually the design of the enemies and the weapons themselves more than how they all behave. You can also easily avoid 75% of the enemies by waiting a bit, which was helpful with in VR. 


[b]Atmosphere, theme[/b]

This is where the real value of the game lies, its world, its civilization, its beings, its technology... etc. It's gore, but not really scary, I don't think there has been a single jumpscare in the whole game. I've been terrorized at times but not by direct violence, it's much more psychological. 

The influence of H.R. Giger is obvious and most people who are familiar with Alien will notice the resemblance with the Xenomorph and it's home world. 
On top of the unsettling depictions of all of this weird bio-technology, where you don't know where the machine ends and the biological starts, many aspects are directly inspired or referencing the setting of LV426 (the eggs, the facehugger... etc).

I also learned about Beksiński while learning more about the game and you can really see the game as a mix of his depressing style and Giger's art. It's also how I would picture civilizations of older or more advanced species in Lovecraftian story. 

The fact that it lacks a narration makes you wonder about the meaning behind everything. There's themes of birth, sexuality, exploitation, spirituality, civilization... 

First of all, I see this world as humanity's doing. It doesn't look like it's a humanoid alien race, but actual humans, who built this place. Maybe on Earth, maybe not. It's probably too metaphorical to really matter, but it's still interesting to imagine the lore behind all of it. 

It feels futuristic, but it's mechanical technology contrasts with how we tend to picture a dystopic digital future. It's some kind of mechanical cyberpunk dystopia.

You encounter many different species, some born from the collapse of this civilization and humanity, some exploited or bio-engineered by us. Suffering and exploitation are an integral part of everything, even while the civilization was thriving. It is built on horror. Everything is made in the image of the human body, of which you find hints in everything around you, it's hard to wrap your head around this world that seems to worship the body's physicality while also disrespect it so much in it's real biological form. 

The game's name to me refers to humanity's relationship with itself, with life as a whole, seen as a means to a technological end. Our world has been built on the exploitation of a workforce as long as we've had social classes, from slavery to serfdom to today's proletariat. That's not even considering the catastrophic toll "humanity", or really, the way it organizes production and exploitation, has on life on Earth as a whole. Factory farming also isn't really that far from what we see depicted in this hell world. 

I don't see this place as hell, it's very physical, concrete. It would seem meaningless if it wasn't for the very ending. All of the elements of this last place and it's puzzle makes you understand what the protagonist was chasing all along. It's a mystical spiritual place you try to reach after a lot of struggle, like in the movies Stalker or Annihilation. 

Everything leads up to this weird climatic (and anti-climatic) place, where pain reaches it's apex but also allows you to reach a spiritual goal by joining a collective consciousness or mind, and entering a place that you've been chasing all along. 
Maybe it's about the shit some can go through to reach a religious heaven, which in the end doesn't show up even show up, as the events unfolding in the game show. You're only left with the pain just as you thought you could finally reach nirvana. 
The relationship between suffering and a spiritual goal also reminded me of the movie Martyrs, one of the rare ones I've seen where the story had a real meaning and impact to me. 
Or it's just pure nihilism about how life is suffering, we try to give it meaning, and in the end you die. 

There's a lot of lore that is shown in the artbook and I may get things wrong in my interpretation. It is such a rich universe, I wish more could have been shown. 


As I understand it, the game was very divisive among the community expecting it. Some criticize it as a walking simulator, but it's also the fact that it was apparently supposed to be bigger than it ended up being, that it was over hyped and over-sold...

The steam page at the time said "Scorn takes place in an open-ended world with different interconnected regions." and it's very clearly not what we got. 

It seems like it was rushed, a lot of content and playability cut, but the end result by itself was a very good experience to me.

The false advertising would have been my only criticism, but luckily I only purchased and played it a while after everybody.

Scorn is a surreal, atmospheric first-person horror adventure that defies traditional genre boundaries by plunging the player into a grotesque biomechanical world inspired heavily by the works of H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński. Developed by Ebb Software, the game is less about conventional storytelling or action-based gameplay and more about immersing the player in an unsettling, decaying environment where every surface breathes, bleeds, and oozes with organic decay. It’s a game that deliberately obscures meaning, offering an experience that feels more like exploring a waking nightmare than progressing through a clear narrative. For those willing to embrace ambiguity and slow-paced exploration, Scorn offers a hauntingly unique vision unlike anything else in the horror landscape.

From the opening moments, Scorn sets the tone with eerie silence and a palpable sense of isolation. There is no dialogue, no exposition, and no guidance beyond the player’s instinct to move forward and interact with the world. Instead, the game relies on environmental storytelling, allowing players to piece together the narrative — if one exists in a traditional sense — through observation and interpretation. The setting is a decaying labyrinth of flesh and machinery, where everything seems to be both alive and dead at once. The architecture pulses, moans, and reacts, creating a deeply immersive and disconcerting atmosphere that lingers long after the screen fades to black.

Gameplay in Scorn is a mix of environmental puzzle-solving, exploration, and light combat. The puzzles are intricate and often abstract, requiring patience and careful attention to the grotesque machinery scattered throughout the world. These challenges are not merely mechanical obstacles; they’re tightly woven into the fabric of the environment and often involve disturbing interactions with the biomechanical world, such as inserting limbs into organic interfaces or operating gruesome machinery. The satisfaction of solving these puzzles lies not only in the intellectual challenge but also in how they deepen the player’s immersion in the alien logic of the world.

Combat, while present, is minimal and intentionally awkward. The game arms the player with organic, weapon-like tools that are slow, clunky, and uncomfortable to use — a design choice that enhances the feeling of vulnerability and helplessness rather than power. Encounters are tense and often best avoided rather than confronted head-on. This decision will likely divide players: those expecting more traditional FPS mechanics may find the combat frustrating, but others may appreciate how the combat reinforces the game’s oppressive atmosphere and sense of unease.

Visually, Scorn is nothing short of stunning — in the most unsettling way possible. The use of texture, lighting, and environmental detail is meticulous. Every corridor, chamber, and grotesque structure contributes to the game’s otherworldly aesthetic. There’s a tactile, almost sickening realism to the organic materials that dominate the game’s world, and it’s this visual design that elevates Scorn beyond a typical horror experience. The sense of scale and dread is omnipresent, with the game world feeling hostile, indifferent, and utterly alien. Sound design complements the visuals beautifully, using ambient noise, subtle audio cues, and disturbing biological squelches to keep players constantly on edge.

One of the most compelling — and controversial — aspects of Scorn is its complete lack of hand-holding. There are no tutorials, mission markers, or overt narrative cues. The game demands that players figure things out on their own, sometimes wandering through its decaying corridors with little sense of direction. For some, this design choice will enhance the feeling of being lost in a bizarre, uncaring world. For others, the lack of clarity may feel frustrating or alienating. But Scorn is unapologetic in its commitment to this design philosophy, and it’s part of what gives the game its unique identity.

In terms of narrative, Scorn is open to interpretation. There is no dialogue, no text, and very few overt story beats. Instead, the game invites players to engage with its symbolism and visual metaphors. It’s a meditative experience — one that encourages reflection rather than explanation. Some players may see themes of birth, death, transformation, and futility woven through the grotesque imagery and quiet suffering of the protagonist. Others may simply experience it as a beautiful, horrifying journey through a surreal biomechanical landscape. Either perspective is valid, and part of the game’s strength lies in this ambiguity.

Ultimately, Scorn is not a game for everyone. It’s slow, abstract, and deeply disturbing — a far cry from fast-paced horror shooters or narrative-driven thrillers. But for those with the patience and curiosity to engage with its world on its own terms, it offers a deeply atmospheric, artistically ambitious experience that lingers long after the final scene. It’s a testament to the power of visual design and mood to tell a story without words, and a rare example of a game that feels like a piece of interactive art. Scorn may frustrate, confuse, or even repel some players, but for others, it will be a haunting masterpiece that rewards introspection and immersion above all else.

So, I went into this game mostly blind, like seeing the pictures and a trailer or two.
I went in with the expectations of seeing art, environment and other stuff akin to what I've seen in most Alien material.
As in, the design of the Xenomorphs, their hives, the ship that's shown in the first 2 movies.
At no point did I expect to actually see them in the game, though it would have been a neat easter-egg.
But all that bone-structure and architecture, that's what I mainly expected, and got.
I didn't mind that the game could've been an entire WalkingNoCombat thing, with its puzzles.
That would have been just fine, but here's the thing... there is more than walking, just not combat.
What you have, is danger, with attempts of defenses.
See, the first 1/5 of the game I really enjoyed playing, even getting the first tool-gun was okay.
Since it is first used on passive things and a puzzle, I wrongfully assumed the game would just be a slow but okay ride.
But no, then we get to 2/5-4/5 of the game, where 2 gun mods, not tools, is introduced, as well as 3 aggressive creatures.
First 1, as others have said, is a "chicken" with ranged and melee attack.
Second 1 is a weird "dog", also with ranged and melee attack.
Now they can be killed with the tool, since you don't get the first gun mod until early 3/5.
But they hurt good, and there ain't a dodge feature, only manual movements.
Now around this time, I did read up here and there about this "combat", and I've concluded it all down to this lesson.
You can fight, but it is best to just backtrack-run along a few corners and roughly 30 sec.
Wait, and they'll mostly hide away so you can walk pass.
If they reappear, just get further away while out of line of sight, that often works too, making you save ammo.
Cause this is another thing, there literally isn't ammo for every creature, at all, so run and hide more than fight.
"But hey, what about that tool, you said it can kill too, I can save ammo that way."
Why yes, you can, BUT, around 3/5, the 3 creature appears, and unlike the first 2, this one acts different.
Third 1, "Bulky", won't stop chasing you, and takes more shots than the rest, does only melee, and hurts too much.
So the tool won't work here, so try and save ammo mainly for "Bulkies", and only use on "Chicken" and "Dog" if needed.
These 3 creatures are organic, and only appears during late 2/5 to the end of 4/5 of the game.
During this part of the game, it mostly looks organic/parasitic, and barely what I expected.
But hey, maybe the story can explain it.
Don't worry about spoilers, cause if I told you based ONLY on what the game tells me, then I learned NOTHING.
Yes, 8 hours, and I didn't learn a single thing about what's going on.
At BEST, maaaaybe, I learned there was an ancient race, which is now gone, and a parasite thingy exists instead.
Why? How? When? Who? At this point, maybe even Game Theory can have a legit answer.
But hey, we still got that 5/5 of the game left, right? Well... kinda.
At first, I was sooo thankfull for what I witnessed and thought we could be back at the same stuff again.
At first, yeah.
Then a sudden boss fight.
Here's the thing, the game NEVER helps you directly, it's all up to you to figure out what to do at any given time.
No text, no truly obvious signs.
Just... minor things that you may or may not notice is actually what you have to do in order to progress, even in "combat".
Maybe I just sucked at the 2nd boss fight, but that one didn't make it clear to me how to beat it.
First one had a weakness that was only slightly glowing, giving a hint to try and shot there, but 2nd boss didn't have that.
I died a lot and got hurt a lot, before realising it was immune to all damage, EXCEPT, using the last 4th gun mod.
Shooting a grenade into its open back when it reloads.
Oh right, during middle 4/5, you get the 3rd gun mod, try and only use it on "Bulkies", kills them in 2 good shots.
So yeah, I had a fair amount of downs throughout the middle parts of the game, only adapting when I knew more.
But that aside, I still.. somehow, enjoyed the game overall, but only juuust enough, and also cause I got the Ribbon.
See, getting that Completionist Ribbon is pretty straight forward.
Just play the game through, and you get 11/12 Achievements.
Get the last one by starting the game again, get to the puzzle that requires you to open a door by 2 people.
You did one of 2 options the first time, now just do the other option, get that Achievement, done.
Exit the game, uninstall to get that 50GB back, and use that for something else now.

So yeah, that's my story and experience with this game, a game I thought to be one thing, but turned out another.
A game I weirdly did enjoy enough to still Recommend, but still want to beat the hell out of if I ever have to play again.

Scorn is a totally unique game that is not for everyone. The environmental storytelling is incredible, the art is jaw-dropping and intricate, the grotesque scenes are picturesque and uncomfortably beautiful. There are many things I would describe as gut-wrenching and disgusting, but as someone who has played countless horror games, I found that to pull me in to the experience even more. I enjoyed the puzzles and figuring out where to go quite a lot. The game does not give a shit about holding your hand as there is no dialog, no hints, you have to pay attention to detail and find your way through this dismal, broken world. I totally loved that about this game. Each level is DENSE and very complex to digest. There's so much to get a grip on in each area, and it feels as if every nook and cranny has been lovingly crafted by a team of fine artists. The gore is abhorrent, the body horror had me reeling and leaning away from the screen. The monstrosities that loom over you in this bleak world are ominous and vaguely sad. Everything drips in the classic art style I've come to understand from East European game developers- a collective consciousness utopia inevitably ending in disaster that is a staple in portraying communist authoritarianism. Games like Stalker, Darkwood and several others also feature this theme, and Scorn portrays it with aplomb. I highly, highly recommend this to fans of other East European sci-fi and horror, you'll likely fall in love with it immediately. 

That being said, the combat is definitely the biggest detractor to the fun I had in this game. The clunky movement and gunplay forced several restarts to some relatively easy to kill enemies, and before you get the shotgun(?), the pistol(?) is very underwhelming. As a horror game with puzzles, it's a fantastic experience and I had a lot of things to reflect on after finishing each chapter about what I had just seen. As a horror game with combat, it's more stiff than the original Silent Hill or Resident Evil in terms of movement. You fire slow, you run slow, you reload slow, and enemies have an unusually good chance of hitting you with attacks, in particular the enemies that look sort of like chickens. The final boss also had an annoying habit of firing 3 grenades but 4 explosions would happen, which killed me multiple times. I was not frustrated by the austerity of the world or puzzles, I was only frustrated by the handful of enemies and the fact that I couldn't quicksave to skip the cutscenes that have to play before each encounter.

No matter if you like this sort of horror
or if you [i][b]like[/b][/i] this sort of horror,
you will probably enjoy this game.

Scorn is an experience, a good and very unique one at that! For me, reviewing Scorn means I should describe and rate its 5 main aspects, which, in my opinion, are the following: 


[u][b]Worldbuilding & atmosphere[/b][/u]
At the forefront of the Scorn experience is its worldbuilding and atmosphere. The world of Scorn has been deliberately and meticulously crafted to be a layered, biomechanical spectacle.

While the surface layer is a vast, barren landscape consisting of little more than an eerily empty desert shrouded in the foggy whispers of death; the sparringly placed (or perhaps simply the few remaining) structures speak tales of a once great civilisation of intelligent humans or humanoid creatures that has abandoned this place long ago. For reasons one can only speculate.

Inside these structures we find elaborate, carefully crafted interiors of mechanical excellence, covered in organic tissue that lives and breathes. Inspired by life and the natural order—birth, death, and rebirth—it is exceptionally fitting that these ancient structures now lie in decay while fleshy, cancerous growths and twisted, hostile lifeforms have overtaken the vast halls and countless chambers once called home by the much more civilised race that originally designed and built it.

With this combination of pristine Alien-looking architecture layered with organic but unwelcoming life thriving in its own way within the remnants of a long-forgotten history, Scorn has managed to make each corner of the world incite a very primal feeling of terror, fear, and a general feeling of unease. Never quite sure what new horror lies around the corner, and yet the only way forward is to push through.


[u][b]Level design[/b][/u]
As one might expect, the worldbuilding directly translates into the level design. Each major area in the world of Scorn feels like one giant organism of interconnected pathways in a labyrinth-like structure. The great level of detail put into every sinister crevice of the world makes for a great exploration experience.

Something I really loved is that on top of this, Scorn does not hold your hand along the way. It is entirely possible to get lost or even miss important areas, though fortunately never in a way that you get stuck later on. This intentional lack of guidance deepens the feeling of being alone in an unforgiving world where nobody is on your side and the only way to survive is to be deliberate and smart with everything you do.


[u][b]Soundtrack & ambient sounds[/b][/u]
Everything mentioned above is compounded by the sound design. The OST—music consisting largely of droning notes and atmospheric background noise with thumping, metallic groans, ritualistic chanting, and more mixed in at the right moments—adds to the dark and unsettling aesthetic of the world around you. Sometimes even the absence of music stirs the feelings of despair and loneliness you'll find yourself become familiar with as you progress through the path laid out before you.

Add the ambient sounds and background noise of this frightening and dangerous realm, and you got yourself a soundscape that grips you tight and deepens your immersion into the world. You never know for sure if the sound you just heard is an active threat, or just an ambient noise of the eroding realm being slowly consumed by a fleshy, organic evil.


[u][b]Gameplay[/b][/u]
Something that struck me by surprise is that Scorn is, at its core, a puzzle game (a genre I love). The physical puzzles aren't too complicated most of the time, but there is a second type of puzzle element: safely traversing the labyrinths. Enemies might crawl in and out of the organic material on the floor and walls, ammo and health is somewhat sparce, blocked pathways have to be cleared, unlockables are sometimes hidden, etc. It all makes for a solid mix of exploration, problem-solving, problem-avoiding, resource management, and occassional combat.

Worth noting is that while as a gamer I'd say the combat and some of the puzzle mechanics feel a bit clunky, as a puzzle and storytelling enthusiast I feel that the way these things are handled makes perfect sense given the biology of who we play as, their state of mind, and the unfamiliar biomechanical nature of every tool or weapon available. It increases the immersion and sense of urgency/danger.


[u][b]Storytelling[/b][/u]
Thankfully there are no quests, marked objectives, dialogue, or other such traditional aspects of a videogame storytelling. However, the storyline is absolutely there if you pay attention to the environment and its inhabitants, the recurring symbolism in all its many forms, and use your imagination to fill in the (intentional) gaps. It's a worthwhile storyline as well, I might add!


[u][b]In conclusion[/b][/u]
• Worldbuilding & atmosphere: rich and beautiful in a hauntingly disgusting way; 11/10
• Level design: perfectly matches the worldbuilding and serves the game's purposes well; 9/10
• Soundtrack & ambient sounds: deeply unsettling, dark, atmospheric; 10/10
• Gameplay: good mix of elements, could be smoother but it adds to the experience; 8/10
• Storytelling: environmental, nuanced but very intentional, minimalistic but profound; 9/10

Scorn isn’t a game. It’s an autopsy of existence performed in real time.
Every corridor pulses like a vein, every machine breathes, and every puzzle feels like an act of self-harm in the name of progress. There’s no dialogue, no guidance, no mercy, just you, a fragile being navigating the carcass of a civilization that long ago fused life and machinery into something both divine and monstrous. The gameplay itself is slow, deliberate, and cruelly tactile, forcing you to touch everything that disgusts you. It’s not about shooting or surviving; it’s about enduring. Every moment reminds you that to move forward, you must surrender a little more of yourself. But what elevates Scorn beyond horror is its philosophical depth. Beneath the layers of flesh and steel lies a mirror and in that reflection, you see humanity’s true nature. We, too, are parasites feeding on our own god, the Earth. Destroying the visible divine while worshiping invisible constructs. As Scorn unfolds, it becomes less a nightmare and more a revelation: that creation and destruction, life and death, progress and decay are all the same process. The ending is devastating, yet fitting. There’s no triumph, only transformation. You don’t win; you become part of the system. It’s the most hauntingly honest ending imaginable because it captures the fate of every living thing: absorption into the cycle. Scorn is an experience for those who look beyond the surface. For those who find beauty in decay and meaning in the void. It’s art, horror, and philosophy merged into one biomechanical prayer. A disturbing masterpiece that doesn’t just show you hell it reminds you that you were born from it.

Scorn: A Horrifying Journey Through Art, Gore, and Confusion

1. Hook
"I entered Scorn expecting puzzles and horror, but I left wondering if my insides were supposed to look like that."

2. Key Features

The atmosphere is a perfect mix of grotesque beauty and why-does-this-room-feel-alive.

Puzzles that make you feel like a genius one moment and an absolute fool the next.

Minimal narrative, but who needs words when the environment screams discomfort at every turn?


3. Personal Experience
At one point, I solved a puzzle and felt unstoppable—until I realized I’d trapped myself in a biomechanical hallway that looked disturbingly like an esophagus. It’s fine. Totally fine.

4. Relatable Humor

Every lever you pull looks like it’s going to do something cool but ends up causing trauma—both in-game and emotional.

The gun looks amazing until you realize reloading feels like assembling Ikea furniture with one hand.

"Is that wall breathing?" is a question you’ll ask yourself far too often.


5. Pro-Con List
Pros:

The art design is both stunning and stomach-turning.

Solving puzzles feels incredibly rewarding (after 45 minutes of crying).

Truly unique; nothing else feels quite this weird and unsettling.


Cons:

There’s no tutorial, so good luck figuring out if that alien tool is a weapon or a dental device.

Walking around makes you feel like you’re trespassing inside someone’s digestive system.

It’s less “horror” and more “existential dread with extra goo.”


6. Final Verdict
Scorn isn’t just a game—it’s an experience that will leave you questioning your humanity and your gag reflex. If you enjoy puzzles, grotesque art, and a complete lack of hand-holding, dive in. Just don’t expect to sleep soundly afterward.

[h1]Wake up. Time to die.[/h1]
Straight up, Scorn is not a game for everyone. It just turns out that this is the perfect game for demented sickos like myself.

The only real critique I have of the game is its price and runtime. The game itself is really only about eight hours give or take (I have a few more hours on the GOG version), which makes it extremely difficult to justify the $60.00 AUD price tag. It is also a shame considering the artbook and soundtrack are also fantastic. Definitely only get this game on a steep discount, especially if you are unsure whether or not you will enjoy this kind of a game.

Scorn also runs perfectly on the Steam Deck. I was playing on the maximum graphics settings with AMD FSR set to performance mode. It both looked fantastic and ran increadibly smooth without any issues or bugs. My only recommendation is to play with some really good headphones, since the audio design should not be missed out on. If you have a Steam Deck, and feel like traumatising the person sitting next to you on the bus, then look no further!

The gameplay itself is very simple. Walking through various scenes and locations broken up between the occasional puzzle and combat encounter. The movements and gunplay are very slow, which might turn a few people off. I did not mind this, but only because I am more adjusted to slower paced shooters anyway.

While on the topic, combat is purposefully cumbersome in this way, and I feel this is where the game loses a lot of people. The majority of players I witnessed seem to have the false impression that they have to kill every single enemy they come across, in the process wasting their scarce resources, and then proceed to complain about ‘forced combat encounters’ when in reality you can theoretically get through most of the game without needing to kill anything. 

Aside from a select few that will encourage combat, the majority of smaller enemies will spawn in on ‘patrol’ and then despawn at the end of their route. If you do not want to waste your valuable health and ammunition, you can simply break line-of-sight and wait for the enemies to move on. If you do decide to engage in combat, get a couple of hits in, run behind cover, let them spit their acid at you, and then repeat. It is dead simple once you get the hang of it.

I do appreciate that there is an animation for almost everything your character does, making the world feel very tactile and real. While I do think part of the intrigue of Giger-esque art is the viewer is only left to speculate what mechanical functions these contraptions have, I think Scorn strikes the perfect balance of intractability with these devices, while still keeping the majority of these machines mysterious. While traditionally gameplay to me is the most important aspect of a video game, I approached this game from the perspective of it being an interactive artbook and was not disappointed in the slightest.

Speaking of which, what can be said about the artstyle that has not been already recited thousands, if not millions of times over? It is gruesomely gorgeous! Wearing the inspirations from both H.R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński on both its sleeves. Despite the obvious comparisons though, I feel that Scorn does retain its own identity apart from both Giger and Beksiński, and that partially comes from the uniquely strange and esoteric universe the developers have built. In true Giger-esque fashion, you will come across various contraptions, devices, and machines that you can only theorise as to their function. Piles of humanoid and not-so-humanoid bodies clambering up the walls, hinting at some greater struggle, extremely Beksiński-like. In this way, it gives the impression that the developers of Scorn both respect Giger and Beksiński and understand their work, in all its cryptic intrigue.

It is because of this reason, that to me, this is where the real horror of the game is. Naturally, horror is a very subjective concept, what might be scary to me might not phase you in the slightest. This game is a perfect example of this, since to me the true horror comes from the atmosphere, the environment, monolithic structures, and glimpses into atrocity. There is something about the strangely familiar yet completely alien environment that Scorn depicts throughout its runtime that fills me with such a unique feeling of dread and unease, unlike any other horror game has managed to capture before.

While there are a few monster enemies scattered throughout the game, they were not the scary part to me. What was scary was the implications that the world and environmental storytelling convey. The horror that gets to me the most is when there are just enough pieces scattered here and there to get your imagination going and inevitably fill in the blanks between them. An audience’s imagination of what something [i]could[/i] be will always be infinitely more terrifying than any writer, director, or designer could say or show it to be.

This is also true for the story, and the greater lore. There is no dialogue to convey the narrative to the player, no recordings, notes, or documents left behind, which I love. Scorn takes the ‘show, do not tell’ philosophy of storytelling to its most literal, leaving only for speculation into the specifics. This removes the inevitable frustration of bogging down the story with long exposition and endless collectable notes to comb through, and simply just [i]shows[/i] you instead. If you do not understand what you are looking at, good. That is the point! Naturally, this kind of story telling should not be applied to [i]everything[/i], it is perfect for Scorn and the world it depicts.

I only wish we could have seen more of the game, especially the last section of the game that takes place in an entirely new location that is distinctly different from the rest of the architecture prior. One can only pray that an eventual sequel or continuation of Scorn will be greenlit someday. I crave to see more of the horrific lore and witness the rest of this dark world the developers have built.

In summary: Scorn is a short game, so get it on sale. It will not be a game for everyone, but if you are a H.R. Giger or Zdzisław Beksiński fan, you will love it. If you are looking for something completely different, immersive, artsy, and esoteric, you will also love this game. Conversely, you will probably not like this game if you are looking for in-depth combat mechanics, fast-paced gameplay, or an easy-to-understand narrative.

If you are on the fence and buy this game on a discount, simply strap yourself in for the ride and just take your time with it. Look around, drink it all in, absorb the atmosphere and the world around you. I think you will be glad you did!

Probably the best immersion of atmosphere that I have ever experienced. It is not a "game" like the others; it is more of a simulation of solitude, with an atmospheric pressure so intense that it becomes difficult to think, hard to breathe, and hard not to get lost. The many landscapes of mechanical bodies blur love, war, procreation, the art of giving life, and taking it away. The enormous buildings induce vertigo—what are these nurseries, often transformed into slaughterhouses? By combining Zdzisław Beksiński's work with Hans Ruedi Giger's, a new dimension is created in their art, as if they were destined to meet, with one being nothing without the other, as if they were formed from the same skin.

The atmosphere in Scorn is suffocating, eerie, and profoundly alien. There is no dialogue, no guiding narration—only the sound of wet, pulsing textures, bone creaks, and distant groans. The absence of music amplifies the sense of dread, replacing it with ambient biological sounds that make the world feel alive, or perhaps dying.

This is the perfect biochemical purgatory, with a striking similarity to H.R. Giger's Necronomicon artworks.

“H.R.Geiger the Game” is the shortest way one could describe [b]Scorn[/b].

[h1]X-Factor[/h1]
Of course, the main draw of this title is its aesthetic, everything is biomechanical, the environment, contraptions and creatures built with bone, flesh and sinew.

Also spotting Ambiental sounds rather than a full-on soundtrack to keep you immersed in its eerie world.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The shooter elements are light and focus on bullet economy, often pushing you to avoid enemies when you can.

The puzzles are what’s required to progress from one area to the other and showcase the many biological interfacing and animation of the aesthetics.

[h1]Story[/h1]
Is there one?
You tell me as it’s almost all ambiental storytelling where everything in the environment looks suspiciously like a phallus.

But it makes you feel immersed in an alien setting where these things may be the norm for them but quite strange for us.

[h1]Downsides[/h1]

The immersion is many times broken by how unnecessary the process to access the next area is.
For example I had to pick a shelled creature from a grid place it in a tray, attach a clamp to it, put it in another machine that would cut it out of its shell, drag the creature to a hole in a wall to give it another clamp on its hand, drag it into a room where I jammed its hand into a meat console.
Why did I do all of this?
Just to open a door...
Even worse, in many cases you could’ve just squeezed through the gaps that gate you of from the next section or vault over using a very climbable surface.

Another criticism is that it didn’t fully take advantage of the setting, many times I didn’t “feel” like I was inside a biomechanical being despite looking like one.
The many elevators, flat floors, consoles, handrails, and guns made it look like the game was set in a spaceship that just happens to have an organic look to it.

The creature variety that you can interact with in the shooter part of the game is almost nonexistent and some puzzles are poorly communicated.

Also a very blueballing ending to boot, I’m sure people wouldn’t mind much some of the flaws it Scorn had a satisfying conclusion

[h3]TL;DR: Two things Scorn will leave in the history of video games: the imaginative memories of its unsettling art, and one of the worst examples of game design ever. [/h3]

H.R. Giger, you all know him. Maybe not by name, maybe you've never seen any of his work, but I really think the design of the Alien is in the collective imagination, even for those who haven't seen the films.
In addition to revisiting Giger, you should also discover Zdzisław Beksiński, another lovely artist with a troubled life and works that make your hair stand on end.

Combine the devastating and disheartening sensations of these two artists, animate them with the "body horror" by David Cronenberg, spine-chilling audio effects, a first-person survival horror gameplay, and the environmental storytelling made famous by the "Souls" series.

If you have enough imagination, you're already frightened and/or excited, and you should be, because [b]Scorn is truly one of the most impactful and chilling immersive experiences I've ever played.[/b]

It was actually an almost obvious idea - to make a video game using an insane imagination like Giger's - but it had never been done before.

I won't tell you anything about the game or the plot itself: it lasts about 7 hours, and it's an experience you HAVE to try.

Unfortunately, for some damned reason, at a certain point, the game designer of Scorn decides that [b]instead of creating an epoch-making masterpiece of survival horror that would set the standard for eternity, they prefer to make a bad FPS.[/b]

Including weapon combat in a game of this kind was truly one of the most unfortunate choices I've ever seen in my forty-year experience career as a gamer, and I see that on the internet, nearly everyone agrees unanimously.

To make you understand: most of the game you'll be using a single weapon, namely a tool with a moving part that acts as a plunger, and which can also be used to strike enemies.
It shoots two shots in succession, then it needs an infinitely long time (in terms of FPS) to reload, and the average enemy requires 3 shots to be taken down.
Add to this the protagonist's very poor movement agility (for obvious reasons you'll discover while playing) and the inability to make a decent circular strafe, and - icing on the cake - the checkpoint saving system that will force you to repeat entire minutes of slow walks and animations after each death (fascinating the first time but monotonous from the third onwards).

However... if you have the patience to overcome the really heavy frustration of the second chapter, the game then closes with a breathtaking third one that will leave you with a persistent sensation under your skin, and goosebumps all over your body that will return every time you think back to it.

It's not little, but if I think about what it could have been, I kick myself (an action that was probably considered normal in the world of Scorn).

It's a deeply visual narrative and while that's interesting in its own merits, the overly designed levels might also make you feel lost pretty quickly, which might be the point, but a very big turn off to some. But if you are willing to go deep and explore and find out how things work on your own, then this might be a very intriguing experience.

About the narrative, it is overall very simple. The character wants to get from point A to point B. But the motives behind his actions, the background story, the worldbuilding and the reasons for all you see are left VERY ambiguous and if that's not your thing, another turn off. If you enjoy some cosmic horror mixed with body horror and like to think that the ambiguity of it all that makes it scary and fun, then this might be your thing. The narrative will leave you wondering... A lot. A LOT. If you have 10 questions, it will answer one of them, and leave half-answered two, and the rest, it will leave them behind quietly while it takes you forward. Maybe asking the "WHYs" isn't the point, and getting the "BECAUSE's" is far from being it either.

Just enjoy the ride. Enjoy the nightmarish visuals. The violence, the body horror, the linguering disturbing questions. The suggestive horror. The game might not be scary in a traditional sense, but it'll sure make you disturbed by what it has to show you... As well by what it doesn't show, or tell you. It's a cool a experience, but like I said, not a rewarding or pleasant one. 

I'm recommending because, despite its faults (and a very annoying bug towards the end that made me restart the level), I found myself intrigued, immersed and interested in a way very few games did. If you like that sort of stuff, then go for it.

If you want something more traditional, this might disappoint you a lot.

[b]In-depth -[/b] So imagine if HR Geiger and Alex Grey were the art directors for an atmospheric horror video game and you would get Scorn. Have played video games for the better part of three decades and I have never played anything quite like this game. From start to finish; everywhere you look, everything you do, every single step of the way you are confronted with horrifying imagery that keeps you unsettled and grossed out for the duration of the game.

Everything you think you know about video games is wrong when you play Scorn. There are no tutorials. There is not a single word spoken. There is no "music" only horrific ambiance that is used for dramatic effect and for unsettling you with shear silence. There is only a minute Heads Up Display and in fact it's more of a heads down display. Everything is unsettling and grotesque, literally e v e r y t h i n g. The weapons; the enemies, the viscera laden bio-mechanical technology all around you, the main character, the story, the actions you must undertake to progress, anything at all that you see anywhere at anytime might make you want to hurl.

On the other hand, after you really start taking it all in and noticing what the theme is, the game really starts to shine with an unforeseen splendor that you were too horrified to notice before. The cohesion of everything I mentioned above and how every single speck unifies with and adheres to the theme, transform this into a gestalt that was clearly crafted using an elegantly horrific design.

The story itself is also not traditional and you're going to have to make up your own mind about what happens but be forewarned that the ending is not for everyone. Other than that I truly enjoyed what it took to get through this game. It really feels like a task was completed after the emotional price I paid to progress in this game. The story does a fantastic job of elevating the main themes here by making you really feel the weight of your actions and it does so in many different ways. It is painfully emblematic of the famous Thomas Sowell quote: "There are no solutions. There are only trade-offs"

These non-traditional and unique choices will also likely turn off a lot of players and, I would almost recommend using a guide unless you are someone that wants to go in blind but, be forewarned you are going to be punished for thinking that this game is like any other video game. The games is not very intuitive or easy to understand so getting lost is a near certainty.
What a wild ride. Not for the squeamish; but one of the most creative things I've seen in awhile.

[h1]Poetically morbid[/h1]
Should you happen to have at least a passing interest in narrative techniques, you’ve probably come across the rule of “show, don’t tell”. As in the room isn’t just dark, it is the faint ember of a candle barely letting your eyes to make out the outline of the door on the other end. The idea being that the exposition is significantly more compelling when the viewer can experience the scene rather than be given dry statements to accept as facts. This notion is arguably even more vital to visual medium of filmmaking. Would you rather be told by narrator or other characters that the hero is an experienced fighter or watch an action scene proving the point? The answer is rather obvious.

Many games, including the title of the day, are beyond a shadow of a doubt cinematic experiences with little beside interaction and the viewer immersion to distinguish between one medium and the other. Despite being avidly visual in nature, Scorn takes the idea of “show, don’t tell” to its extreme end and to deliver what I deem to be one of the most profound gaming experiences I’ve had in years. Without uttering a single word.

[b]Living, breathing world[/b]
Scorn unceremoniously dumps the player onto the surface of an alien world. Literally, without preamble or a warning, the protagonist falls to the ground and thus the journey begins. A single glance at the surroundings is enough to tell this is not a place of warmth and safety. Everything is organic – the walls are shaped out of bones, joint together by muscle and sinew, wet and glistening as if the tissue was freshly exposed. While the grotesque bio-machinery is undeniably alive, the place is otherwise forebodingly empty with only dark ambient and occasional pulse heard from behind a wall to keep the player company during these first steps.

In short, Scorn leaves it up to your eyes and imagination to make a sense of your surroundings and you will take away from the experience as much as you choose to. Whether you focus entirely on navigating the ossified corridors or dedicate additional time to explore, is left entirely at your discretion. Truth be told the game’s morbid aesthetic is not for everyone, nonetheless this title is undeniably crafted with an exquisite attention to detail. Be it monumental structures, perpetual faint mist or discreet soundtrack – Scorn’s atmosphere is thick enough to be carved out with a knife.

[b]Watch and learn[/b]
Before anyone gets an impression that Scorn is a glorified walking simulator, fret not. This title is foremost a puzzle, made all the better by its alienating style of delivery. Luckily, while the HUD is kept to the absolute minimum as to allow for maximum immersion, crucial hints like health bar or objective marker can be brought up, should the player need them. Furthermore, even in its visual storytelling, this title doesn’t leave you entirely without guidance. Most of the progress is hindered by some manner of closed door, giving a plain indication that some interaction with nearby bio-machinery is needed to unlock the way forward. To give credit where it is due – the puzzles are complex enough to feel satisfying to solve.

As soon as you get used to general gist of forging the path ahead, you will learn that you are not alone in here. For better or worse, Scorn steps in to give the player an extra hand in form of a weapon. The bizarre device utilizes interchangeable endings to serve as both a tool and a gun, capable of warding off creatures inhabiting fleshy overgrowths strewn across the facility. Combat element hardly switches the pace to that of an action title though. To be fair, fighting is quite awkward and rather unforgiving. Resupply stations are few and far between and mostly it is a wiser idea to sneak around threats rather than confront them directly. Assuming the claustrophobic corridors of the facility will leave enough room to remain hidden.

[b]From Switzerland, with love[/b]
While they are lacklustre at times, the game mechanics of Scorn sufficiently set it apart from walking simulators. Then again, this title is primarily a visual experience, to the point where I am tempted to compare the sensation to visiting a virtual art gallery. One entirely dedicated to a certain swissman by the name of Hans Rudolf Giger, an artist best known for designing the Xenomorph of the Alien franchise. Although the pitch-black menace is by far the best known among Giger’s works, the most prevalent theme of his art would be all manner of bio-mechanical constructs. Those consistently incorporating human body as just another component. Often in a manner evocative of a sexual act mind you, giving an unnerving, visceral quality to the stylistic. Taking into account Scorn is essentially a 6 hour-long love letter to this very aesthetic, the game is directed exclusively towards mature audience.
[url]https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3359719151[/url]
Whether you consider the distinct art direction of Scorn virtue or vice is a matter of taste. What is arguably a master’s stroke is how this visceral quality has been integrated into the gameplay. Dubbed by the developers “full body awareness” is a set of impressively detailed and realistic animations accompanying any environmental interaction. Most importantly to the gameplay loop, these allow the player to keep inspecting the condition of their avatar, as to put things bluntly, progressing through the game is going to hurt. This title doesn’t hand out a key, to operate the door controls – it grafts one directly onto your hand’s underside leaving your appendage bleeding in the process.

[b]Polarizing abstraction[/b]
For all of my fondness to Scorn’s visual prowess, I have to admit this is an utterly alienating experience. As mentioned previously, the game does not utter a word, also meaning not a shred of explanation is given to the player. In my book, unyielding dedication to atmosphere is a boon, however I can wholeheartedly understand the critics, who give up on a title seemingly devoid of objective. Likewise, apart from the gun designs, the combat is largely underwhelming. I am glad it is there though, for sheer diversity it brings to the table. Without it, this title would’ve overstayed its welcome long before the credits roll.

Ultimately, I acknowledge Scorn as a mixed bag, nonetheless I fell head over heels for its visuals and atmosphere. Perhaps I had to grit my teeth a little throughout the middle part of the game, although I am more than happy to have done so as once the developers play their hand during the final act, it is gruesomely majestic. Bearing in mind this title is primarily a visceral feast for the eyes, I can easily recommend Scorn to any horror fan, willing to pick a game for distinct visuals. However, should you happen to be a type who values gameplay over the [i]artsy-fartsy[/i] nonsense (which is perfectly understandable standpoint) don’t come anywhere near this title since it will flatout let you down as soon as the initial impact of its brutality subsides.

[h1] Interesting Puzzle Game in Desperate Need of a UX Designer [/h1]

I [i] really [/i] tried to enjoy this game, and I'll keep trying, but this game is perhaps the best example of why "User Experience" designers are important. 

This game has a very barebones aesthetic in terms of UI and Storytelling, and at first it seems to work really well. There's basically no formal narrative, the story/lore is very subtle and plays out through the environment and puzzles, and no tutorial. That's not a problem, however, because piecing together what the game expects you to do is intuitive... in the first 30 minutes. 

When you first encounter an interactable object, a circle with a dash through it appears and you get an "error" SFX when you try to interact with it. Then when you encounter an item you [i]can[/i] interact with, the circle appears "filled" and has no line. The game teaches you that when you see these circles, you know whether or not you can interact. Then, when you finally solve your first major puzzle room, there's this sense of accomplishment that you were able to figure it out without any help. It's great! Then you move on to the next major puzzle room...

WELL LO AND BEHOLD, the game breaks its own rules on the second puzzle. Both circles appear on the same interactable object at varying times, but neither of them work and there's no "error" SFX when you do try to interact when you can't. So within 1 hour the user interface just starts lying to you. Then, when you finally do solve the puzzle, it opens a door that leads to...

A dead end. With nothing there. Nothing to interact with. Nowhere to progress. You're stuck in a room with nothing to do.

I'll keep playing, but something so egregiously dumb as switching what your UI means within the first hour of the game (without telling the player and leading them to think the game is broken) coupled with a cutscene of a door opening that leads nowhere is pants-on-head dumb design. 

Note for the devs: For your next game, hire someone that knows what a good user experience looks like.

There are a few problems with the game even when considering the "Universe" as the main  "concept" of the game. Typically, you can't have such a poor sound design if the goal is to catch the players into your atmosphere. I understand that we are living on a silly and dying world, but even in such a case, musics and soundtracks can be used. You can introduce travelling point of view or cinematic to highlight the landscape or peculiar elements of the decor. Finally, you can put discret texts hidden in the levels (such as drawings on the wall) that would help the players to "get" the story you want to tell.

1. You will like the game for the visuals, and that alone will be enough to carry your enjoyment for $40.
2. You won't like the game, and the visuals are the only compensation for what is otherwise a game dragged down by a developer's pursuit for art over playability.

Those are the two possibilities for you. If you like graphics, and are a graphics fiend, I guess you'll enjoy it. I admit, the game looks good, for a while (not sure why, but, for me, rainbow colored polygons started replacing the textures of the environment mid-playthrough -- I've refunded the game so I don't know how much worse or better it would have gotten). It seemed to get worse the more stuff I unlocked. And that's especially annoying since the game is so driven by its visuals.

Detailed Opinions (no spoilers): 
           The game is relying too heavily on a dedication of time that just isn't worth its weight in substance.

           The environment is truly great. That's the only real praise you'll read of it. It's so great that you want to explore every inch of the world you're in. But I couldn't. The game was so closed off from itself, you can't explore anything beyond the boundary it limits you to, which makes it seem like your walking a tight rope over an open valley. You are so painstakingly limited by the linear structure of the story and the map boundaries (which is supposed to keep you moving forward, but boringly-so), that I feel like the developers shot themselves in the foot by taking away the player's freedom to look deeper into the detailed world they created, which is a damn shame. The world is practically begging to be explored, only for you to be cut off by the developers to keep you along their boring and confusing plot. 
           After a point, I stopped wanting to explore and really dedicated the focus to just progressing through the game itself. But nope. I got through the first three sections and I realized the game is just a waste of my money. The gameplay takes away any story they had made with it's bounded structure and it tries to excuse itself with mini-puzzles. It literally felt like I was only walking around, doing random, inexplicable puzzles, and the only reward was a new environment that was just as disappointing as the last. If all you want is to walk through a detailed world and look at it from afar, in motion blur madness, then I guess this game is for you. I just don't think it's worth $40, and I don't think it's fun or enriching in any capacity.
