Man, this one is... really tough. I've been following along since the game's kickstarter, which I found out about within a few weeks of it closing. Through the devs being general assholes about backers asking for more than one update a year. And all the trailers and announcements since. I was hyped; I'm a huge fan of both Giger and Beksiński and this game, at almost every point, feels like you're playing or moving through one of their paintings (by which I mean, original, uncensored, penis/vagina/breast Giger, too here).

In Scorn, you'll find an atmosphere unlike any other game you've played. You'll find an ambient sound track that fits it perfectly, and a world designed insanely well, that's so alien to you that you'll struggle to understand the basic function or purpose behind more than half the biomechanical structures and constructs you'll find throughout the game. And I think this is what Scorn is best at. Which sort of sucks, as nothing about this best part has anything to do with being a videogame. You can do every last bit of it in a movie.

You might notice my playtime, and that's about half of my issue with the game. Leading up to release, Ebb said the game would take between 10-14 hours to complete, which is great--that's the average length of most horror games, like Amnesia Rebirth, Soma, Resident Evil 7 & 8. About two weeks before launch, Ebb mentioned in an interview the game would be between 8-10 hours, which is a significant difference from what was said before, but still isn't world endingly short. The final duration you see from my play count is actually longer than the full length of the game; I actually restarted it to get the single missable achievement the game has, and had to replay an entire act. [b]You're looking at a game that will take between 3 and 5 hours for most people to play.[/b]

The other gripe I have with Scorn is gameplay. The gunplay is bad, half baked and doesn't really need to be in the game. The puzzles are really, really simplistic and you probably won't find yourself stuck on them all too often. That said, I should mention I was raised on Myst, Riven, Gabriel Knight and the Crystal Key, so my bar for what constitutes a puzzle, much less a challenging one, may be higher than most. 

At the end of the game, Scorn felt worth the experience, but wholly unlike what the game was sold as. It's barely a game, the combat is a bad kind of jank, requiring you save ammo for only one of the three enemy types in the game while you run in circles hitting enemies with the melee weapon, and waiting for it to recharge. I would recommend waiting for a sale; at $40 this is a really tough sell, especially with games like Amnesia Rebirth (which starts at $5 cheaper and is twice as long, with actual gameplay), SOMA (which is one of my favorite games ever, is twice as long, and $10 cheaper), Resident Evil 7 (which has gameplay, is twice as long, and will actually scare you, unlike Scorn, which is more of a creeping dread without any scares) and Resident Evil 8, which while not as scary as 7, has a bunch of replayability through its other modes.

I wouldn't recommend Scorn unless you can get it for $20 or less.

The combat adds nothing of value to the game, actively turns the atmosphere from dour to infuriating, and should have been removed altogether.

I hadn't heard of scorn before it's launch, so I didn't have any previous expectations going in. I saw like 2 minutes of video showcasing the visual style and immediately stopped watching to avoid any spoilers when I realized I wanted to actually play the thing myself. So what I did know going in is that Scorn was a puzzle game with some slow combat. Something like Myst in H.R. Giger-land with some guns for flavor. 

Scorn is like 1/4 of one of those things. It nails visual and audio presentation. It looks and feels like taking a tour through a Giger landscape. There's the good. Now the bad-ish.

 It has too few puzzles to be a full on puzzle game. Most of the "puzzling" is which way did I want this elevator to go. There are a few "proper" puzzles, but if you went in expecting something in the vein of an old school puzzle/adventure game, then you'd be disappointed with the number and complexity. 

 Then it has too little combat to be a full on shooter. You don't see your first enemy until about halfway through if you're moseying through to see the sights. And oh boy is combat clunky. Not because it's slow. Which it is and isn't. It almost made it. The few weapons are melee, revolver equivalent, shotgun equivalent, and grenade launcher. Grenade launcher sounds great, but you only get it at the end and use it to solve "puzzles". Shoot grenade to break the chain to open the door. Like 3 times. 

Melee has 2 charges and recharges extremely slow. Actually everything does. Which wouldn't be a problem, but they don't feel powerful enough to justify it. If you give me 3 enemies at once, which is a lot for Scorn. And I have to use 4 out of 6 shots to kill 1 of the enemies and then switch to Melee. But melee takes 4 hits to kill the doggos and only has a charge of 2. So you have to dance around dodging acid spits while it recharges, which wouldn't be a problem, BUT you move at like 3/4 of the speed required to dodge. The range on the doggo spit is longer than the visual, so you'll think you're safe, then lose 3 bars of health. The little spitters basically have auto-aim unless you get around a corner, which isn't always available, and chargers Exist.

The point being that it feels bad to never finish a fight better off than you started it. I didn't get through a combat encounter once in the entire game without losing a way bigger chunk of health than was comfortable. And the nearest health station for more ampules, might be 30 minutes away. And maybe I'm just bad at it, but then I couldn't avoid it.

Whoever said you could avoid combat was a motherfucking liar. Here's how enemy AI worked for me. If I get close enough to the spawn point to trigger aggression, they'll follow me a set distance. If I go backwards out of that distance the way I came in, they'll despawn and the cycle repeats when I get close to the trigger again. If I go forwards I die because there's a door in the way and you can't dodge for shit. Coupled with things just getting spawned behind you half the time for the lolz. I'm looking directly at that hallway that spawns bulls in-front of AND behind-you at the same time, but only AFTER you go down the hallway, which is a dead end to get the health refill down there. Actual bullshit.

So no matter which side of gameplay you enjoy more, there's not enough substance and too much funk and the two sides DO NOT mesh well together. Scorn would have been a better game if it was all puzzler. It also would have been a better game if it was all shooter with tighter mechanics and better level design for that type of gameplay. It also would have been a better game if they just cut all gameplay elements besides walking through the fantastic landscape their art team made. Nobody wins here.

Which funny enough is the moral of the game. Which I think is some Grade-A Bullshit. The first character doesn't win, so he decides to make sure the second character doesn't win so we all have to go down in this dying hell-scape together. Spend half the game fighting with this parasite, finally get rid of it at the end and then he just swoops back in deus-ex-machina style at the very last second. You get a "fuck you, nobody wins, doesn't that suck" 30 second cutscene and then get kicked back to the menu. It honestly feels unfinished. Like they switched it up and cut so many things over the course of development and whoever had control at the end just made up this cop-out ending at the last minute. 

With more development and expanding on the theme, it could have worked. But it didn't and I finished the game just kind of disappointed with every aspect except for the parts where I got to just walk around looking at the world.

Scorn is a tragedy.

You can already guess how this review will go, I will praise the tone and atmosphere. Which I absolutely will, credit where credit is due. But Scorn's flaws are too numerous and large to overlook. It's a game that I think people will continue to look back on or point toward as one with its own captivating visual style in a sea of bland first person shooters. What Scorn manages to accomplish with it's environments is an amazing feat of game engineering and design.

But the flaws that Scorn has are too deep and numerous to overlook. The game is very short and too deficient in most of the criteria you would judge a game by.

It's puzzles are both too simple to be truly engaging to the level they have the potential to reach and also criminally few and far between. In the game, depending on what you consider "puzzles," I would say I recall there being about 3, and none of those I felt really engaged you past something in the ballpark of minigame or quicktime event. While I didn't think that the game was going to have Destiny gunplay or anything, the unknown world and its mysteries seemed to be a setup that lent itself heavily towards environmental puzzles or more complex activities where you need to decipher how to use an interface, or item, or machine to proceed. And indeed the puzzles in the game do have a lot to do with using the latent technology of the areas, but a lot of these are straightforward sequences where you just interact with something and it kind of does what it needs to by itself. Scorn seems to be so afraid of explaining any of its world to anyone that it would rather have puzzles solve themselves than allow you to delve into it. One of them it moving objects with a crane, and well, everyone knows what a crane is. This is a thing we do in our own world. No one can extrapolate anything about Scorn from the operation of a crane. Many of the other puzzles are likewise.

The combat... The combat is so bad I want a hand-written apology for it from the developers. Again, I didn't have any high hopes for it to begin with, but I would say its inclusion actually takes away from the game rather than add to it, its poor quality feels like it was a feature checkbox that needed to be checked, that maybe if it had no combat the creators of the game worried that this would not draw a large enough crowd, and I guess I can't fault them for that, but combat almost doesn't even fit into the world of Scorn hardly. It's an exception, a thing that you do not see recreated or even hinted at very much in the bleak setting except for when it finally culminates in what may be gaming's worst boss fight ever. Curiously, while the puzzles and other aspects of the game jealously guard information about Scorn's settings, the weapons overflow with intriguing ideas about the world-- the tooth bullets, the flower-like pods that hold both ammo and health, the unique "weapon switching" all have little things to say about Scorn's world, which is why it's so surprising how underwhelming it is. I wonder if the creators of the game had things they wanted to communicate but had no other avenue than the weapons?

But the worst aspect of Scorn is that it doesn't say enough. The "story" of the game is only a story in so much as it is a recollection of events and nothing more. When you play Scorn, you know that things designed so meticulously must be that way for a reason. But unfortunately, for the most part this information is kept secret. The thing that frustrated me the most was that Scorn can be so captivating and have such a rich world, but go to great lengths to keep you from being able to appreciate the deepness and richness of the lore. I have heard that an edition of the game comes with an art book that has notes on the setting, and to my knowledge this is the most information about the game and any of its creatures or places. That in order to even know the names of these places, you'd need an add-on item from a more premium edition of the game I think says everything that needs to be said. I empathize with how hard it must be to try and communicate and specific information in this game without ruining immersion. Like can you imagine how jarring it would be to be walking around a rib-cage like hallway of curved bone structures and then suddenly see a big sign that says "Factory This Way." Or maybe they are more interesting in sparking conversation without confirming anything is interpreted correctly or incorrectly. But there are way more methods they could have used to talk about this game that they declined to use. Why not have the first playthrough be as it is now, and then add a "New Game+" type of mode that includes commentary? That way you could protect the experience of the first time through but still let people become engrossed in the lore and touch on some of the intentions of the game. But we don't even get that. And of all the things that hurt this game, I think that the game is so secretive about things that are worth knowing and talking about is the greatest flaw of all.

[b] The Positives [/b]
The atmosphere is probably the best part of this game. The entire game takes place in an ungodly biomechanical hell that always seems to have a new level of "what in the god damn?" to throw at you. This along with the surprisingly well put together animation leads to a pretty unique experience all things considered. This however, is where the positives end.

[b] The Negatives [/b]
Scorn isn't actually a game, it is an interactive walking simulator. Despite being given the "Puzzle" tag, this game has only one actual puzzle in it. It also only has one non-linear decision in it. Both of these come within the first act of the game, meaning you experience the most "Game" Scorn has to offer within the first 20 minutes. While there is shooting in this game, it's completely unnecessary since you can run past the majority of encounters. Even if you did want to fight, there's no point since the gun mechanics are incredibly janky and unsatisfying. Towards the end, I found myself more annoyed by Scorn than entertained or amazed. 

[b] Conclusion [/b]
In conclusion, if Scorn was a $15 game, I wouldn't be too disappointed. But since it's an outrageous $40 for what is a literal walking simulator with a highly misleading steam store page description, I am indeed very disappointed. If you have absolutely nothing better to do and enjoy this kind of horror experience, then this game is certainly worth your time. But for $40? it'll never be worth your money.

Scorn is a mixed bag.

PROS
+The game is beautiful in a disgusting way.
+The game is disturbing, just like it wants to be.


MIDDLE
- No dialogue and almost no text. This isn't something that breaks the game, but they didn't compensate for these limits elsewhere. Detailed below.



CONS
-The visual design for puzzles is terrible. It's hard to distinguish what is an interactable element or not. The worst is an egg puzzle early on that really, really doesn't explain itself. With no text or dialogue, visual design was even more important for a game with puzzles, but it feels like they made this part bad on purpose, to spite the player. The corridors also all look the same and it's very easy to get lost, especially during the puzzle underneath the big guy about 2/3 through.

-The storytelling is pretty mixed.

-The art-book is essential for understanding plot elements, but the digital version got downgraded after people had purchased it, which is one of the most consumer unfriendly decisions I've heard in a while.

-The save-points system is abysmal. Dying can send you way back and you have to go through a lot of nonsense to get back there.

-If you get behind on resources, like bullets or healing items, you are behind for the rest of the game. Missing a few shots is enough for this to happen.

-There is a lot of audio clutter, especially around the parasite that is on your back. Every hour or so, it screams at you, you look down and the parasite punches your guts. Also, this is unavoidable damage that can kill you, which is a terrible design choice and forced me to restart a chapter because healing is very limited.

-The boss fight takes way too long and is very repetitive, which is extra frustrating because of the previously mentioned check points garbage.


OVERALL
Scorn is a game that makes almost every decision against the player. It's a game that wants you to feel as much torment as the character you're playing as and expects you to like it. Scorn is a game that hates that it's a game and wants to watch the world burn.

One of the most dichotomous opinions of a game I've had in a really long time.

As a *video game*, this is astoundingly cruddy. Inherently sluggish/frustrating combat even by survival horror standards is compounded in seemingly every way the developers tried to imagine - often not enough room to strafe to dodge projectiles, supremely annoying checkpointing, missable weapons before points of no return that the game later expects you to have (yes, I had to reload from an earlier chapter), no manual saving, a couple of instances of bugged enemy behavior that necessitate particularly tedious stealth/chase sequences, not even any degree of enemy variety to look at, and one pair of back-to-back fights against two identical elites one after the other, after which you're very possibly drained of health refills and then are required to repeatedly damage yourself in order to finish the next sequence.

The worst part of all of it is that this is such a masterwork of visual design and atmosphere and mood, such a singular piece of interactive art, that it had no need whatsoever of any video game DNA, let alone any so poorly shoveled in as to undignifiedly regurgitate all over itself and nearly spoil the entire experience.

If you have a strong appetite for artwork even attempting to approach the likes of Giger or Beksinski, you unfortunately still owe it to yourself to walk the halls and see the sights of Scorn. The long development time shines in every facet of its presentation, and I can just about guarantee you've never seen a game like it, never found yourself surrounded by this particular brand of mesmerizing hellscape. If, however, that in itself does not *acutely* excite you and you still expect to enjoy Scorn as a *video game* in order to feel your money was justifiably spent, I can confidently say you can pass on it.

If you are still onboard, I offer just a few pointers in hopes that it will mitigate/eliminate for you the undue misery that in no small part made up my experience:

- The two most common enemy types are introduced one right after the other. These two types will almost always slink away into some hole avoiding combat altogether if you keep your distance and avoid them for a moment or two.

- Keep your eye out for weird interfaces on walls. Be sure that you have looked around every room in the general area before moving forward. Don't miss weapons.

- Make sure weapons are reloaded before using ammo stations.

- In actuality the 'hurt yourself' stretch is not as bad as it seems like it's going to be; you don't have to be as infuriated and incredulous at the audacity of even such an idea as I was when I ran into it. You'll probably be fine.

I'd really like to, but it feels like the bad just barely edges out the good.

Let's start with the good first.  The visuals are fantastically done.  Scorn shines in the artistry.  The team nailed it there.  Everything looks fantastic.  The H.R. Geiger aesthetic has not been handled better since Aliens in my opinion, and you can see the attention to detail is present everywhere.  Performance is also fantastic.  I'm playing on outdated hardware and it's very smooth.  The team made Unreal Engine 4 behave very nicely.

Sound is a bit so-so.  The effects sounds are fine, but for an atmospheric game I feel there was not enough effort spent on the soundscape.  There is some immersive ambience as opposed to music, but It just felt a bit lacking in that department.

There are puzzles that must be solved for progression, and this has its upsides and downsides as well.  In one sense, some of the puzzles are very clever in their execution.  You have to move real-world objects around to progress, not just "find key to open door", though there certainly is an equivalent of that present here.  The only really annoying puzzle is found early on where you have to slide some "eggs" around on a wall to release the correct one into a machine.  It's just a tedious variation of a "slide the blocks" puzzle.  The other puzzles do not hold your hand in any way.  You MUST figure everything out on your own.  This might be a turn-off to some players as some of the puzzles are not entirely intuitive.  There's a bit of real-world problem solving involved.  On the other hand, the progression is fairly linear so if you're stuck on something it's not to far to backtrack to figure out what you're doing wrong, and once you've solved it, you know for certain that you've solved it.

Combat is where things start to get a bit lackluster.  There are only five types of enemies - including the "boss" fight near the end, and your weapons are woefully inadequate.  For the weapons, there's a melee weapon that doubles as a key.  It can "fire" two shots before needing to recharge.  It's basically a captive piston, and it's pretty weak.  There is a pistol that can hold six shots, and it takes a long time to aim it effectively, but it's also very weak.  The shotgun is VERY powerful, but holds only three shots, and finally there is a grenade launcher.  Unfortunately by the time you get the grenade launcher you use it in exactly one fight, which happens immediately after acquiring it, and after that it's really only used to solve three environmental puzzles.  You can carry only a very small amount of reserve ammo for any weapon, and the refilling stations for health and ammo are very scarce and typically become exhausted after a single interaction.

The enemy types consist of a stationary tentacle that can fling acid at you, a crawling meat sack that will try to vomit acid on you at close range, a smaller meat sack with... baby bird wings?... that will spit a glob of acid at you VERY accurately from a distance, a larger quadrupedal meat sack that will charge like a bull and takes a full magazine from anything to put down, and finally a cybernetic monstrosity that serves as the end boss.  

The combat overall is soured by the fact that the weapons are largely ineffective against the enemies, coupled with the fact that health and ammo is incredibly scarce, so there is zero margin for error.  To fire a weapon you must hold down an "aiming" key, and for the pistol to hit with any degree of accuracy you have to STAND COMPLETELY STILL while aiming, which gives the evil little chicken things plenty of time to land one or two shots on you, which severely depletes your health.  In addition, by the time you get the pistol you're likely to be facing three enemies at a time.  Aiming takes an eternity, reloading takes an eternity, and to avoid getting hit you MUST sprint, and guess what you can't do while sprinting?  Seasoned FPS players will find this frustrating beyond belief.  Combine that with the fact that there are specific cut scenes that involve your life being drained by a full bar as part of the story progression, and if you're left with almost no health after a fight the subsequent cinematic could end you.  Fighting the boss is a bit unintuitive as well, making it easy to waste precious ammo unnecessarily.

The worst bit, however, is the ending.  It's painfully clear how the game had to be cut and its ending tacked on.  Very little is explained or made clear as to why anything is happening, and from what I've read, some of this is explained in the art book as having been kept deliberately vague, but once you get to the ending it feels like the entire thing was a colossal waste of time.  It's not simply the fact that it is a negative ending - that's a common trope within the sci-fi horror genre.  What bothered me is that it felt lazy, or at least rushed, in its execution.  It was definitely a "That's IT?" moment.  Ending a game on a negative note is one thing.  Ending it on disappointment is another matter.

After my own experience, I wish I could recommend Scorn due to the effort involved in creating a very visually immersive environment, but that in and of itself just doesn't seem to be enough to justify the time spent playing through.  It's a largely empty world with very difficult and tedious combat midway through and some puzzles that can be fairly tough at times.  If you can see past the downsides the visuals are fantastically executed.  That being said, it feels a bit unfinished.  Scorn definitely needed more time to complete and a lot more polish to be what it could have been.

I tried hard to love this game...and I did! But I can't recommend it, not without some major caveats.

First things first: the look and feel of the game, its environment, lighting, and sound design, are 11/10. Ebb absolutely killed it and I'm happy they took as long as they did to do so. Fans of Giger, Beksinski, and Cronenberg will be drawn to this game for obvious reasons. In Scorn, your feeble, tormented character wanders around a cold, disgusting, biomechanical superstructure, a monumental and unwelcoming presence which wholly envelops you, making you feel like a speck of dust: small, forgotten, hopeless, and insignificant. Sickening machines of unknown purpose stand ominously next to piles of gore. The croaks and gurgles of ungodly creatures echo through the skeletal halls. Everything you see and interact with is hideous and captivating, in the best way. I'm not only impressed, but inspired by the wickedly immersive and thoughtful aesthetic experience of this game. It's something to aim for. Other studios and projects will struggle to carry tone and artistic vision the way Ebb did with Scorn.

The level design is also phenomenal. Orderly, geometric floor plans are broken by tasteful asymmetry, dilapidation, and corrupted organic growth. Each chapter has its own architectural styles and motifs that gave them a unique flavor as you progress, a reward in itself. Verticality is a huge aspect of the layouts, twisting and folding back on themselves, which succeeded multiple times in making me feel like I had wandered far away only for me to notice that I was above or next to an area I recognized. This is also a huge part of the aesthetic experience, as you'll be shouldering around the tight throat of a hallway one moment, then come out to a stunning, decaying vista the next. There were probably a dozen moments in this game where the view in front of me was so stunning, my jaw fell open and I had to just stop in place and take it in. Even backtracking was rewarding in that the paths in reverse had details of their own.

But wait, how much backtracking? A good amount, and that leads into the first downside...

Initially, the gameplay is not unlike a point-and-click adventure, in that you walk around, find items, and use those items somewhere else. Immediately in the first act, though, after wandering around and inspecting all the interactable things on the level, I was confused. Eventually I worked out that I needed to [spoiler] solve the (now infamous) sliding pod puzzle [/spoiler]. Not only was it too subtle that this was even a puzzle at all, I found the "cues" for what you had to do to solve it kind of unintuitive, already a concerning sign for a puzzle game, made even more concerning by Scorn's minimalist approach. I play a lot of logic and puzzle games, so I enjoy a tricky or "hardcore" challenge like this, but it gives me pause in broadly recommending Scorn. It demands patience in a way that will turn many people off in its first hour (and I've seen many reviews to this effect). To be fair, the puzzles from that point on felt more intuitive. But considering it's the first major roadblock you face, I think the devs could have better eased the player into it, guiding them a bit better. Be prepared to backtrack and search around while you determine if you missed something earlier. And, unfortunately, be prepared to encounter things while you backtrack and search.

So yes, let's talk about the gunplay, this game's weakest point by far. Scorn is not a shooter. I remember early on when it was announced, there was more of a focus on the gunplay, but Ebb seems to have de-prioritized that element, and I'm glad they did. But I wish they went even further. The combat in Scorn is unnecessary and feels stapled on - for example, most enemies you can and should avoid altogether, or fire one shot at then run past them rather than try to kill them. It's like Ebb either didn't want to let people down by removing it, or throw away the weapon art assets and design decisions they'd already worked on, or both. I feel like the combat could be removed from the game and it wouldn't have had less of an impact on me; in fact, its inclusion is distracting and too tastes too "game-y" compared with all the wonder of its environment. I've seen other reviewers hope for something like the "safe mode" in SOMA, which optionally turns off enemy encounters altogether, and I agree. The best compromise I can imagine is for enemies to still be around, maybe [spoiler] still block your path sometimes in the case of the big "charger" guys in the later acts [/spoiler], just not aggro or attack you. Then they're more like an interactable part of the environment and you can consider the impulse to kill them or not.

Other people seem to have crashes and graphical issues and stuff, but I haven't experienced much of that. Assuming they'll patch that out, I haven't factored that into my recommendation.

[b]Overall I would recommend buying Scorn on sale if you are interested in a challenging aesthetic experience over compelling gameplay, willing to play it with patience, and willing to forgive its shortcomings.[/b] The current price point of $40 given its length (appx. 5 to 8 hours) is a bit steep. However I will say that if you're speedrunning this game, you're totally missing the point. Play it slowly. And it /does/ have replay value, but not if you're only motivated by Steam achievements, lol. I will definitely be playing this game again.

Some grab-bag improvements that could be made:
- As many reviews mention, checkpoints should be more frequent, especially right after completing a puzzle. There is no reason to make players repeat these sections if they die.
- Only show controls which display on the pause menu that are currently available and relevant. I was stuck on a part where I thought I couldn't switch weapons, because there's a control simply labeled "Switch", and it didn't do anything. Turns out this "Switch" control is only available during the last 5 minutes of the game - so why is it shown on this screen the entire time? I think it would make more sense to only show that control during the small section where it matters. Similar idea with the weapon and item controls as they're unlocked.
- Would be nice to holster my weapon when I'm just walking around. Better for screenshots and immersion :)

Criticism aside, kudos to Ebb for an incredible art game and I can't wait to see what they do next!

Graphics
An interesting environment that raises questions. After the initial WTF, everything is more or less the same. There's only a handful of impressive/memorable moments. Body horror/gross-out is part of the draw, but isn't used very much. A few graphical errors with weapons and puzzles can be fixed with a restart.

Audio
Generally of excellent quality. Music is sparse, but effective at enhancing the moment. Ambient noise instills fear of what might be lurking behind every corner. Directional audio seemed unreliable at times. Could not hear some enemies until they had seen me.

Puzzles
This is not a puzzle game.

There are maybe five (5) "puzzles" to "solve." Most of them I "solved" as I was trying to learn the rules of the "puzzle." I've seen reviews that mention being "filtered" by these puzzles.
Unless you are extremely impatient, I doubt you could fail to "solve" the "puzzles."

Combat
This is not a combat game.

You are slow, firing is slow, switching weapons is slow, reloading is slow, healing is slow, ammo is sparse, health is sparse, and the damage you do is low.
You almost never need to use your weapons because encountering enemies is rare and they are easily avoidable. That is, until you are suddenly surrounded. 

Stealth
This is not a stealth game.

There is no way to hide from most enemies, other than running far away.
Hiding from enemies in tight quarters is tedious and unreliable.

Story
There is no catharsis to be found here.

Conclusion
This is a walking simulator.

The puzzles give you vague clues of what you're supposed to do, but on the whole it's mostly just trying everything until something works.

Combat is useless. The enemies are pretty dodgy as well. I've had them disappear, and then reappear behind me when there was no way they could have been there.

TLDR: Linear puzzle game with very little shooting and no replayability. Amazing creativity but a big push on the grotesque doesn't always result in a great end product. It's also very short for its price point. If you're truly wanting to give it a go, get it on sales.

Story: So... To my knowledge, there's isn't a single line of dialogue in the game. The past events/story is a bit up for interpretation. By this I just mean, there is a lot to unpack here, but it just stays packed as nothing is really explained. In the game S.O.M.A. you eventually understood what went down and had a reasoning behind everything, but here, you're kinda left to wonder why it all happened, and what the meaning of it all is.

Gameplay: For a first person there is very little action, which fits the general vibe of the game. It's more about getting from puzzle A to B, while trying to deal with the enemies the best you can, and while there is a lot of backtracking, the game feels very linear. 
There are many puzzles and while they aren't explained, they are decent and easy to understand.
You get 4 guns, and one of them you only get 4 bullets of, so its more of a gimmick weapon than an actual one (as almost each bullet is meant for a specific target), heck, even naming them guns is a bit odd.
Ammo is scarce, so are health refills, so looking for them is important. 
Reloading is horribly slow.
The way the game handles saves is, uh, unknown to me, as I never noticed a checkpoint and never got to save manually. I just beat it in one afternoon, and when I died I had a pretty good chunk to redo.
Other basic aspects are fine, but you can get easily think you have more room to maneuver than you really do.

Graphics: It's gray and red. Oh, there's a tad of brown too. There's really not much going on. There is the occasional oooh, that's a pretty building, or... Ooooh, well that's nasty. But apart from that it's pretty drab and forgettable. Which is kinda crazy considering how artistic the game can be at times. The inventory especially caught me off guard, it reminded me of Alone in the Dark 3.

Audio: This reminded me of Agony. Agony was also an agony to play and listen to. I'm not saying the sound is broken, but the ambience is pretty much a gurgling stomach. After a while, it kinda gets to you.

The game heavily focuses on trying to be gory than being an actual enjoyable experience. I mean it's fine if you're gonna do that, but go for broke and make it fun. And while it had some interesting elements, in the end it just all felt like an unfinished product. Concepts and ideas are great, but only when they're put to practice, and there needs to be a hook. At least I got me some sweet pressed baby juice.

Scorn honestly disappointed me on so many different levels.  I will start with a positive though and say that Ebb Software made an incredible looking game with it's own unique style and engaging atmosphere, and that deserves praise for their first game.  It's something most Triple-A studios struggle to pull off these days.  Aside from the intrigue and detailed environment though, Scorn is disappointingly average.  The game mostly consists of walking around doing braindead puzzles.  I have nothing against puzzle games, in fact Manifold Garden is one of my all time favorite games and I've beat it a few times over, but something about Scorn's puzzles just weren't that interesting to me.  The gunplay and combat in the game is so clunky and annoying, it honestly would've been a better experience if it was completely removed.  The ads for the game make it seem like combat played an integral role in the experience and that it would be fast paced and fun.  Instead the gunplay is present about 30% of the game and every time it feels annoying and tedious.  If I came across angry or upset in this review it's just because I'm disappointed with how the game turned out.  If executed properly this game could've been something really great, but instead it's just okay.

It's a beautiful game. I wanted to enjoy the art and storytelling stuff, but a number of horrible gameplay design elements severely detracted/distracted from my ability to appreciate it.

I eventually "figured out" the "combat" (Protip: it's just patience and avoidance, always wait and/or run away. if you're having trouble so you're rage reading neg reviews, adopt a coward's tactics and see if that helps any), but not before becoming horribly frustrated, to the point where I was no longer paying attention to the environment/atmosphere/storytelling aspects of the game (just rage-playing, which isn't good for this kind of game), and even after that, there were a few unavoidable ambushes that killed me (after getting set back and returning to that point, the encounters were rendered trivial by the newfound forsight), and that kind of thing just feels bad. I feel like the frustration and slow uptake is because of how combat and the enemies are introduced to the player? idk, not fighting felt like it should have been intuitive (infact, I played very pacifistic at first, because I felt that suited the forlorn, ruined atmosphere/vibe of the game, until I died a few times because of misunderstanding enemy/game behavior, then coming to the logical, but wrong, conclusion that the game was asking me to fight better to progress).

I loved everything except for the greasy area with the fungus enemies (Act III), but perhaps due to the frustration that place caused me, it kind of overshadowed the rest and highlighted a bunch of other elements of the game that fall short, things I might not have otherwise noticed or cared about if it hadn't so effectively pissed me off.

My playtime is abnormally high because I play this kind of game super slow, died a bunch, and left it paused for an hour while I had lunch, and played the first area again to pick up the alternate act I achievement.

It started off really strong, though I expected more intricate/difficult environmental puzzles after the opening area, that it didn't have that is fine. I also felt like it had a really strong ending (note: you MUST [spoiler]have some healing charges left after the fight in the cathedral area[/spoiler] or you're basically sol because [spoiler]the puzzle solutions after that point require you to take a bunch of damage[/spoiler], which, is honestly a cool mechanic? and I think would have been a better use of your hitpoints than the combat if explored a little better/more, but is seriously unfair because if you're not ready for it you might basically get softlocked out of the ending and have to restart the area).

Leaving a no recommend mainly because the game has plenty of positive reviews. There was a lot I loved, but more I was disappointed by. Give it a go if you think you're interested, but maybe buy it on sale.

But the combat is absolutely awful, with a controller anyway, and why wouldn't I use a controller when the game is clearly designed for it, except when it's not.
The sensitivity option applies to both looking around and aiming, so if it's high enough to be able to quickly turn around and run away from a creature then it's difficult to aim (and there's no aim assist!), and if it's low enough to be able to aim then exploration becomes a chore and running away becomes almost impossible.
Reloading and switching weapons takes forever, so if you miss a shot then you're as good as dead because there's no time or room to retreat and reload. Which is especially a problem when some of the "stronger" creatures take an entire clip to kill.
And then when [i]you[/i] get killed for the n-th time - you have to watch this slooooow death animation before you're presented with "continue" button because apparently developers live in a parallel universe where skippable cutscenes were never invented.

I get that making combat more dynamic would've contradicted the general vibe of the game, but it should not have been added in the first place. The first weapon in the game also acts as a tool, and if the rest of them were also tools and the puzzles revolved around that - I think it would've been a more consistent experience.

I wanted to recommend this game; I really did. 

A lot can be said about Scorn. It's visuals are stunning, the art direction is uniquely horrifying, the puzzles were simple yet compelling, and it's atmosphere is one of a kind. I have never played a game quite like it. I felt that the inventory system was immersive, and it seemed like the game knew exactly what it wanted to accomplish. It didn't overstay it's welcome (literally).

Now, reading that above, I could understand why you - the reader - may be mildly confused to why I don't recommend this game. I'll be honest; Scorn is an okay game, but it still left so much to be desired.

I feel for the people who have followed this project since it's conception. I didn't learn about Scorn until late 2021, so I didn't wait in anticipation for 8 long years for its release. Although I enjoyed this game, I felt like the game doesn't deserve a $40 price tag. Even at the 10% off price that I bought it, I still felt like I was a bit scammed out of $35. I can't believe that the deluxe version is $50! Yes, the art direction of the game was fantastic, but the level design was quite poor in multiple areas. There were a few times were I found myself getting turned around in the linear labyrinth that is Scorn. Just because you make the area look good doesn't mean you throw level design out the window. On top of that, the combat was lackluster, the "boss fight" (if you want to call it that) at the end of the game was slightly frustrating, and the overall fun factor of the game was relatively low.

Sure, make a cool art horror experience, but maybe if it's gonna be 5 - 6 hours long make it about $15 - $20 cheaper? 

TL;DR - Get Scorn on a Summer/Winter Steam Sale; otherwise it's not worth it and overall disappointing for the price.

[h1] I can't reccomend this game [/h1]
[h2] Music: ★★★★★ [/h2]
The music in Scorn is absolutely spectacular, perfectly complementing the game's dark, gory, and bizarre ambiance. The eerie soundscapes and unsettling tracks keep you on edge, making you question whether the sounds you hear might belong to one of the game's annoying monsters, like the mutant chickens or whatever the name of those things are that I absolutely hate. The audio design is top-notch, immersing you in the game's disturbing world.

[h2] Graphics: ★★★★★ [/h2]
Scorn's art direction is a masterpiece, creating a truly unique and haunting atmosphere. The attention to detail in the grotesque environments is incredible, and the game's visuals are nothing short of stunning.

[h2] Gameplay: ★☆☆☆☆ [/h2]
Unfortunately, Scorn's gameplay falls flat and quickly becomes a tedious experience. The game can be summarized in walk puzzle, walk puzzle, walk puzzle and so on, with little else to break up the monotony. The puzzles themselves feel like a chore rather than engaging challenges, and the game offers no guidance or instructions on how to approach them. The exploration is useless everything is empty apart from liking the aesthetics there's no point in doing anything but the puzzles, the game is as empty as my faith in humanity.

[h2] Story: ★☆☆☆☆ [/h2]
Scorn's storytelling is virtually nonexistent, leaving players in the dark about the game's lore and narrative. You are thrown into this mysterious world with no context or explanation, and while this approach may aim to enhance immersion, it ultimately fails to engage the player. Your character seems to understand the purpose of everything around them, but as the player, you are left desperately wanting to know what's going on from start to finish. Apparently, you have to watch the trailer or something for that.

[h2] Combat: ★★☆☆☆ [/h2]
The combat in Scorn is lackluster and unsatisfying. The only weapon that feels remotely effective is the shotgun, which you acquire far too late in the game, around 70% of the way through. The earlier weapons feel weak and ineffective against the game's enemies (Better to avoid them anyway, yes even the fat ones).

[h2] Overall: ★★☆☆☆ [/h2]
Despite its breathtaking visuals and haunting soundtrack, I cannot recommend Scorn. The game's repetitive gameplay, boring puzzles, lack of storytelling, and frustrating combat make for a hollow and unrewarding experience. While the game's aesthetics are undeniably impressive, they are not enough to carry the entire game.

First off I'd like to say, if there was a middle thumb option, I'd absolutely pick that instead. Scorn is not a bad game by any stretch, however, it feels like a concept piece instead of a full game.

Personally I didn't follow this game's development too closely and I didn't back it during its kickstarter run. With this, I had very little expectations for it. Even then, I still felt disappointed and let down.

Yes, the art direction is phenomenal and on a technical level Scorn is super impressive. But this isn't a painting on a wall, its a video game.

Obviously I don't know this for certain, but considering the sheer amount of time this game was in the works, I'd wager there were some serious issues behind the scenes. The game is very short, oddly paced and makes you feel like you've experienced only a percent of the game in its total playtime. I was left wanting more, and not in the good way, I felt robbed.

Not to mention, the game is also pretty different from the minor impressions I got based on the very few trailers I've seen. This is not a survival horror game, its a puzzle/exploration game with combat tacked on. The combat is slow and feels caught like a rock in a hard place. Enemies feel too tanky and abundant for the small amounts of ammo they give you. Not to mention, due to the linear design of many areas, you will often feel forced to trade damage to proceed. You can't even reliably avoid enemies a lot of the time either because rooms are so damn enclosed.

To discuss the actual narrative, I've got my own theories about what it all means, but that's all they are, theories. There is zero dialogue or actual explanation for anything in the game. Whatever it means, you can only guess. Personally I wouldn't mind this if the game was longer and had more meat to it, but as is, it just feels hollow.

The ending is also incredibly harsh. I'd felt like literally nothing I did to get the end actually mattered and I was robbed of any kind of resolution or explanation for anything. I'd hoped the game would throw me a bone eventually, but it really didn't.

Scorn is technically sound for the most part, but I did experience some jank. Occasionally I'd see floating objects or some clipping. I had one instance where a cutscene soft locked me, forcing me to re-load a save, which then resulting in the game sending me back over 40 minutes.

I don't know, all considered, I just feel disappointed. If it were a longer experience with more to it, I think I'd come around to it a lot more. If it featured more focused game design instead of trying to be multiple genre's at once, I think I would have enjoyed it more consistently.

With time, I might come around to liking it more, but as it stands, Scorn leaves me feeling sad and empty.

The visuals, artistry, the mystery world, all of that is awesome, but... 
And that's a big but; I still would not recommend it. Here's why.

Apparently, the game has been released unfinished after more than 10 years in the making, and the gameplay mechanics, especially combat, have been made clunky and too hard on purpose to make the game feel longer: 
- The dodging action has been cut on purpose to make the player dodge by strafing only or avoid combat entirely by sneaking around the enemies
- The [spoiler]health recharge tanks[/spoiler] have been made less than half empty on purpose
- Checkpoints (and that's what grinds me most) that fit the world's lore are missing, where the player could safe his progress, but instead the checkpoints are invisible, arbitrarily placed and too far apart. When the player dies, they never know where they spawn again and what needs to be done once again
- Exploration takes unnecessarily long just to show that something bad happened to the world without anything actually meaningful to discover other than striking landscapes and visceral visuals

Placing fewer, more unique enemies and making them harder, or longer to defeat would have made much more sense and would require the player to be more strategic, analytical and patient. I would have imagined unique enemies having some nasty, gory, gigeresque visceral attacks, as the world's alien biology seems to be out of control. Instead: shout the ugly spitting things in the face; repeat until dead. Some enemies look like they weren't initially planned attacking the player at all, hence the only attack they use is spitting; very easy to implement, much more annoying in combat. Either the combat was slapped on the otherwise fascinating game, or it was left finished. It isn't fun and feels out of place.

It's a walking simulator with an unbelievably awesome aesthetic, though I think the last level was a little bit much to be honest.

The issue is that it seems confused over what genre it is.
Is it a Walking Simulator? Or is it Survival Horror?
It doesn't bloody know and that's the biggest problem.
It shouldn't have combat if it's not going to design the levels around those enemies and more importantly the resources for dealing with them. Game's really stingy on health, which by the way I'm going to go ahead and say that the game shouldn't rely on you button mashing or going into the settings to figure out what button heals you, really stingy on ammo.
And by god you'll need that ammo.
The combat system is just a flaming hot mess that detracts from the core premise of the game.
Next issue is the save system.
Or rather the lack of one.
You can't save. It relies on a series of soft checkpoints and hard checkpoints. Hard CP's are the ones you can manually reload to, like say if you encounter a game ending glitch where a bull bugs out and blocks the tunnel, and these are only available near as I can tell for the beginning of the 'act.' The game is divided up into 5 acts.
Yeah. 5 saves. Or so it seemed to me.
Now if you die, as will happen a lot because some of those situations were absolute garbage fires of level design, you'll go back to a soft save which can sometimes be quite a waaaaays back. Like I'm talking this is a game mostly dominated by walking and puzzles and death can result in you having to do all of it all over again.
You can't manually use these which is just a horrible addition with the combat system or ya know glitches.
The game can be improved by removing or redesigning the combat system and adding a proper save system (that tells you when it's a checkpoint, you could put this on the damn biogun for immersion if ya wanted).
SPOILER PART:

Now the ending... yeah. It's extremely anticlimatic and disappointing. Nuff said. The game's focus on a complete and utter lack of any form of narration or guidance honestly harms the concept as a whole and renders a lot of what you're doing completely random and unconnected. I've seen reviews of people critiquing a lack of narrative, and like I get that, but that's not really the issue. The narrative of a walking simulator is delivered primarily by the aesthetic and the setting and importantly what you're doing in that setting. And if you don't know what you're doing... well, that harms the narrative.

If you are willing to endure suffering caused by truly awful combat mechanics and an excessive number of puzzles, just so you can enjoy the visuals, then perhaps the game is worth considering for a purchase at 25€ or less.

I genuinely wish the game were simply a walking simulator with some lore, but unfortunately, it is not.

Developers, I implore you not to incorporate combat mechanics into a video game if you do not possess the expertise to make them enjoyable.

Switching weapons takes several seconds, cannot be canceled, and reduces your character's movement speed.
There are situations where you don't know if a big or small monster is coming from around the corner, and when the monster emerges, you no longer have time to switch to the right weapon, and you die as a result, because the big enemy can stun-lock you.

This game's world is incredible. There's nothing quite like it in any other media I've seen. It's visually stunning and intriguing, giving the viewer a glimpse into a world unfathomably alien.

Everything else isn't as good.

The puzzles and the manner in which you're given no instructions has a lot of potential. It makes you feel like an interloper in a world much bigger than yourself. However, the linear nature of the middle part of the game and the general lack of interactability makes them not challenging. They feel more like time-wasters than mind-benders (with a few exceptions).

The level design is restrictive and linear. One way the game developers keep you in-bounds is by not having the option to jump. This makes even small ridges wall to the player and movement can be frustrating. The game has next to zero exploration and barely any player agency in the path the player takes.

The combat is probably the weakest part of this whole game (minor spoilers ahead). Health loss is permanent and health is few and a between. You will be lucky to have full health and heals at any moment in this game. You are stuck with the melee option for the vast majority of the game, and it's not a very good option. Enemies are quick to punish even the slightest mistake, and the long cooldown makes combat mostly about running and trying to find cover. The terrible movement and level design exacerbate this by making it difficult to tell what is and isn't the part of the floor you are allowed to walk on. For some reason, you move at a snail's pace when you have a weapon raised. The gun raising and switching animations are way too long and also cripple your movement speed, making combat feel sluggish, awkward, and frustrating. Because of the health system, it's easy to get low health and then get a checkpoint. And because of how few checkpoints there are, dying later can send you back tens of minutes, still with no health and no way to get any more.

The length of this game also hurts it a lot. I wouldn't mind the length if it felt like a fulfilling experience, but it felt like I just finally got my feet under me and the game could finally throw some new challenges at me. Then it ended. I feel like this could be so much more if it just kept building on what it had (plus some balancing and game-feel tweaks).

The weapons especially feel robbed (more spoilers). The first ranged weapon comes with so little ammo that you can barely try it out and learn how it works before waiting forever to get a refill. Honestly considering the risk of the lengthy reload and weapon changing animation, it's probably less risky to just stick with melee in most scenarios. There's no incentive and no spare ammo to learn to utilize this weapon effectively (and no spare health to make mistakes while learning). Then, when you finally get more ammo and better weaponry, the combat feels a bit better (just don't miss because you'll need to conserve bullets to make it past some of the later encounters). And then the combat is over. The better weapon is barely useful at all for the endgame, and then you can't even use it anymore. Then, the final gun is barely even used as a weapon. So much potential, wasted.

So much work went into the world, but not enough work went into making Scorn a fun experience. I enjoyed playing it, but I feel like I would have enjoyed watching someone else play it almost as much (and would have avoided the price tag and some headache). If the developers put more effort into the gameplay, it would actually be pretty good. I almost wish there were a planned DLC or a Scorn 2 planned which could rectify the mistakes this game made. It truly does have a lot of potential.


Tl;dr: world good, combat bad, puzzles disappointing, game short and falls well below its potential.

8 years of waiting ... It's really just a puzzle game. Here's my main takeaways: 

- Interesting setting: it's probably the main selling point. Can't think of another game that pushes the 'biomechanical' look and feel as much or as well in the environment. Enemies just look like uncooked poultry, but the rest is good. Also, somehow, not very scary or creepy. I think that might be due to how the game is just moving from puzzle to puzzle, and ultimately makes me feel more frustrated than anxious.

-Lackluster shooting and combat: the 'guns' feel awful. Combat for the first half of the game is just about taking pot shots and then running for cover. The final weapon only needs to be fired 3 or 4 times. The enemies is this game are painfully uninteresting.

-Bare-bones story: there isn't really one. Why are we here? Why this red infection stuff? Why is biotech based entirely on solving puzzles? Does the ending only exist to cop out of an explanation as to why we did any of this? Lots of moments with little to no payoff. By the end I still know nothing to the point where even guessing is grasping at straws. Pretty disappointing. 

- The puzzles: the actual *meat* of the game. Only a few puzzles that were really just mind-numbing, fewer that were fun. Many of the puzzles were unintuitive, or force the player to walk mazes, or just take ages to wait for parts to move. Frankly, these felt like a waste of time, possibly unnecessary padding. Definitely the hardest part is just finding the will to backtrack and try to find objectives. You can end up running around on 1 hp for a lot of it due to the save/checkpoint system.

If you're interested in puzzles and HR Giger environments in a game that can be completed in less than 6 hours, maybe worth a try.  For me, however, I thought this game would have some more substance in terms of combat, suspense, or horror, so not much for myself to enjoy. Not a bad showing for a game ... but 8 years since announcement and all the hype was worth about 6 hours of play time, a few ooh's and ah's, and a lot of puzzles. If this game had instead better shooting sections (or none), less puzzles (or none), and more focus on the unique scenery, there might be a cool experience here. And the price?! Definitely not worth $40 USD. As is, it's just too slow for too little substance.

[I]Scorn[/I] is an example of how stunning art direction and truly masterful environmental storytelling can be ruined by absurdly poor game design. Without the rage-quit-inducing combat, this would easily have been one of my favorite games, a must-play for surreal cosmic body-horror fans. At it stands I can't even recommend it.

Much of the game is walking-sim-style exploration with satisfying, visceral puzzles. Hooray for that. Two thumbs up. But then around the mid-point combat is introduced. The fact that it's very difficult, at times unfair, and very plentiful is bad enough. But the real issue is a save system that makes me pull my hair out: it's automatic, invisible to the player (you have no idea when the game is saved), and with save points very far from each other. The cost of death can be having to repeat long, tedious, and challenging segments of the game. And here's the cherry on top: this automatic save can easily have you at just one hitpoint and with no ammo.

We can all write long essays on how this awful design could have been fixed without negatively impacting immersion. Just look at the many excellent horror games that do it right, or at least much better than [I]Scorn[/I]. It's hard to understand why the devs made such a horrible misstep when they got everything else so right.

I persevered and finished the game, all the way to its glorious ending, which may be one of the best I've ever experienced. Everything is just ... wow. I am awestruck. But getting there was often the opposite of fun.

Maybe modders will be able to fix this game. Until then, you are better served watching a playthrough than playing it yourself.

Instead, Scorn's gameplay feels artificial, screwed on for padding. I can see how its mechanics could be tightened up or removed altogether, and I can also see how it would shrink the playtime to a couple of hours at most. That would've disappointed even more people. Not me.

[h3]I Want to Get off Mr. Bones' Wild Ride[/h3]
The visuals made Scorn's bitter pills easier to swallow. For performance, the world's being baked-in solid and guarded with abundant invisible walls. You may click a hotspot to watch alien contraptions unwrap, yet can't interact with 99% of anything. Can't leave a mark on a wall, jump over a hump, or throw a shadow on the floor, despite having a visible body. Even the guns are designed not to produce dynamic lighting effects. In a way, the limitations consolidate the alienating settings of Giger, Barlowe, and Beksinski with their semi-synthetical unlife. The soundscapes adhere by creating an aura of another dimension. The echoing growls in the slurping corridors, all the wheezing and sleazing. Then, sparse cosmic tunes ringing through the howling wind take you straight to the lonely surface of Venus.

I felt her scornful gaze from the moment I arrived. Stepping through these otherworldly hellscapes, one probably feels as helpless as a drop of water on a dry sponge. This world is designed to consume, distort, and abuse your flesh, which, in turn, abused my trypophobia. If it decides to chew on you, there's nothing you can do to prevent this from happening. Scorn's hell is a heartless poultry farm ran by a sex cult, a glorious biopunk parade of entomorphic meat bundled in carapace and wobbling muscle piles warping into shapes designed to incite a glimmer of faint recognition. Your own permeable body changes, getting grossly "upgraded" along the way. Creepy on paper.

In practice, the game's safe, lethargic flow and poor timing for scares doesn't translate well into horror. Still, it excels at evoking existential dread. Coming from implications of pain and ill will. It's in the body horror of the unholy amalgamations of flesh interpenetrated with foreign matter. In the freakishly contorted forms of miserable beings, longing for death yet fearing it still. Such is the pathetic nature of things, a morbid display of scorn. It's as if the remnants of these merciless biomachines of methodical madness, after ages, maybe millenniums, are still channelling the sadistic pleasure its engineers took in a mockery of life itself, eternally projecting their will on the undead biotic hell you're thrown into like a torn puppet.

Not necessarily out of the desire to hurt you. Sometimes the horror hides in the indifference of a perpetrator or lack thereof. You've been put through a grinder, made feel every second of it, and there's no one to twirl their moustache about it, the architects of this funfair of misery are probably long gone. Or is it hatred as expressed by AM in I Have No Mouth? The world teaches you to be just as cruel as it is, you can't progress without committing crimes against conscience. Once, I found a different way to solve a puzzle. Like when I didn't kill an egg creature to get its arm. I freed it, pushed it around, looked in its fearful eyes without mercy, to then leave it forever stuck in one of the machines. I didn't enjoy being me and I think I wasn't supposed to. Like I wasn't supposed to enjoy the rest of the game, it seems.

[h3]Dragging Through the Motions[/h3]
Mainly, you aimlessly lug around, blindly sticking your limbs into alien apparatuses, forced to put your trust into something that violates you without blinking. Scarcely, you're given compelling redesigns of your standard sliding, rail, and maze puzzles. They are intuitive, reward spatial thinking and, much like the exploration in-between, most of them are but boring busywork. You always know what you have to do and how to accomplish it. Getting there is just a matter of patience. The level-scale puzzles are particularly abysmal since levers and buttons are usually far from one another and your character isn't exactly a sprinter. With the amount of disorienting backtracking and repetition, initially I thought the game was pulling my leg. Nope, it insisted on ennui until the end.

I was so fed up with every area I roamed that all of them lost their gloss to me long before I left. There are never that many places to go, which is a relief, considering how quickly the act of hauling ass becomes mundane, and I wouldn't call this "exploring in a non-linear fashion" or say the regions are "interconnected". You linearly progress through the levels and even this is sluggish enough. Coming to a dead end and realising the need to backtrack through the whole location was the greatest kind of scare this game produced. Go turn a knob, run somewhere else to push a thing, return and stab a spot, miss something, look for it for an hour, poke it. Repeat ad nauseam, trying not to get lost in the similarly unique environments while occasionally taking breaks for some mediocre riddles and uninspired shooting, inserted for no one's pleasure.

[h3]Salt and Awe[/h3]
Most of the enemy designs are kinda dubious. The first ones are some acid-spitting... uh... poppy bud monsters? Way to make a first impression. It was a lame creature and an even lamer fight, which lacked any semblance of impact. It took so many hits and I took even more because of the terrible movement and that garbage "melee gun", although using any gun here is a torment due to how clunky the simple process of aiming is. Still, the other guns are significantly better, yes. In a sense how being waterboarded is better than being waterboarded and electrocuted simultaneously. Thankfully, they at least use bullets. Of course, reloading them means slowing down to a crawl, giving enemies free hits on you. And you don't get that many heals! Like ammo, those serve as a weak incentive for the increasingly laborious exploration.

During which, I was trying to kill a chickensh*t poppy bud fast and move on. It killed me. Every time I died, I had to replay another completely linear section, typically consisting of riding the damn Undercity elevators and watching drawn-out animations. Tedium is the only palpable punishment Scorn dispenses in droves. It's poorly calibrated. Going for that Survival Horror clumsiness, its combat ended up lacking the suspense and gratification to support it. I felt like it got in the way, often literally when trying to run past monsters, getting stuck on them or the scenery. It was annoying. I won't be telling you about the rest of what's on offer, there's no point. All of it sucks. Before witnessing it, I kinda enjoyed the chores. Afterwards, I barged through on salt and awe.

[h3]Still Art[/h3]
As it stands, artistic talent alone doesn't make good game designers. Scorn's world is engaging on a cerebral level, yet laсks tangibility. Hiding behind the fabulous looks and themes, I found its malnourished gameplay, and being infested by the undercooked ambition, it's a deformed parody of itself. A colossus standing with one crutch in the puzzles and one in the shooters, cracking at the seams. But it holds, for its paint is a brilliant concoction. Created on the backs of strong ideas and legendary aspirations, Scorn is a vision manifested purely artistically. Alas, I deem this offering insufficient for the medium. It's a great experience at the expense of being a bad game. A bad game that has so much to give, go figure. In the end, I don't deny Scorn its artistic merits. But who said that art can't sh*t the bed?

Giger, which im ok with, but i wished there were more of beksinski in this, which was mostly limited to the one outdoor area you visit after the prologue.

It wasn't really a walking sim, but i kind of wish it was because the gameplay that is there was honestly some of the most frustrating gameplay i've ever engaged with. The combat doesn't just feel sluggish and slow, which i can deal with, but it feels half-baked and unfair. I rarely vocalize my frustrations when i play videogames, but in the final boss-fight(s) i genuinely bellowed in frustration. The fight was incredibly contrived in that you cannot crush the baby on the stand, you have to crush it when it is inside the mech suit; frustrating in that the weak spot is only visible after you wait for a long time, or you shoot the boss several times, which gives you a timeframe to run up to the weakspot that is too short and you end up missing the timeframe; far too long in that you have to attack the weakpoint 4 times, then there is a second phase which is poorly telegraphed how you're supposed to fight back. If you lose in the second phase, you restart the whole thing.

The bossfight is not the only issue with the gameplay, more generally it feels like you cannot avoid attacks and that you take too much damage. The tracking on the enemy attacks is insane. You keep getting stuck in the geometry.

I love the visual aesthetic, it is simply gorgeously morbid. Despite the frustrating gameplay, i wish the game was longer, or had the interesting moral choices that the devs talked about us having to make. There are plenty morally abhorrent or questionable decisions the player makes, but they are not decisions you have any say in. You must do them to progress. There is one choice the player has a say in early on in the prologue, but it serves to purpose, as right after you do it there is a big timeskip, and the decision is never relevant.

It is a game that is fantastic to look at and engross yourself in, but i would recommend you look up a playthrough online instead of playing it yourself.

Received this game via Humble Bundle, which is the main upside to this, because i'd be fairly annoyed if I'd paid $40+ for what turned out to be a ~4 hour game (in game time) for me.

My first downside was the mouse movement, which actually caused me to get dizzy for a few minutes every time I started the game.

The puzzles are decent but there's only four of them if you count the beginning area. This seems to be the main focus of the game because the enemies are somewhat avoidable for the most part (only learned this later) and the story is non-existent. You wake up and begin exploring through the world trying to do...something. It's never explained or hinted at what needs to be accomplished, except maybe survival. The enemies are my primary annoyance. Until the middle of act 3 I was under the impression that the enemies were just that - enemies. It was my impression that you had to kill any enemy nearby to anything that you can interact with, because logically they'd be able to hit you while you're doing something else right? Wrong. Enemies will wait for you to finish doing your thing before they resume firing upon you. 
Three of the enemy types in the game are ranged damage, technically, as one of them needs to be somewhat close to you to fire. I've been hit through walls and seemingly solid objects by projectiles, and one enemy is able to track your movements and fire at where you're running to, which is quite frustrating. Best dumbest moment was when I started up the game, loaded into my save and immediately had an enemy shooting at me before I was able to control my character.
Your melee weapon is 2 hits before it has to recharge, which is less than useful for most combat situations given that the only thing you can kill in 2 hits is a long ranged enemy that will usually get off 2 shots before you can get close. The pistol is the same damage as the melee, only ranged. Stay still to focus your shot, which only becomes useful if you're making the first shot. Otherwise enemies can run up on you pretty quick. The shotgun is nice, doing 3x the damage of a pistol shot but only gets 6 shots per ammo station that you find every so often. The pistol is easily miss-able. The shotgun seems more obvious but could also be skipped if you're not paying attention or exploring.

As you progress in the game you'll find health kits/blood packs. No station that recharges your health vials will ever give you a full charge and it's very easy to be running empty or close to it all the time. I certainly was. Health button has to be held the entire animation or it won't go through, and can be interrupted by some attacks that knock you down. Couple that with situations in which you're faced with 2-3 enemies and you can be going through health at a rapid pace. Gold star awarded for having cutscenes/scripted moments in which you take unavoidable damage that further drains your health resources. Second gold star for having a late game mechanic to stick your hand into a shredder in order to regain use of it for 10-15s before it becomes unusable again. Considering there's no wandering hostile enemies in the act where that mechanic is, I don't see why there's a point to limiting your healing when you're under a time crunch to get to what you need to do anyway. 

But the nail in the coffin for me was the ending, which was so disappointing that it left a sour taste in my mouth and I felt as if all my time playing this game was a complete waste of time. 

3/10 for the visuals & music. A shame the rest of it is so disjointed and messy.

Kickstarter and trailers promised a horror game. Early trailers showed the use of guns with a hint that, just because there are guns, doesn't make it an action game.

However, the enemies in this game move quick, sometimes quicker than you. They have long-ranged projectiles and very good aim. You cannot out run their attacks if you were already close - you will get hit. Your best bet is to cheese the enemies by running in circles around the level, if any loops are available, or get behind something. You will have a close-range "weapon" that has 2 hits before a lengthy cooldown. You cannot help but GET CLOSE to kill these enemies. And there will be more than you ought to deal with for a game that wants to deny its title of being a "non-action" game.

Yeah there's not a lot of action alright - not a lot I can fucking DO about some of these enemies except get killed and hope that RNG is better next time. Most of the time I had to run away and wait for enemies to just leave as they crawl back into the environment. Later, I get better weapons but health and ammo is slim. The issues with slower movement and enemies having long-range projectiles still existed but was better.

Speaking of "figuring out when" to conserve resources and dying, later in the end-game, there is a game mechanic that requires you to take damage over time to solve a puzzle.

Let me say that again: THERE IS A GAME MECHANIC THAT REQUIRES YOU TO LOSE HEALTH OVER TIME TO SOLVE PUZZLES.

Tie that into the conservation design of this game and you have a recipe for screwing over your players and calling it "good game design". I almost forgot. You take health damage during cutscenes animations too. I hope you weren't finally making progress at 1 HP.

I had been waiting for a while for this game, and I think I admittedly got it mixed up with Agony as far as some expectations were concerned; because I thought this was a game based on "a soul in hell trying to escape" with some shooter elements, but mostly horror. This had more or less no effect on my opinion, because I'm a fan of shooters and horror alike regardless. That being said:

I didn't really feel "scared" by anything in Scorn. It's just kind of gross and unsettling. I know it's based on H.R Giger's art, and I wanted to play a horror game for Halloween; but it wasn't very scary. It was just kind of disgusting and visually repulsive, because of all the flesh everywhere. Which, to some people, is scary. To me, it isn't; and most of my actual time playing, most of the game, was centered around these "diseased" biomechanical areas which make up most of the game. I thought the clean, biomechanical, alien looking areas in Act 5 were visually appealing. Everywhere else felt like I was walking through a shitty, gassy stomach.

Which kind of brings me to my point. Some people feel as though the fact that it's linear, and that it has no other endings is something of artistic value. Maybe? But it doesn't really add to my appreciation of it either. There are only 12 achievements to get in this game, and you get 11 of them based on a single choice you may or may not make at the beginning of your journey, before there is any danger. People love to criticize open-world games and games that aren't linear nowadays; and that's fair, but so is my own opinion:

The fact that there are no other endings and virtually no other content gives this game literally no replayability whatsoever. There is nothing you can change to fit a different playstyle, nothing you can do to alter the story (whatever the story is meant to be in the first place.), and no "actual" narrative. Even the most recent patch notes refer to a "getting stuck in the hurt machine." I looked at that, and said "which one?" There is no dialogue. It's so completely and utterly linear, that basically I found myself resigning any kind of critical thinking ability I had, to "Just find the interactable shit. You'll get through the story that way."

While some people think this is artistic, I feel as if it's kind of lazy. I don't even say this with any offense meant to the developers; it just feels unpolished. Making it so there is only one "outcome" that's meant to be depressing isn't profound to me, it's boring. Making it so that the protagonist seems to know where he's going and what he's doing while the player remains clueless doesn't necessitate being thoughtful to me. It feels like any deductive ability the player has is stifled by how narrow and linear it all is, including exploration. You don't really find anything that kind of clues you in. Even at the end, you don't even know where the hell you're going, if the portal you were intending to step through before Randall from Monster's Inc kills you goes anywhere that would've been able to repair your innards, or you'd start new life, etc. Most people don't find the shit in the can artistic, so giving people nothing doesn't really feel inspiring or anything either. It just kind of leaves a bad taste in your mouth where you're wondering why the hell it cost 40$.
