﻿I love Giger's work. I do not love it this much - you can consider the +1.5 rating I've given as an acknowledgement of a very well-rendered visual and auditory presentation of a Giger-esque setting. Literally every other aspect of Scorn is appallingly bad. The game qualifies for me as no more than a walking simulator, as it makes obvious within the first hour of the experience (as you do genuinely nothing else). Leisurely strolls to and fro a linear factory of some variety, pulling tendon levers in the right order, is not my idea of a good spooky time. Combat is... horrid. The character has no jump, a pitiful sprint, no way to climb, no dodging ability aside from taking advantage of the tumor-looking foes' inability to handle you running in circles around them. The guns, despite being biological in almost every way, require little shotgun pellets that you daintily slot back into place, and run out of if you aren't using the melee.... gun? to dispose of the less threatening mold rat beasts. The puzzles are not interesting (I enjoyed a single one, so I can't fully say that) and the problem-solving of the environmentals is a straight shot if you aren't obligated to backtrack by design. There are.. theoretically story beats to pick up on, which you definitely won't figure out beyond "place make people, people make resource, resource.. exist" unless you read the few paragraphs of text that are apparently in the art book. There are... maybe four cinematics, which are somehow the thing I was looking forward to in a.. video game. Lastly, and most egregiously in my mind, the game's setting suffers from a reversed technology trope - super intelligent societies that use their incredible developments to somehow make things more complicated than they are today. Why in the world do you have... on-rail push carts... in a setting like this? Why is there an entire system to replace ball-trap elevators that swivel you around ONE ROOM? Don't buy this game, and honestly, I wouldn't even watch it. Buy the art book if you want. Heck, look up Giger's work and enjoy that instead.

The music is also a class act in ambiance and atmosphere - the sound design on this game is so, so, so, sick.

However... The game itself seems confused. I am someone that would've enjoyed this game more as a puzzle game rather than a shooter, but the game is really a 60% puzzle/walking sim and 40% shooting. For a long while in the game you will only have a melee gun that is god awful to use. Many, many times there are puzzle pieces that are hard to find in the expansive environment. There were a few times that I was truly stumped and had to use a walkthrough, and a few solutions I have no idea how you would even solve that on your own without just... trying everything.

Saving is also an issue, as the game has no quick saves except in between Acts. The game doesn't tell you anywhere that it will save before you quit. I understand the want to not have players reload saves to cheese things, but if it was communicated I think would've hated the concept less. You felt very trapped, and while there is an argument for immersion, I can't say I liked it personally.

I've been eagerly awaiting Scorn ever since it first debuted on Steam Greenlight, but now that I played and finished it, I'm just sad and disappointed. Gorgeously disturbing art and atmosphere can only take a game so far when everything else about it is a janky underdeveloped mess.
Years before release, Scorn's developers have been showing off the game's nifty combat system and importance of moral choices on the progression - all of that is gone now. The released game is a clunky linear puzzle game, where you can expect to play such bangers as:

* A convoluted sliding tile puzzle.
* Guide-a-light-through-a-maze puzzle.
* Align asynchronous rotating disks puzzle.
* And the all time classic - light up all the nodes puzzle!

The fact Scorn wraps such trite exercises into its gorgeous Geiger/Beksiński art style feels utterly insulting.
But then "combat" is introduced three chapters in, and it gets so much worse! Your fragile, lumbering, meat-man with slow, imprecise short range attack on a 10 second cool down is suddenly pitted against aggressive fast-projectile-lobbing damage-sponges. And so, you die, and die and die and die some more, each time sitting through a painfully slow death animation and a lengthy load time, then get respawned at the last checkpoint that may often be 15-20 minutes ago, forcing you to redo puzzles, or re-watch long unskippable cutscene animations. Health and ammo recharge stations don't regenerate, so if you used one up, then got mauled or missed a few shots shortly after, you might as well restart the chapter and lose hours of progress, as Scorn has no qualms about soft-locking progression and generally wasting player's time.

I am not mentioning the game's story because there isn't one. You just move from one gorgeously grotesque setpiece to another without any real connection, until your meat-man is murdered in a convoluted, completely undeserved way, and the credits roll.

Don't bother playing Scorn - it's clunky and boring, with a borderline broken checkpoint system, and no respect for player's time. If, like me, you were allured by the art of HR Geiger and Zdzisław Beksiński - watching a LongPlay on youtube will be a much better experience. Don't waste your money, especially at the current asking price of $40! Holy crap it's not even close to worth it!

So I guess if you're a big fan of body horror (and I am), it's a fun game to look at for a while, but that's literally all it has. Combat is some of the worst I've ever played, gameplay is frustrating, the story...isn't, and the ending made the whole thing feel like a waste of my time. The worldbuilding, such as it is, feels like a paper-thin layer atop a vast abyss of gore, misery porn, and so much Freudian imagery that H.R. Giger is sitting up in his grave saying "I appreciate the tribute, but maybe [i]tone it down[/i] a little?" Dear God if I never see another disembodied penis and/or butthole for the rest of my life it will be too soon.

The compact puzzles are also good, they help give some variety to the gameplay.

Scorn on the whole as a game though, feels really lacklustre.
I can see in the reviews that some people write it's difficult. I disagree - I'm generally not good at shooters at all, and still managed to complete the game.
But playing this, more often than not, feels like a *chore*. The combat feels clunky. You'll be trying to kill the mutated leftovers of a butchers shop while handling what feels like a freight ship, waiting around corners to snipe meatbags, moving slowly forward to be sure you don't aggro to many mobs.

70% of the level design, not the art but the part where you use the space as a game, feels uninspired. The last area mentioned above felt different simply because I wasn't walking along 12 corridors which felt almost identical, but had landmarks and memorable spaces to navigate through.
The world itself is carefully crafted, but this also comes with an extra challenge. It's alien, and there's no text in the game, so little to nothing is explained. This isn't new. Other games such as Rainworld have done variants on this as well.
But here, your ammo is limited. Your life is limited. And the game doesn't save often. If you're like me, this means the player becomes very cautious about trying different stuff if you think it costs life or ammo. I looked up wikis more than once, simply because I didn't want to waste ammo or life and then have to redo many minutes of the game.
I wouldn't call it good game design if the player either has to replay entire sections because they ran out of ammo or health, or had to check a wiki to solve puzzles or progress. Make no mistake, strictly as a game Scorn is relatively simple. This shouldn't be necessary. If you get ambushed by a walking blood sausage and die, you're going to be repeating the exact same stuff you did 5 minutes ago. This sucks the freshness right out of the game.
So, buyer beware: if you buy Scorn, buy it for the concept art and mild gory creepout. Don't expect a Doom run-n-gun shooter, or a hardcore puzzler.

TLDR: great art and concept. Meh execution.
Watch a youtube video of someone playing the game if you like the art, or buy the game cheaply on sale.

While Scorn provides a stunning visual and audio feast, its gameplay, storytelling, and amount of content leave me decidedly against recommending this game to all but the most hardcore alien-horror enthusiast. 

Scorn is a first-person horror/puzzler set on an alien factory world straight out of the nightmares of H.R Giger and Riddley Scott.  You explore post-apocalyptic bio-mechanical labyrinths of flesh, chitin, and bones where the race of the planet was experimenting with bioengineering to outpace a devastating infection/biological weapon ravaging their people (my own theory because the game does not provide firm lore). The art style is the game’s selling point. I got through the game to see the whole thing. At some points I was struggling with the gameplay loop and combat, but I pushed through because of the detailed and creative world that Scorn presents. I cannot stress this enough; it is a good-looking game! 

However, there is a lot to dislike. First, I dislike how the story is told and its world is presented. The worldbuilding is completely absent. It presents you with the gorgeous and engrossing world but tells you absolutely nothing about it, aside from what you can glean from small details that leave you with more questions than answers. The game could have added needed length and reason to explore by feeding the player lore to make for a satisfying world and an engrossing story. Along with worldbuilding, the story telling is absent. Aside from moving to the next area of the labyrinth, you have no idea why you are doing what you are doing until the end of the game. What meager story elements contained in the game are even told in a confusing way, with the intro cutscene telling a part of the story that should have been told after act 2. I should not have to go back and play the game’s intro again to put some pieces together. 

Next the gameplay loop leaves something to be desired. The gameplay loop looks something like this: You wander this gorgeous labyrinth, soaking in the sights and sounds. You come upon an interactable alien device. If you can interact with it, great, you solve its puzzle and gain a way to move forward somehow. If you cannot interact with it, you make a mental note about where it is and then you move on. Enemies dot the map from act 2 on. You either run away from them or suffer through the game’s terrible combat. That’s pretty much it. I would have liked for it to have been punctuated by story telling elements or dialogue or something to diversify the loop. 

The game’s combat is bad. I feel like the game cannot decide if combat is important or not. There are various enemies, there are boss fights.  But there is not enough ammo or health to engage in regular combat. I get it, its not a shooter. Then why is combat so prevalent? It hard to describe why the combat is so bad. Its slow moving and its weapons are not fun or satisfying. For example, the first weapon you get basically gently slaps a target 2 feet in front of you. Even the most basic enemy takes more than one hit. The first two hits happen one after another, but if you want to shoot again, you must wait 5-7 seconds, which gives the enemy time to hit you because you are at point blank range. You will lose health on most combat encounters.

All in all, I loved its atmosphere and art, but just wished it gave you more than it did. Its 6-7 hour playtime was a bit short. Its worth a buy on a major sale for lovers of alien horror who don’t mind mediocre gameplay to get a great visual experience.

The problem with this game fundamentally is that it feels like it has a bit of an identity crisis, specifically in terms of gameplay. The beginning of the game is a puzzle/walking simulator with some very cool and unique puzzles, but also some very frustrating ones. But later portions of the game are plagued with very underbaked combat that really bog down the experience.

The issue with some of the puzzles in Act 1 is that they rely on you just stumbling across the 'thing' that activates another 'thing.' But because of the very faithfully created Giger environments, you're gonna be crawling around at a snail's pace for hours just hoping to stumble across the correct 'thing.' But that isn't the majority of act 1 and I still very much enjoyed it for what it is. It's mostly there to get you acquainted with the world and the controls and it does so very well.

Next in Act 2, you're given two weapons, with a very unique ammo and health system. Like one in a robust shooter/horror game like Resident Evil. But this isn't that style of game. The actual combat is VERY underbaked. Fighting enemies feels like trying to kill small dinosaurs with a paintball gun and one of those electric thrusting dildo machines. I get making the player underpowered for the sake of tension, but this was just more annoying than tense. The reach on the dildo feels inconsistent, and missing even a single shot from the gun feels like a kick to the balls considering how scarce ammo is and how much HP the enemies have. Also dodging attacks is near impossible. The little chicken guys have near laser precision on their shots, and the big bulls are twice as fast as you and can kill you in two hits. The combat only starts to feel a bit better once you get the shotgun. But by then I felt like it was too little too late. Over all, Act 2 is by far the worst of the 3, and this is mostly due to its over reliance on the combat.

Act 3 was much better than 2, mostly because the combat is relegated to 2 simple boss fights that are actually pretty decent. Instead of being straight combat, the two bosses are more like two very similar puzzles, each with their own spin on how to solve it. The third act is overall much shorter and simpler than the first two, but after the utter frustration that was act 2, I actually welcomed this. The only problem with act 3 is that its actually possible to softlock yourself after a certain point. SPOILERS: [spoiler] at some point, the parasite that has attached to your character will start to grow mold on you. In order to continue the game, you need to activate certain machines that will break the mold for you, but you'll take damage OVER TIME from this. If you don't have enough health or medkits when you reach this part of the game you simply will not be able to move forward. [/spoiler] While I understand that this is supposed to create tension, I plainly just think this a bad idea and should've stayed on the cutting room floor.

As for everything else, the story, atmosphere, sound design, environment design, character design, etc. it's all a 10/10. Its really a shame that I found the actual 'game' part of this game very frustrating. I really REALLY  want to love this game, and its a story and world that I'm gonna think about a lot, and its even inspired me to do some more Giger style art myself. But This wasn't the game for me, and I can't recommend it either.

A potentially great tribute to H.R. Giger ruined by some poor game design decisions.

I was aware of the controversy around this game so I went in expecting a 'walking simulator', a living 3D art museum. What I was not prepared for was an FPS game, complete with boss fight! Somehow this cheapened the whole experience for me.

The devs are free to do what they want but I really felt that they missed a great opportunity to create something ground breaking but instead we get sliding puzzles, door locks, Doom style weapons, button operated lifts etc, like any other game in the last 10 years,

Also, I suffered through most of the game with very low FPS because the game does not run well in fullscreen mode on a second monitor. The FPS got so bad in the boss fight that I stopped playing and figured out that I needed to run it in windowed mode on 2nd monitor or fullscreen on the first monitor.

I would love the devs to create some DLC or a sequel, as long as they can innovate and not dress up a dull game in alien goo.
It has it's strokes of genius, but it's gameplay and story issues are manifold.  A cripplingly unpolished mess with a terrible resolution to it all.

I had rather low expectation about this but it still ended up being worse than I thought. It is actually a pretty bad and underdeveloped game.

The only good thing about Scorn is of course visuals and while I agree that visually game is pretty creative and unique it gets partially negated by a poor level design. Levels look extremely repetitive with the same corridors and the same circular rooms being everywhere. Game jumps from astonishingly beautifull landscapes to boring copy-pasted locations that become annoying pretty fast.

Everything in Scorn that is not Visuals is just horrible.

Sound design is nonexistent, there is literally no sounds and no music besides some boring ambient on the background.

"Open world" advertisement is a lie. Game is super linear. All your hopes to explore a dark and twisted world of Scorn will be crushed into endless invisible walls and permanently locked paths. 

Scorn has no story and no lore. I mean no story and no lore at all. If you expect to learn something about this world you gonna get disappointed. The protagonist wakes up in the middle of nowhere and starts doing strange thing for no reason at all. You know, even cheap and trashy indie horrors usually provide some lore through document scattered around or whatever. But Scorn gives you nothing.

Gameplay is mostly walking around and solving puzzles that vary from average to ridiculously stupid like you enter a belly of a gigantic monster (that actually looks pretty cool) and suddenly you are solving a puzzle with a ball moving through a maze like in some old game from 80-s. That looks completely out of place and breaks all the immersion. There is combat but it is super basic, boring and is there for the only reason of wasting your time.

Scorn is clearly underdeveloped. You know that game is underdeveloped heavily when a brand new (and pretty interesting) mechanic gets introduced 5 minutes before the game ends. There clearly was supposed to be more but it is not there. I don't know what happened to the developers but in the current state I only recommend this with a big discount and only if you are really into that type of visuals.
If a game could be carried by art direction alone this would be game of the year. Too bad it can't and this gameplay is so boring it would be more fun to eat soggy toast.

It is said that the developers have spent years on the graphics and atmosphere of this game.
The effort shows, and is very impressive. 
However, if would have been nice if they had spent at least five minutes on the development of the gameplay.
For example, an option of a simple ‘save game’ function is absolutely necessary for this confrontational setting.
After a death, the forced re-entry point, can be minutes before the time of departure, the result being that it gets extremely tedious repeating the same parts, over and over again. The ‘baby in a bubble’ combat is a good example of how tedious it can get. If you die at the end of a lengthy combat sequence, you have to re-start, way before the battle commences. In addition, there appears to be a game stopping bug after the first stage kill. Although ‘white highlighted’, you cannot interact with the ‘wounded boss’ weapon, and you are stuck, for ever( i.e. the ‘cut scene’ does not happen)     This where I left it for now. not worth anymore cursing time….

The atmosphere and late game visual design is so good, but the experience is such a slog that it's hard to say it's worth it. Map aesthetics are a little hit and miss, with everything looking great, but throughout the short runtime each chapter takes up, they overstay their welcome. It makes the maps obnoxious to navigate. Not in a "surreal and disorienting" way, but because of dull repetition.
Geiger's work is grotesque and erotic. That's like, the whole deal. The game captures of of this in the last act, but most of the game is just the bio-mech gore. It's not bad so much as a lost opportunity.
The design gripes don't make the game unplayable though, it's pretty nice to walk around. Until you get interrupted by the puzzles or combat.
The puzzles are dull. The game launches with an obnoxious sliding block puzzle. There's the "rotate one piece and adjacent pieces rotate" flavor puzzle. Probably some others that I already forgot about minutes after finishing the game.
It's boring. It's not thematic. It's a sliding block puzzle except it's eggs.
The combat isn't any better. There's less than a dozen encoutners, and they revolve around slapping whatever you want to fight twice, and then turning a corner. The guns are a generic pistol and shotgun type weapon, which work fine, but you could remove all of the combat and have a sub-par puzzle game. Then you could remove the puzzles and have a pretty interesting walking sim.
The ending is really cool. Might even be worth going through the other 4 acts.... but also maybe not worth the time.

The atmosphere, visuals, puzzles are all great, but the combat is just so bad and stupid that I have to give it a negative review. Reloading and switching weapons make you slow down and there's you can't strafe properly, and when you take damage by the time the animation ends you'll get hit again if you're fighting multiple enemies

Scorn is a great concept and not quite a game to be honest. You'd do better watching a play through. The world is cool and super dark and the design choices are all well done but it doesn't actually make a game. It's a walking simulator between different unconnected and unexplained areas where combat is just an afterthought and more of an inconvenience than any kind of enjoyable component. If you want to understand anything of what it contains you need to get the art book alongside.

The narrative for this game is so weird that  I can't begin to sum it up, and the ending is such a downer that I don't believe it's worth the effort trying to make sense of it. As for the game-play, well, describing it as boring would be an understatement.

It takes about an hour to get going, which even for a walking-simulator is pretty lethargic, and when it does get some life to it it comes in the form of puzzles that aren't particularly stimulating but have been dragged out to a tedious degree. Other than the impressive visuals and grotesque environments, I wouldn't even say its atmospheric as you "explore" during this opening period, as there's no music and barely any ambient sound either.

Just when the ending seemed like there might be something "nice", given how sordid and disturbed the rest of it is, it finished right back in utter grimness. To be frank: I don't care that it's horrible, its  just so f*ck*ng boring and pointless, and sh*t, that peeves me. No recommended, unless you like really weird sh*t or hate yourself.  Anyone who tells you this is fun to play, is lying.

Scorn has incredible art design and creates an equally gross and engrossing atmosphere. It is drippy, and infected, and fleshy, and moist. However, its puzzles are mediocre at best, its combat is clunky and best when it's avoided, and its narrative is murky and unsatisfying. It's only recommendable to people who can overlook everything else if they get a good Horror atmosphere.

The art is great, but that's about it.

The game is artificially extended with slow walking, slow animations, backtracking, and other tediums. But overall is actually quite short. 'Combat' is tedious and frustrating, if you miss a shot or two, you're dead. And if you don't die there, you die later because you don't have enough ammo or health to proceed to the next 'checkpoint', and you can more or less softlock yourself forcing you to revert to an older save.

The most egregious issue is the bugs. I had to look up walkthroughs to figure out if I just wasn't doing something properly only to see others do exactly what I had done without issues, loaded an earlier save, played through more tedium to reach the spot where the bug prevented progress, and voila, i was able to continue. I got it on sale for 13 bucks, and I'm glad I did. If not for the bugs, the game has a playtime from start to end of ~3-4 hours, and fails to introduce or use new gameplay mechanics effectively. The puzzles are either simple, or tedious. There was a crunch for time before release, and it shows with the lack of care put into polishing the actual gameplay/story beyond making it a visual piece. If you like giger-esque art and you're getting it for that, expect a gruelling experience. If you like action horror games? Theres not much action. If you like walking simulator style atmospheric horror games? You probably wont get very far either. It's more or less a visual piece with a few gameplay mechanics haphazardly tacked to it to make it sell better. But if you got the game and enjoyed it? I'd recommend trying 'Riddick: Escape from Butcher Bay' as a comparable (and more polished) experience.

Scorn -- One of the most visually stunning and interesting puzzles that I've played to date. Man, I wish I could recommend this. 

I purchased this game shortly after it came out, and in a couple of sittings I cleared acts I - IV. Up to this point, the puzzles were fun enough, and the game did an excellent job indirectly leading you in the right direction. There was "some" back-tracking, but not enough for me to leave a bad review.

This game felt too thin, with too little substance stretched over a very short playtime that does not justify its asking price. It harbours and hogs gameplay mechanics to prolong an experience as intriguing and captivating as observing concept art. Far too little and too late is an accurate description of Scorn, as it extends what little gameplay there is in a game that can be finished in four hours to obscure how barren it is. Speaking of barren, Scorn's Story.

Scorn dumps you in its world clueless with no hints, no markers, no objectives, designed for blind playthroughs, if you will. I initially liked that until I learned this method extends to the game's story. Far from what I would describe as environmental storytelling, Scorn instead walks the path of no showing and no telling. With not a single piece of dialogue, the game does not establish characters, plot or narrative, not even through other means. When I discovered a moral choice in the game, I was amused at how poorly implemented it was. This moral choice only serves to make the game feel unfinished. It's a single moral choice. One of its kind, of little impact and importance. It further establishes the feeling of what could've been, of lost potential, of snuffed excitement.

Visually, Scorn is striking and sombre, yet appealing and unique. It is, undoubtedly, the game's most substantial positive element. The puzzles often blur the lines between puzzles and basic problem-solving. The combat is tedious and monotonous. Once a second enemy enters, the player will take damage no matter what because wielding a thruster tool against projectile-launching enemies in confined spaces is stupid. I felt like the player and enemy characters were designed for different games. It was definitely bothersome fighting far-ranged enemies with a limited close-ranged weapon capable of two strikes at a time, and it added to the dull nature of the combat. I discovered that enemies mostly chase the player for a very short distance before stopping and even exiting the area; from then on, I simply went along with my business and did not engage in combat unless absolutely necessary. The other much more powerful weapon is only used for one section before being rendered useless; hell, the combat, in its entirety, is in two sections, and I'm using both "combat" and "section" very lightly.

The Cream does not recommend Scorn at its full price; get it on Game Pass instead if you want to play a concept art exhibition with a few "puzzles", frustrating combat, and soft locking. Oh God, the soft locking!

It's 95% walking simulator, 3% puzzle game, 2% souls-like. The good things are that the graphics and atmosphere are amazing, the puzzles are satisfying and the game is overtly erotic (though it's very niche, you need to be into hardcore s&m and be a switch to enjoy what's going on). The bad stuff is a lot. The game is not scary at all. There is no dialogue at all although the story could be interpreted as something about relationships or wars? I'm not sure. It leaves a lot to interpretation. The combat is frustrating. Very little ammo is available and the melee weapon is horrible. A lot of the game is just running around and that gets extremely boring quick.

To summarize: if you're into Aliens or Lovecraft AND you're a switch who's into hardcore S&M AND your tolerance for boredom is high you'll like it. Can't recommend it for the vast majority of people though.

I like Cronenberg, I loved Little Nightmares and Soma, and I have an appreciation for Giger and what Ridley Scott did with his ideas. These are all clearly influences on Scorn. I dunno. i followed the development of scorn since its initial announcement where it was unclear what type of game it was going to be. it was clearly going to be heavily giger (and beksinski) influenced in its visuals, and that was enough to pull a lot of people into the hype. sadly, it feels like the early trailers being largely/completely devoid of gameplay wasn't coincidental and was just representative of what had been developed for the game to that point. it really feels like all the art concepts, materials, models, shaders, pre-fab level parts, etc were created first, and then gameplay was kind of tacked on in the last year or two, which makes it not particularly fun to play!

before going into specifics, i want to clarify that i am not predisposed to dislike a game like scorn, nor did i go into it with unrealistic expectations. i like horror games, i like walking sims, i like puzzle games, i like fps games, i like games that are not direct in their storytelling, i like games that can make you feel miserable (ie: pathologic 2). i really just don't think these things feel like a cohesive final product in scorn though. 

[u]visuals:[/u] visually i don't think i have to say much beyond the game is stunning and so much thought seems to have gone into every element of the visuals, from obvious things like textures, models,and animations, to deliberate sight lines from different parts of the maps. you could easily set your computer to screenshot scorn every 5 minutes as you play and have 90% awesome pieces of art.

[u]sound:[/u] i think the sound was also quite good an contributes immensely to the atmosphere as a whole. it was understated and largely ambient sounds and environmental noises. everything sounded suitable gross, or mysterious, or vacant. i only really noticed music coming in once, and thought the track was nice, but me "not noticing" a soundtrack isn't a sign of a bad soundtrack at all since i absolutely adore the trent reznor/nine inch nails soundtrack for quake as well.

[u]story:[/u] there's no traditional story in scorn, and i don't recall any dialogue or text through my playthrough (outside of text in the menu/ui). there is still environmental storytelling and some in-game cutscenes that highlight things occurring and changing throughout the playthrough. i thought seeing how things developed with the player character was interesting, and i thought any non-enemy characters that showed up alive were able to communicate emotion in a way that resonated with me.

[u]puzzles:[/u] so the puzzles... with few exceptions i really felt like the puzzles throughout did not seem realistically integrated into the environment and were super simple to work out. there wasn't anything really unique or novel with the types of puzzles either, they reminded me of the ads i get on free duolingo for puzzle game apps. i know puzzles in other games are mostly the same handful of puzzle types over and over again, but doing a puzzle in any other random game rarely pulls me out and shatters my immersion like it did for me in scorn where the puzzles interrupted the pacing and felt hard to justify their inclusion in a space that otherwise felt cohesive (largely due to the strong art and sound direction).

[u]combat:[/u] i saw reviews on steam and elsewhere online around the game's launch complaining about the combat, and i figured people just didn't have the same tolerance for jank/kinda cruddy fps combat that i have, but nope, i was wrong, the combat is abysmal and possibly the worst fps combat i can think of in recent memory. ultimately, combat fails because aiming and reloading take absurdly long, ammo capacity is low, and enemy placement often has them body block you in corridors or gang up on in you a space that is very difficult to avoid physical or splash damage from them. it doesn't translate into a survivor horror kind of stress and item management, it just becomes a slog of a cover shooter. i am not trying to turn scorn into doom eternal or anything, but i kept feeling like if i was in the player character's position i would have abandoned the weapon(s) after about 2 enemies and just fought from there on with my bare hands. i feel like i could do more damage more quickly with uppercutting some monstrosity than i could with the weapons in game.

i will post one spoiler here (spoiler tagged) that touches on my most frustrating experience with the [u]combat[/u] and [u]save system:[/u] [spoiler] there is a (tedious) boss battle towards the end of the game, and after defeating it i gained the "grenade launcher" equivalent weapon. i didn't know how it worked or what it was at first, so i shot a few shots, damaged myself, and then realized i used all my ammo. i figured i'd load from checkpoint and get my health back and all that ammo, but the checkpoint took me back before the boss! i guess there are either 2 bosses back to back or one enemy-type boss twice depending on how you look at it, and i tried to reload between the fights without knowing there was a second. maybe player error, but i don't know any other game that doesn't save after a boss fight if you're given full control of your character again without a boss present. i died over a dozen times in those boss fights cuz i was stuck with a save at low health and no health resources, and i had to keep watching the same cutscenes each time without an option to skip. [/spoiler]

i am often drawn to games with strong visual presentations regardless of genre, and that can be enough reason to warrant a purchase from me. scorn's grotesque visual splendor was my main interest in playing the game, but the visuals alone were not enough to carry me through the trials and frustrations of its gameplay and have an overall positive reflection on it. i think an extraordinarily patient person may enjoy this game for its gameplay, but i think most people who recommend it are doing so for its incredible setting and atmosphere. i think i would have greatly preferred a version of scorn that focused on only one type of gameplay vs. the one we got that ended up flirting with multiple genres but only developed them on an incredibly basic surface level.
